_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 93_ 

## **4.1.2 Quarterly production in mining and utilities** 

As noted earlier, UNIDO also compiles and publishes sub-annual IIP data, which enable a more detailed and timely analyses than those based on annual national accounts. These data encompass four industrial sectors: mining and quarrying (ISIC Rev. 4 section B), manufacturing (section C), electricity and related industries (section D), and water supply and related sectors (section E). 

Mining and electricity production indices are available for more than 100 economies, representing about 80 per cent of global mining and utilities value added, while data on water supply and other sectors included in ISIC Rev. 4 section E cover around 60 economies. Due to this limited availability of quarterly data as well as insufficient coverage for calculating country group and regional aggregates, this section is excluded from the analysis. Annex C summarizes the main characteristics and methodological aspects of these indices. 

Recent developments in the mining and electricity sectors are illustrated in Figure 4.3. Global mining and quarrying activities have followed a volatile trajectory, registering only a modest production increase of 2.4 per cent in cumulative terms since the first quarter of 2022, the first year free from most pandemic-related disruptions. Production levels in this sector have remained relatively flat across both industrial and industrializing economies. Recent quarterly data indicate moderate growth of 0.73 per cent in industrial economies, while output in industrializing economies recorded a slight short-term decline. Given the dominant share of industrial economies in global mining output, the global growth rate largely reflects their recent performance and longer-term growth trends. 

Global initiatives aimed at reducing the environmental impact of mining activities, as discussed in Section 4.3, will likely contribute to increased instability in the sector’s prospects. At the same time, advances in technologies related to energy, batteries, machinery, and transportation may stimulate demand for minerals and metals, potentially leading to higher production levels in the sector. 

In contrast, the production of electricity and other utilities classified under ISIC Rev. 4 section D exhibited stronger global momentum, increasing by 6.5 per cent in cumulative terms since early 2022. When disaggregated by country group, industrializing economies recorded a steady and sustained expansion, with electricity rising by more than 17 per cent over the past ten quarters. Conversely, industrial economies experienced a pronounced slowdown in recent years. In the most recent quarter, electricity output in industrializing economies continued to expand robustly by 1.1 per cent, while it declined by 0.81 per cent in industrial economies.

_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 96_ 

## **4.2 Structure and transformation of mining and utilities industries** 

In previous editions of this Yearbook [37; 56; 15], the transformation of mining and utilities sectors has been analysed through the lens of structural business statistics (SBS), focusing on value added, employment, and investment by activity classification according to ISIC (e.g. ISIC Rev. 4 sections B, D, and E). While this approach provides essential insights into the economic structure, performance and transformation of these sectors, it often cannot reveal the underlying dynamics of specific mineral commodities that are increasingly shaping global industrial development. 

In response to the growing importance of critical raw materials, strategic resource dependencies, and increasing energy demand, this section introduces a product-level perspective. Drawing on information published by World Mining Data (WMD) [54], the analysis shifts focus from aggregated industry indicators to monetary values and physical production volumes of individual mineral commodities. This approach enables a more granular understanding of global mining trends and a better alignment with resource security and sustainability topics. The emphasis on product-level data complements previous analysis based on industrial activities, offering a multidimensional view of the transformation underway in the combined mining and utilities sector. 

Global production of mineral raw materials nearly doubled over the last four decades, underscoring the intensification of industrialization and the broadening of resource demand across sectors. According to WMD 2025 data [57], total world mining production (excluding bauxite)[INFO-CIRCLE] surged from 9.6 billion metric tons in 1985 to 19.2 billion metric tons in 2023, a 99.0 per cent increase. This represents a compound average annual growth rate of approximately 1.8 per cent, underscoring the resilience of extractive industries. Sustained expansion led to the highest recorded level of production in 2023, reaffirming the pivotal role of mineral commodities in the global economy. 

## **Global production of mineral raw materials: regional shifts and emerging leaders (1985–2023)** 

In the past forty years, global minerals production has experienced significant regional shifts, as illustrated in Figure 4.6. Asia has emerged as the leading contributor, tripling its output to surpass 12.0 billion metric tons in 2023, which accounts for more than 60 per cent of global production. Concurrently, Northern America, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Oceania have overtaken Europe, indicating a notable reconfiguration of the global mining landscape. Indeed, Northern 

## **World Mining Data (WMD)** 

World Mining Data [54] is an internationally recognised annual statistical publication issued by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance. It provides comprehensive mineral production data from more than 160 countries, dating back to 1984, presented in both physical quantities and monetary terms. The data serves as a key resource for raw material policy analysis and commodity forecasting. The World Mining Congress (WMC) [55], founded in 1958 under UN auspices, plays a pivotal role in supporting data collection through dedicated questionnaires. National Committees of WMC member countries are among the primary contributors to the dataset, alongside other entities such as embassies and foreign trade representatives. Publicly accessible mining statistics from reputable sources, including the United States Geological Survey, are utilised for validation and

## **Mineral composition: fuels dominate, yet non-fuel minerals continue to rise steadily** 

The composition of global minerals production can be broadly categorized into two groups: first, _mineral fuels_ , which include coal, petroleum (incl. natural gas liquids), and natural gas, and second, _non-fuel minerals_ . Although the term ‘non-fuel minerals’ is not used in the current version of WMD, it is nonetheless useful to employ such a category in further analysis to streamline findings. It encompasses iron and ferro-alloy metals like cobalt, nickel and titanium, non-ferrous metals such as aluminium, lithium, and rare earths, industrial minerals including phosphate rock and kaolin, and precious metals like gold and silver.

--- end of page.page_number=111 ---

_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 99_ 

In terms of volume, production is overwhelmingly dominated by mineral fuels, as shown in figure 4.7. In 2023, these amounted to approximately 16.6 billion metric tons, exceeding the volume of non-fuel minerals, which were estimated at 2.6 billion tons, by more than sixfold. Over the past four decades, mineral fuels production has generally followed an upward trajectory, with occasional declines in specific years such as 1991–1993 , 1999, 2009, 2016, and 2020. These fluctuations are likely attributable to geopolitical developments, global economic downturns, or shifts in energy policy. By contrast, non-fuel minerals have shown more gradual growth, yet their production has more than doubled since the mid-1980s, reflecting sustained demand for raw materials essential to industrial production, infrastructure, and technological advancement. Although petroleum, among other products, is classified as fuel, it also serves as a feedstock for a wide array of manufactured products. However, the available data do not differentiate between its use as a fuel for energy generation and its use as a material input. A further methodological consideration of significance pertains to the standardization of units within the data illustrated. 

To present all production figures in metric tons, data compilers, such as the contributors to WMD, have applied conversion factors to harmonise disparate mineral raw materials [57, pp. 10–11]. This practice enhances comparability across commodities, yet it also introduces interpretative nuances, particularly when analysing energy-related materials.

## **Mineral fuels from 1985 to 2023** 

A comparison of mineral fuels over time makes it essential to distinguish between their physical volume—measured in metric tons after harmonisation—and their energy content, expressed in tons of coal equivalent (TCE). This dual metric reveals important shifts in the global energy landscape between 1985 and 2023, as shown in Figure 4.8. In 2023, steam coal was the dominant fuel by mass, with a production volume of approximately 7.0 billion metric tons, contributing 41.7 per cent to the global mineral fuels production. However, its energy content was significantly lower, amounting to 5.2 billion TCE or a share of 27.7 per cent. This discrepancy underscores steam coal’s relatively low energy density. Nonetheless, its share in both mass and energy terms increased compared to 1985, indicating a strong expansion in absolute output and a growing reliance on steam coal in certain regions. By contrast, petroleum, with a lower production volume in 2023 of 4.5 billion metric tons, yielded a much greater energy output of 6.5 billion TCE, thereby overtaking steam coal as the leading energy source when measured by calorific value. Interestingly, petroleum’s share in the fuel mix declined between 1985 and 2023 from 32.3 per cent to 27.0 per cent by mass and from 40.6 per cent to 34.9 per cent

Natural gas demonstrated a notable discrepancy between mass and energy content. Perhaps most striking is the case of uranium, which, despite a negligible production volume of just 62,297 metric tons (share almost 0.0 per cent), converted into an extraordinary 1.0 billion TCE (share of 10.4 per cent) in 1985. This highlights the exceptional energy yield of nuclear fuels and their disproportionate contribution to total energy supply. However, by 2023, uranium’s energy share declined to 6.0 per cent, despite a slight increase in mass, pointing to a relative stagnation or decline in nuclear energy’s role within the broader mix. Lithium, a non-ferrous metal among the highly concentrated commodities and known for its decisive role in energy storage solutions, has recorded the most pronounced production dynamics in most recent years with a growth rate of 160.2 per cent between 2019 and 2023. Australia led global production in 2023 with a share of 40.8 per cent, followed by Chile, which also anchors the strategically significant Lithium Triangle, a region comprising Chile, Argentina, and the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Collectively, the triangle contributes over 25 per cent of global lithium output, underscoring its importance in the global energy transition. China and Zimbabwe, with a global share of 21.3 and 6.8 per cent, are other major producers. Rare earths likewise witnessed substantial growth of 89.2 per cent during the same period, driven by increasing demand for components used in electronics, renewable energy technologies, and defence applications. China dominates mining of rare earths, accounting for more than 66 per cent of global production. Also, China emerged as the leading producer of 26 distinct mineral commodities, reaffirming its central role in global supply chains for numerous mineral raw materials. 

This dominance also raises broader questions about strategic dependencies and development opportunities—issues explored in greater depth by the United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD)’s recent analysis of critical minerals and their role in sustainable industrial transformation [59]. The global reliance on a few key producers poses risks for countries seeking secure access to essential inputs for clean energy and digital technologies. UNCTAD emphasizes the need for resource-rich developing economies, particularly in Africa, to move beyond raw material extraction by investing in domestic refining and processing capabilities. Such investments can drive industrial development and enable these countries to capture greater value from their mineral wealth. The current boom in critical minerals presents a unique opportunity for sustainable transformation, provided it is supported by inclusive governance, transparent contracting, and equitable benefit-sharing. Also, strengthened international cooperation and adequate financing mechanisms are essential to bridge existing investment gaps.

## **4.3 Environmental impact of mining and utilities** 

Mining and utilities generate significant environmental pressures, including land degradation, water and air pollution, and GHG emissions. As a result, environmental considerations have become increasingly central to policy discussions in these sectors. Similar to the environmental analysis of the manufacturing sector in Section 3.6, this section offers a non-exhaustive overview of the main environmental challenges linked to mining and utilities. The use of examples and isolated figures throughout reflects the limited availability of consistent, comprehensive data on these topics. 

Mining activities are a major driver of land degradation, contributing to deforestation, soil erosion, and water depletion. Gold and coal extraction together account for most mining-related forest loss globally, responsible for 36 per cent and 34 per cent, respectively. While the impacts of gold mining are distributed across several countries, coal-related deforestation is heavily concentrated in Indonesia, which accounted for 57 per cent of global tree-cover loss linked to coal extraction between 2000 and 2019 [60]. In Mongolia, an estimated 72 per cent of land is degraded due to desertification and mining activity, among other factors, with coal and gold extraction playing a significant role [61]. Moreover, mining frequently takes place in ecologically sensitive, biodiversity-rich areas, contributing to habitat fragmentation and species loss [62]. 

Mining operations also pose substantial risks of water and air pollution. Toxic by-products, waste rock, and tailings may contaminate water bodies for decades after mine closure. One study estimates that 23 million people globally live on floodplains contaminated with potentially harmful levels of toxic waste from current and historical metal-mining activities [63]. Air quality is also affected, as blasting, excavation, and ore transport release dust and fine particles containing heavy metals, which could increase the risk of respiratory and other health risks. 

As expected, electricity generation accounts for a significant share of global CO2 emissions, as it produces the energy required to power households and all other economic activities [64; 65]. But mining and water provision are also highly energy-intensive sectors. For example, examinations of drinking-water utilities have shown consistently high and rising energy intensity over time [66]. Mining also requires substantial energy, particularly during comminution and through the fuel used for mining and transport equipment. As easily accessible, high-quality mineral deposits become depleted and global demand for mining products grows, the sector’s overall energy consumption is expected to rise further [67; 68]. 

Mining and utilities have significant environmental impacts though comprehensive data remain limited 

Mining operations could exacerbate deforestation and land degradation including in ecologically sensitive areas 

Toxic waste contaminates air and water and poses health risks over decades 

Mining comprises energy-intensive activities and drives CO 2 emissions 

--- end of page.page_number=121 ---

_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 109_ 

Despite this high energy use, mining accounts for a relatively small share of global GHG emissions, between 4 and 7 per cent, because of its limited weight in the global economy.[INFO-CIRCLE] Moreover, only a small portion of these emissions results from electricity use; the majority stems from fugitive methane released during the extraction and handling of coal, oil, and natural gas [69]. 

These environmental pressures are likely to be intensified by climate change, including through greater water scarcity and more frequent extreme weather events. Addressing them will require improved land rehabilitation, decarbonization of operations, stronger watermanagement systems, and enhanced engagement with affected communities. 

Global policy frameworks increasingly target environmental sustainability in mining and utilities. Common instruments include environmental impact assessments, environmental taxes, green-finance incentives, and international cooperation to strengthen responsible practices. These measures seek to reduce habitat destruction, pollution, and emissions while advancing circular-economy approaches, technical capacity, and the transition to low-carbon energy sources. 

Countries are increasingly adopting policies that aim to balance economic priorities with environmental sustainability by setting carbonneutrality targets, promoting cleaner technologies, and reinforcing regulatory frameworks. However, gaps in implementation and enforcement remain widespread, including limited monitoring capacity. Expanded global data collection and strengthened statistical systems would further support these efforts, by enabling more robust assessment and monitoring of the ecological and health impacts associated with mining and utilities. 

INFO-CIRCLE These estimates include only emissions released directly during mining operations or indirectly from the use of electricity, heat, or steam; fugitive methane emissions are also included. _5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 111_ 

Industry remains central to development strategies around the world, but the context in which it operates is changing rapidly. As documented in the earlier chapters of the _Yearbook_ , global manufacturing continues to expand, but trends in output, trade, productivity, and emissions have become increasingly uneven across regions and country groups. Progress towards the industry-related SDG 9 targets is generally offtrack and unlikely to be achieved without a significant acceleration in the years remaining until 2030. At the same time, the sector is being reshaped by decarbonization pressures, digital technologies, shifting trade patterns, and changing labour markets. 

The thematic chapter of the _Yearbook 2024_ [37] reviewed the last three decades of industrial development, summarizing major trends observed globally and across regions and industries, and documenting the scale of the sector’s transformation. 

In contrast, this thematic chapter of the _Yearbook 2025_ takes a forwardlooking perspective instead. It focuses on the main changes expected to shape industrial development in the coming years, including the shift towards production that is greener, more digital, more globalized, but also increasingly exposed to shocks. On this basis, the chapter considers strategic responses aimed at ensuring that industrial statistics continue to support evidence-based policymaking for a sustainable industrial future. Furthermore, it critically assesses existing gaps and challenges in this area of official statistics, outlining how standards and frameworks may need to evolve to meet the broader and more complex data needs in the years ahead.

Industrial statistics are at a turning point, requiring modernization to remain fit for purpose

Advancing the modernization of this field has become increasingly urgent. First, the rapid transformation of industrial activity risks rendering existing statistical standards obsolete or insufficient for future policy needs. Second, major international statistical frameworks have recently been revised, already incorporating many of the changes needed to better capture current and future economic structures. Together, these developments create a window of opportunity for developing the next generation of industrial statistics. 

The objective of the chapter is therefore to identify the key emerging policy themes and structural transformations that will shape future demand for industrial statistics, outlining the response required to ensure they remain relevant, consistent, and fit for purpose. This analysis is framed within the broader context of recent changes to international statistical frameworks and the expected areas of methodological work in the coming years. 

The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. The next section presents the major transformations reshaping industrial development and industrial policy, and examines how these shifts alter the demand for industrial statistics. Section 5.2 then discusses the statistical implications of these changes and discusses how existing and emerging

Section 5.3 turns to cross-cutting challenges in the compilation and production of industrial statistics, including response burden, data integration, data quality, and timeliness, and explores how future frameworks may mitigate these issues. The final section concludes by outlining the rationale and main directions for the forthcoming updates to the international industrial statistics standards, highlighting how these revisions can support the development of future-ready industrial statistics. 

## **5.1 Transformations shaping the industrial landscape** 

A set of structural changes, operating on both the short- and long-term, are reshaping the trajectory of industrial development worldwide. Recent UNIDO publications have highlighted several cross-cutting, interrelated megatrends: the green and energy transition, digitalization and AI, reconfigured global value chains, demographic and labour market shifts, the growing importance of innovation and intangible assets, and an increasing emphasis on resilience to shocks [10; 70; 71]. 

Each of these transformations changes what needs to be measured and therefore has significant implications for industrial statistics. Three features are especially relevant from a statistical perspective. First, these changes are multidimensional and require information from domains that extend well beyond the traditional scope of industrial statistics. Second, they are interdependent, which calls for an integrated statistical system capable of linking information from multiple sources and domains. Third, they evolve over long periods but can shift abruptly in response to shocks. Monitoring them effectively therefore requires a combination of high-frequency indicators and long-term structural measures. The main megatrends are discussed below, with an emphasis on their implications for industrial statistics. 

## **The green and energy transition: decarbonization, circularity, and resource efficiency** 

As discussed in Sections 2.2 and 3.6, manufacturing is a major source of global GHG emissions and resource use, accounting for 17.5 per cent of global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion. If emissions from industrial processes are added, this share increases further. Energyintensive industries, such as steel, cement, and chemicals, make particularly large contributions. The left panel of Figure 5.1 shows that the sector’s energy consumption has continued to rise, although at a

At the same time, there is evidence of an emerging, but incomplete, decoupling between manufacturing activity and emissions. In a growing number of high- and middle-income economies, industrial emissions have started to decline even as output has continued to expand, driven by energy efficiency improvements, the increased reliance on lowcarbon power generation, and structural shifts towards less carbonintensive industries. However, current trajectories remain inconsistent with the steep reductions in industrial emissions required to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement [73]. 

The mining and utilities sectors have a key role to play, as they supply many of the critical resources required for the energy transition and provide essential activities such as energy generation, waste management, and recycling, all of which are fundamental to environmental sustainability. Industrial policy is increasingly expected to accelerate the diffusion of low-carbon technologies and promote energy and resource efficiency, while managing the distributional consequences of the transition, ensuring just outcomes for workers and regions that depend on emission- or material-intensive activities. At the same time, industrial strategies designed to support the emergence and

scaling of green industries (e.g. electric vehicles, renewable energy technologies, or recycling machinery) are gaining prominence in many countries. 

These policies significantly increase the demand for detailed environmental information on industrial activities, including disaggregated data at the level of specific industries or products, rather than aggregate measures for broad sectors. Beyond CO2 emissions and energy use, a more comprehensive measurement framework is needed to capture other GHG emissions, water use and pollution, material extraction and resource depletion, land degradation and land use, and other environmental pressures.

Green industrial policies require detailed data on emissions, energy and material use, and environmental impacts 

A consistent identification of “green” manufacturing activities and products in industrial statistics has also become essential, including activities related to material recycling and product repurposing. Existing work under the system of environmental-economic accounting (SEEA) and the environmental goods and services sector provides useful building blocks for defining these activities and products in a way that is consistent with national accounts [74], as it will be described later. 

Finally, the green transition requires statistical systems capable of linking industrial performance to broader environmental and social outcomes. This requires greater integration of industrial statistics with other sources such as energy balances, emission inventories, labour and household surveys, agricultural statistics, and land registers. 

## **Digitalization and AI** 

Advanced digital production technologies, many of them powered by AI, are enabling new forms of smart, connected production, often referred to as Industry 4.0. These technologies are transforming how industrial firms produce, organize, and compete [25]. Evidence from recent research indicates that the adoption of digital technologies is associated with substantial productivity gains, and that investments in these technologies can help lagging firms catch up with the productivity frontier. However, the extent of those benefits depends heavily on the presence of key enabling conditions, particularly access to the required skills [75; 76; 77]. 

Digitalization and AI are not limited to production processes. They also change how industrial value is created and captured. A growing share of manufacturing companies derive income from the provision of digital services related to their products. 

At the same time, digitalization raises new challenges. The diffusion of AI and automation is reshaping the organization of work, skill requirements, and the distribution of employment within and across

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 115_ 

economies. Uneven adoption of digital technologies may exacerbate existing gaps in productivity and competitiveness between leading and lagging firms, sectors, and regions. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face particular constraints: many continue to lack adequate digital connectivity, relevant skills, or access to advanced digital tools, reinforcing a widening digital divide [78]. Policies aiming at supporting the adoption of advanced digital production technologies should also consider critical enabling factors, such as digital infrastructure, governance systems, data security, access to finance, and skill development. 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Many SMEs lag in digital adoption, risking competitiveness and innovation gaps 

From the point of view of statistics, these transformations have several implications. First, there is a growing demand for systematic information on the adoption and use of digital technologies in manufacturing and related industries. This includes granular information disaggregated by industry, firm size, ownership, and region. Meeting this demand requires integrating questions on digital technologies into business and industrial surveys, and linking them with other sources of information on digital readiness, such as indicators on connectivity, cybersecurity, and digital skills. 

Second, digitalization increasingly blurs traditional boundaries in industrial statistics, particularly between manufacturing and services and between tangible and intangible assets. As manufacturers expand their service-based activities, it becomes more difficult to capture their full value creation using concepts and classifications focused primarily on physical goods. This raises questions about how industrial statistics should treat service activities carried out within (digitally-enabled) manufacturing firms, as well as how to account for non-manufacturing companies that provide production-related services to the manufacturing sector. 

Industrial statistics need to measure novel concepts related to digital technology adoption and impacts 

And third, understanding the impact of digital technologies on productivity, workforce dynamics, and inclusiveness requires closer integration between industrial statistics and other domains, including labour, education, and skills statistics. 

## **Globalization, GVCs, and supply-chain reconfiguration** 

The expansion of global value chains (GVCs) has been one of the defining features of industrialization and trade over the past decades. Production processes have become increasingly fragmented across borders, with different stages of design, component manufacturing, assembly, logistics, and support services located where firms perceive comparative advantages. GVCs have supported export growth, productivity gains, and structural transformation in many economies, while also creating new forms of dependency and vulnerability [79]. 

**==> picture [69 x 42] intentionally omitted <==**

## GVCs 

remain engines of export growth, but also channels of vulnerability 

--- end of page.page_number=128 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 116_ 

Recent crises, including the COVID-19 pandemic, regional conflicts, rising trade tariffs and climate-related disruptions, have exposed these interdependencies. They have revealed the extent to which industrial production in one country can be affected by events taking place in another. Disruptions can propagate rapidly through supply chains and severely impact globalized enterprises that rely on just-in-time delivery of key components, leading to production delays [23; 80; 81]. 

Partly in response to these developments, industrial policy has resurged worldwide, as countries seek to strengthen diversification, resilience, and economic security [10; 82]. The general policy challenge is therefore to deepen and upgrade GVCs participation as a channel for industrialization, technology diffusion, and job creation, while managing risks related to trade protectionism, logistical bottlenecks, climate shocks, and the concentration of critical inputs in a limited number of producers [83]. 

To support these policy objectives, timely and granular statistics are essential. Beyond measuring domestic production and trade flows separately, it is increasingly important to understand how firms and industries are integrated into cross-border production networks, what determines their participation, and where value added is generated along supply chains. Given the speed at which shocks circulate across production networks, developing high-frequency indicators of production and trade is also crucial. 

Comprehensive information on the activities of multinational enterprises, the extent of foreign ownership, and the degree to which domestic firms participate in exporting, importing, and supplying inputs to GVCs is equally important. This underscores the need to integrate statistical business registers (SBRs), SBS, and trade microdata, and to strengthen statistics on foreign affiliates and enterprise groups.

## **Demographic change, jobs, informality, and inclusion** 

Demographic trends are reshaping the global supply of labour and the composition of the industrial workforce. UN population projections indicate that the world will continue to grow in the coming decades, but with marked regional differences: populations are ageing rapidly in many countries, while a large and growing youth population is concentrated in others [84]. Urbanization and international migration further alter the geographical distribution and skills profile of workers. These contrasting dynamics create very different policy challenges. In ageing economies, concerns focus on labour shortages, the sustainability of social protection systems, and the need to retain workers in productive employment. In younger economies, the priority is to 

Manufacturing’s share in global employment declined to **14.1%** in 2023, down from 14.6% in 2012 

--- end of page.page_number=129 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 117_ 

generate sufficient decent jobs for a growing working-age population and prevent underemployment and informality [85]. 

The manufacturing sector remains an important source of decent work, particularly in low- and middle-income economies. However, as shown in Sections 2.2 and 3.4, its sustained capacity to provide employment appears to be at a turning point: over the past decade, manufacturing’s share to global GDP has kept increasing, but its share in total employment has declined. Underutilization, labour market insecurity, limited access to social protection, and high rates of informality remain important concerns across regions [86]. 

In addition, industrial restructuring, globalization, digitalization, automation, and other factors affect different groups of workers unevenly, depending on their skills, gender, age, and location. Women, in particular, remain underrepresented in many industrial occupations, especially in higher-skilled, higher-paid jobs and in leadership roles, even as their overall participation in the manufacturing workforce has increased. Persistent wage gaps underscore these inequalities [39; 87]. Similar challenges apply to other groups, including youth, migrants, and persons with disabilities, who may face higher risks of exclusion or vulnerability during periods of rapid change. 

Industrial statistics must therefore go beyond aggregates of production and value added to capture who participates in industry, under what conditions, and with what outcomes. To design policies that promote quality job creation and address inequalities, policymakers require granular data, at minimum disaggregated by sex, age, disability status, type of employment, occupation, and other relevant characteristics. Moreover, the focus on inclusion requires analysing the entire distribution of employment outcomes, rather than relying only on averages that may obscure important disparities. Meeting these needs calls for stronger integration between establishmentbased industrial surveys, labour force and household surveys, and administrative records on employment and wages, supported by the use of common identifiers to facilitate data linkage. 

Where informality is widespread, SBRs and standard establishment surveys capture only part of industrial activity. Measuring informal industrial employment and output requires special approaches, including dedicated modules in labour force or household surveys, mixed survey designs, and methods to estimate non-observed activities. 

## **Innovation, R&D, and the growing importance of intangibles** 

In the digital age, value creation and productivity growth in manufacturing increasingly depend on knowledge, design, software, data, and other intangible assets, rather than on physical capital alone [88; 10;

89; 90]. As documented in Section 3.2, this shift is reflected in the rising importance of technology and knowledge-intensive manufacturing industries. In many sectors, competitive advantage now depends on the ability to develop new products and processes, protect and leverage intellectual property, and use digital technologies to organize production and supply chains more efficiently. These changes are mirrored in companies’ balance sheets and in national accounts, where investments in intangibles, such as R&D and innovation-related activities, constitute a rapidly growing share of GDP and are becoming stronger predictors of manufacturing performance than investment in physical assets [91; 92]. 

**==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Intangible assets are gaining predominance as drivers of industrial competitiveness and productivity 

The growing prominence of R&D and innovation is closely linked to the megatrends discussed above. Digitalization expands opportunities to embed intangibles in products and production systems. Participation in GVCs often relies on product design, process know-how, quality control, and relational assets. In this context, R&D and innovation form part of a broader set of industrial capabilities that encompass technological and non-technological elements. 

These trends have important implications for industrial statistics. First, they increase the need for robust and detailed statistics on R&D and innovation in industry, which remain limited or absent in many economies. Such information is necessary to understand which industries and firms invest in R&D, design, data, and other innovationrelated activities; how this investment is financed; and what outcomes it generates in terms of new products, processes, and intellectual property. 

Second, the growing importance of intangibles calls for a broader scope of investment and capital stock. Many traditional surveys remain rooted in outdated statistical frameworks and focus primarily on tangible assets such as machinery, equipment, and buildings, while treating intangibles as intermediate inputs, if they are captured at all. Aligning industrial statistics with the revised macroeconomic standards offers a pathway toward more comprehensive measurement of intangible assets. 

Third, intellectual property indicators, such as patents, trademarks, and industrial designs, offer valuable complementary information. When compatible classifications and identifiers are used, these data can be linked to traditional industrial statistics, enabling analysis of innovation dynamics. Finally, industrial statistics must be complemented by broader innovation surveys and by both qualitative and quantitative data on management practices and organizational change. This is especially crucial for SMEs, which often innovate without formal R&D expenditure or rely on non-technological forms of innovation. Capturing these activities is essential for understanding the full breadth of innovation across industrial systems.

## **Industrial resilience and shocks** 

The past decade has underscored the vulnerability of industrial sectors when facing large and overlapping shocks. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, different regions have faced climate-related events, geopolitical tensions, and conflicts, with worldwide impacts. The re-emergence of trade protectionism adds another layer of uncertainty. 

The issue of industrial resilience was already discussed in the megatrend of digitalization and GVCs, but this is not purely a supply-chain issue. It also highlights issues about industrial structure, diversification, technological capabilities, and social protection. 

From a statistical perspective, the key consequence is the need for flexible and responsive statistical systems that can react and adapt to emerging issues while at the same time preserving consistency. They should include a battery of industrial indicators that can capture both the short-term impact of shocks and the structural factors that shape resilience or vulnerability. This includes more timely indicators of production, employment, trade, and inventories, and information on exposures to specific risks. It also calls for greater use of highfrequency data, including from non-traditional sources.

Agile, reponsive statistics, capable of rapidly measuring impacts while maintaining consistency, will be increasingly needed 

## **5.2 Aligning industrial statistics with future needs** 

The megatrends described in Section 5.1 directly affect what industrial statistics need to measure and how they are produced. Many of the conceptual tools required to respond to these new demands already exist in the international statistical frameworks, including the updated system of national accounts (SNA) 2025 [93], the system of environmental-economic accounting (SEEA) [74], the fifth revision of the ISIC [94], the third version of the Central Product Classification (CPC) [95], and the forthcoming 2028 update of the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (HS). Other adjustments will require new methodological guidance and integration across statistical domains. This section outlines how these frameworks can be leveraged to keep industrial statistics relevant and fit for purpose amid ongoing and anticipated transformations in industrial activity. 

## **Rethinking the scope and boundaries of industrial statistics** 

**==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

New and revised international standards provide a toolbox for modernizing industrial statistics 

As summarized in Section 1.2, current international standards define industrial statistics as covering mining, manufacturing, and utilities. This core scope has long provided a solid conceptual foundation and remains valid. However, the transformations discussed above 

--- end of page.page_number=132 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 120_ 

increasingly challenge the traditional boundaries of what should be considered _industrial_ for statistical and policy purposes. 

GVCs spread industrial activities across borders and blur the separation between sectors. They involve the participation of domestic, foreign, and multinational enterprises (MNEs) connected through complex production networks. Although international manuals provide definitions and guidance on global production arrangements, such as contract manufacturing, outsourcing, and factoryless goods production (FGP), applying them in practice is often difficult and may lead to counterintuitive outcomes. 

The green transition depends not only on what happens within manufacturing establishments, but also on upstream and downstream functions such as engineering, design, industrial R&D, maintenance and repair, recycling, and end-of-life management. Similarly, the digital transformation erodes the traditional boundary between manufacturing and services, as production processes become deeply integrated with software development, data processing, and platform-based business models. These developments suggest the need for information covering broader industrial ecosystems or production systems, rather than narrowly defined industrial sectors. 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

The boundary between manufacturing and related services is blurring, challenging traditional sector-based measurement approaches 

A review of the scope of industrial statistics could therefore consider how to define and classify industrial services and activities that support or are closely linked to industry, while maintaining coherence with ISIC, CPC, and SNA. Flexible thematic groups, such as green industries or digital-intensive industries, could be developed to answer specific policy questions. This would enable industrial statistics to better capture emerging realities while preserving the core definitional structure that ensures cross-country comparability. 

## **Classifications for a changing industrial structure** 

Classifications of activities and products are at the core of official statistics. They determine how establishments are grouped into industries and how goods and services are categorized, ensuring that national data can be compared internationally. The ISIC classification of economic activities and the CPC classification of products therefore play a central role in ensuring that industrial statistics remain aligned with ongoing transformations. 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Classification systems are at the core of official statistics and are essential modernization building blocks 

ISIC Rev. 5, endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission in 2023–2024, preserves the broad structure of its predecessor while introducing some refinements to reflect new forms of production and the growing importance of services, digital activities, and environmental management. For industrial statistics, some of the improvements include: 

--- end of page.page_number=133 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 121_ 

- A finer breakdown of repair, waste management, and environmental services, supporting better identification and monitoring of “green” industries; 

- Enhanced classification of information and communication, data processing, and platform-based activities, improving the statistical visibility of digital services that are increasingly integrates with industrial production; 

- Clearer guidance on contract manufacturing, outsourcing, and FGP, helping ensure more consistent and transparent measurement of GVCs. 

CPC Ver. 3, adopted in 2024–2025, provides a revised and more detailed product classification aligned with ISIC Rev. 5 and other macroeconomic standards. For industrial statistics, key implications include: 

- Identification of green and low-carbon goods, circular economy products, and environmental services produced by industrial establishments; 

## **Main international classifications relevant for industrial statistics** 

   - International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities (ISIC) [5] 

   - Central Product Classification (CPC) [95] 

   - Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (HS) [96] 

   - List of Industrial Products (LoIP) [97] 

   - Standard International Energy Product Classification (SIEC) [98] 

- More explicit classification of digital products and services arising from industrial activities; 

- Improved consistency in classifying industrial output by type of product, including intangible or knowledge-based outputs, in line with SNA concepts. 

In addition, the HS classification remains the primary international standard for traded goods. The forthcoming 2028 revision, currently under development, is expected to introduce new subheadings for environmental and health-related goods, advanced “green” technologies, waste and scrap categories, and products relevant to circular economy and hazard management. These updates will allow trade statistics to better capture the evolving composition of manufactured exports and imports. 

Looking ahead, it will be important to continue identifying research needs and potential future revisions to ensure that international classifications remain responsive to the transformations taking place in industrial sectors.

The adoption of SNA 2025 as the new international standard for national accounts marks a major milestone for economic statistics in general, and industrial statistics in particular. While the update retains the core structure of SNA 2008, it introduces new or expanded treatment for digitalization, globalization, emerging

For industrial statistics, this implies that surveys and administrative data used to compile industrial output and investment need to collect information on the expenditures on these assets; the bundling of physical goods with digital services or embedded software; and the integration of digital technologies into industrial production processes. These improvements will help industrial statistics to reflect more accurately the growing importance of digitalization, AI adoption, and the role of intangibles in industrial activity. 

The SNA update devotes substantial attention to globalization and global production arrangements, providing refined guidance on MNEs, special purpose entities, GVCs, FGP, merchanting, and outsourcing arrangements. This has several implications for industrial statistics: 

- The delineation between domestic and foreign production, and between resident and non-resident units, needs to be reflected in business statistics and in the profiling of MNE groups;

The recent national accounts update better reflects the global production arrangements shaping manufacturing today 

- Guidance on accounting for outsourcing, contract manufacturing, and ancillary activities, which affect how industrial output is attributed to establishments in different economies, thereby improving consistency between industrial statistics, trade statistics, and balance of payments data; 

- The focus on thematic or satellite accounts (e.g. on the digital economy) increases the demand for detailed data from industrial establishments. 

The SNA 2025 also broadens the national accounts framework to better account for well-being and sustainability, including more explicit treatment of natural resource depletion as a cost of production, distributional measures, and links to environmental-economic accounts. For industrial statistics, this will result in a more comprehensive reflection of the inclusiveness and sustainability dimensions of industrial production. 

## **Integrating environmental-economic accounting into industrial statistics** 

Environmental pressures and the green transition feature prominently among the transformations shaping industry, but traditional industrial statistics remain largely focused on economic variables such as output, value added, and trade. The SEEA provides a conceptual and statistical framework to bridge this gap by integrating environmental information into the same accounting structure as the SNA. 

**==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

The SEEA framework connects industrial activity with energy, water, emissions, waste, and natural resource use 

The SEEA Central Framework, adopted in 2012, consists of several complementary elements. First, physical flow accounts, organized as physical supply and use tables, record the flows of natural inputs, products, and residuals between the environment and the economy, 

--- end of page.page_number=136 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 124_ 

by industry and product. Second, environmental asset accounts record stocks and changes in stocks of individual natural resources in volume and monetary terms. Third, accounts for environmental protection expenditure, environmental taxes and subsidies, and environmental goods and services link environmental policy instruments and markets to industries and institutional sectors. The SEEA Ecosystem Accounting, adopted in 2021, extends this approach further by quantifying ecosystem extent, condition, and services in a way that can be linked to economic activity [105]. 

This framework directly addresses several of the measurement challenges that industrial statistics must overcome to remain future-ready. First, it provides a coherent mechanism to link industrial activities to their resource use and environmental pressures, including energy and water use, GHG and air pollutant emissions, waste generation, and material flows. This information is essential for tracking resource efficiency, environmental performance, and the decoupling between emissions and production. Second, it provides a way to identify industries producing environmental goods and services, which can be useful for monitoring activity in “green” industries and the transition to sustainable production. And third, it supports the analysis of how industrial activities affect ecosystems and the services they provide, including land-use change, degradation, and restoration. 

Despite these advantages, SEEA implementation remains uneven across countries and often partial in coverage, in part because of its significant data requirements. Moreover, environmental statistics are still often compiled separately from economic statistics, leading to inconsistencies and limited integration across domains. A more comprehensive and harmonized implementation of the SEEA offers significant potential benefits for industrial statistics. It would strengthen the capacity of NSOs to measure the green transformation, assess environmental impacts with greater level of detail, and provide policymakers with integrated information to design and monitor sustainable industrial strategies. 

## **Linking industrial statistics with other domains** 

As emphasized throughout this chapter, many emerging policy questions concerning industry cannot be addressed using industrial statistics alone. Understanding the implications of industrial transformations for decent jobs, wages, innovation capacity, external competitiveness, inclusiveness, and other dimensions requires integrating information across multiple statistical domains. This integration could draw on several established international standards, including but not limited to: 

Two main manuals in the SEEA family: 

Central Framework and Ecosystem Accounting

The adoption of environmental accounting remains low worldwide, limiting its contribution to green industrial policymaking

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 125_ 

- Labour statistics, guided by International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS) resolutions on statistics related to labour force, employment, working time, wages, and occupational classifications. Linking business statistics with labour force surveys and other demographic and social data could provide information to analyse the distributional and inclusiveness dimensions of industrialization, including gender and youth employment, informality, skills, and job quality. 

- R&D and innovation statistics, guided by the Frascati Manual [103] and the Oslo Manual [104], respectively. These frameworks define concepts, classifications, and survey methodologies for measuring R&D expenditure and personnel, as well as innovation activities in the business sector. Integrating these statistics with structural and performance indicators from industrial statistics would provide a more complete understanding of the role of innovation and intangible assets in industrial development. 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Complex policy questions require industrial data to be integrated with labour, trade, and innovation statistics 

- Trade and balance-of-payments statistics, including the 2025 update of the Balance of Payments Manual [100] and forthcoming revisions to the International Merchandise Trade Statistics and International Trade in Services Statistics manuals. These standards offer guidance for measuring cross-border flows of goods, services, and capital, including digital trade and services supplied by industrial firms. 

- Energy statistics, which can be linked with industrial statistics to obtain detailed information on energy production and consumption by industrial establishments and on their progress along the energy transition [106]. 

Taken together, these options suggest that the future of industrial statistics may lie not in expanding as a standalone statistical domain, but in deeper synergies within an integrated system of economic, social, and environmental statistics. 

## **5.3 Cross-cutting challenges in the production of industrial statistics** 

The adaptations described in the previous section would allow industrial statistics to better respond to the data needs arising from the transformations reshaping industry. However, these conceptual advances also interact with multiple, often simultaneous operational pressures faced by NSOs. This section highlights some of the most important cross-cutting challenges in the compilation and dissemination of industrial statistics that must also be addressed to maintain data quality, increase efficiency, and ensure industrial statistics remain fit for purpose.

The future role of industrial statistics lies within a broader integrated system, not in isolated efforts

## **Response burden, non-response, and declining survey participation** 

Business surveys are typically demanding for establishments. They request detailed information on output, inputs, employment, investment, products, and technologies, often at high frequency and for multiple reference periods, using concepts that do not always align with business accounting practices. At the same time, firms face increasing and overlapping reporting obligations, including tax, social security, regulatory, and other statistical requirements. These pressures are particularly acute for SMEs, which have fewer administrative resources. International frameworks highlight the importance of considering response burden when collecting statistical information [107; 108]. 

A related challenge is declining response rates. Many NSOs report increasing difficulties in recruiting and retaining survey respondents, particularly among small firms and in sectors with high turnover. The United Kingdom’s labour force survey, although a household survey, illustrates this trend: full response rates declined from 48.2 per cent in 2010 to 17.4 per cent in 2024 [109; 110]. Similar patterns are observed in many other countries. If not adequately addressed, these trends can introduce bias and threaten the representativeness of industrial statistics. 

To mitigate these challenges, many NSOs are adopting an administrative data-first approach, surveying establishments only when comparable data cannot be obtained from existing sources, such as tax filings, financial statements, or employment reports. Non-traditional data sources, including big data, could also serve as complements. Implementing such approach requires well-established data flows, robust data governance frameworks, and clear methodologies for integrating data sources. When surveys remain necessary, several improvements could help reduce burden and improve participation: careful survey design and sampling strategies that avoid repeatedly burdening the same units; the use of web-based questionnaires and pre-filled forms; responsive collection strategies targeted at highimpact non-respondents; and clear communication about the purpose 

## **Survey frames and complex enterprise structures**

Producing high-quality industrial statistics depends critically on the quality of the underlying survey frames. SBRs are widely recognized as the backbone of business statistics, providing coherent frames for sampling and integrating data across surveys and administrative

sources [111; 112]. However, in many countries SBRs remain incomplete or outdated. Gaps are common with respect to SMEs, industries with high firm turnover, and establishments operating in the informal sector. 

Globalization and new business models introduce additional complexity. Enterprise groups are becoming increasingly multifaceted, with operations spread out in multiple industries and jurisdictions. FGP and outsourcing blur the link between the location where goods are physically produced and the units that own the products, technologies, and intellectual property. 

These issues challenge the ability of SBRs and survey frames to correctly identify statistical units and to attribute industrial activity to the appropriate resident entities. Meeting these challenges requires prioritizing the coverage, quality, and maintenance of the SBR; establishing a dedicated large case unit (LCU); expanding the use of administrative data for business profiling; and aligning national practices with international guidance on enterprise groups and global production [112].

High-quality business registers are essential for sampling, data integration, and analysing business demography 

## **Data sources and data integration** 

While surveys remain indispensable in many cases, the pressure to reduce response burden and increase timeliness and granularity is accelerating the shift towards multi-source statistical systems. Administrative data, including tax records, social security registers, customs records, business licensing, and many others, can play a central role in this transition, especially for structural variables like turnover, trade, employment, and firm characteristics [113; 114]. 

At the same time, new types of data are becoming increasingly relevant for industrial statistics. Satellite imagery, scanner data, web-scraped data, and other digital traces hold significant potential for measuring specific aspects of economic and environmental activity (see, for instance, the resources available in [115]). 

A major challenge lies in linking survey and non-survey data sources. The adoption of unique identifiers that allow consistent linkage across datasets would significantly facilitate integration. When they are not available, probabilistic matching can achieve reliable results when based on robust methodologies. Additional challenges commonly arise, including data access restrictions, limitations in legal frameworks, and the presence of intrinsic biases or quality issues in nonsurvey data.

Industrial statistics increasingly combine surveys, administrative records, big data, and other non-traditional sources

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 128_ 

## **Timeliness and quality trade-offs** 

Industrial statistics are used both for structural analysis and shortterm monitoring of economic activity. Data users increasingly expect timely, high-frequency indicators of industrial activity with minimal publication lags. Meeting these expectations requires balancing difficult trade-offs between timeliness, coverage, granularity, and accuracy. 

For industrial statistics, improving timeliness without jeopardizing quality often requires a combination of measures. These include, among others, redesigning survey instruments and collection modes; expanding the use of administrative and high-frequency data sources; and applying model-based estimation and nowcasting techniques to produce preliminary estimates. New methodologies, including machine learning tools, can greatly accelerate data production while maintaining or even improving quality. These include, for example, automated classification, anomaly detection, or imputation techniques [116]. 

## Machine learning methods 

applied across the data production cycle can improve timeliness while 

maintaining or improving other dimensions of data quality 

## **Methodological modernization and process integration** 

In addition to new data sources and methods, addressing the challenges presented requires a modernization of statistical production processes and infrastructure. Applying a statistical business process model to industrial statistics can help identify opportunities for standardization, automation, and reuse of tools across surveys and domains, ultimately leading to improved efficiency and consistency. It can also contribute to a more robust data and metadata management, supported by stronger integration and clear governance structures [117; 118]. 

For industrial data in particular, given its complex classifications, multiple disaggregations, and frequent revisions, well-designed metadata systems are essential to ensure that users can correctly interpret statistical outputs and that data can be consistently linked across domains and over time. Strengthening these systems is therefore essential for making industrial statistics more agile, interoperable, and responsive to the evolving needs of policymakers and other users. 

## **Dissemination, communication, and AI-readiness** 

There has never been a greater demand for reliable, accessible, and timely data. As evidence-based policymaking becomes more deeply embedded and as analytical tools grow more sophisticated, the need for disaggregated, high-frequency indicators continues to rise. At the 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Statistical business process models can streamline industrial data production and support end-to-end modernization 

--- end of page.page_number=141 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 129_ 

same time, the way industrial statistics are disseminated and communicated is undergoing rapid transformation. Some users look for concise summaries and policy-ready dashboards, while others expect open, machine-readable datasets with clear licences, rich metadata, and tools that enable automated processing and reproducible analysis. Ensuring that dissemination systems serve this increasingly diverse spectrum of users is now a central challenge for producers of industrial statistics. 

Confidentiality and data protection remain essential considerations. As dissemination becomes more granular (by industry, region, firm size, or other attributes), the risk of disclosing sensitive information grows. Statistical offices must continue to apply robust confidentiality safeguards, including SDC techniques, when releasing detailed data to the public. 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Dissemination should cater both human and AI users through open, 

interoperable, and machine-readable data and metadata standards 

A new and rapidly growing dimension is the AI-readiness of official statistics. While dissemination platforms were traditionally optimized for direct human use, industrial data are now increasingly accessed by AI systems that retrieve, read, and synthesize information on behalf of users. This shift rises the importance of standardized formats, semantic consistency, consistent identifiers, and machine-readable metadata, enabling AI tools to interpret and combine statistical content correctly. Dissemination systems must therefore be optimized simultaneously for human interpretation and automated consumption, ensuring clarity, transparency, and interoperability [119]. 

## **5.4 Conclusion and the forthcoming revision of the international standards for industrial statistics** 

This chapter has shown that industrial statistics are at a turning point. Structural transformations in industry, including the green and energy transition, digitalization, the reconfiguration of GVCs, labour market shifts, the rising importance of innovation, and growing concerns about resilience, are reshaping what policy makers need to know about industry and how industrial development should be measured. At the same time, statistical producers face mounting operational pressures related to response burden, non-response, integration of multiple data sources, timeliness, data quality, confidentiality, and dissemination. 

Both the megatrends reshaping industry and the mounting cross-cutting challenges call for a renewed approach to industrial statistics 

Section 5.2 described how many of the conceptual tools needed to respond to these demands already exist in the form of revised international frameworks and classifications. However, the current industrial statistics standards themselves still reflect an earlier generation of industrial structures, policy priorities, and statistical practices. They 

--- end of page.page_number=142 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 130_ 

no longer fully match the information needed to design, monitor, and evaluate industrial policy in a rapidly changing world. 

The existing manuals have provided a robust foundation for industrial statistics for many years. They standardized key concepts, classifications, and indicators; supported the development of national industrial survey programmes; and guided international reporting, including for SDG 9. However, they pre-date many of the conceptual, policy, and statistical developments discussed in this chapter, leaving important gaps where updated guidance is needed. 

In response, UNIDO and the UN Statistics Division have initiated exploratory work on the future of international standards for industrial statistics. The directions under consideration include: 

- Aligning definitions and measurement concepts in industrial statistics with the SNA 2025 and the SEEA, including for digitalization, globalization, and environmental and distributional aspects; 

## **Current industrial statistical standards** 

   - International Recommendations for Industrial Statistics (IRIS) [4] 

   - International Recommendations for the Index of Industrial Production (IRIIP) [99] 

   - List of Industrial Products (LoIP) [97] 

- Clarifying the scope of industrial statistics, including the treatment of industrial services and industry-related activities, drawing on updated SNA guidance; 

- Fully leverage updated classifications to identify green, digital, and high-technology industries and products; 

- Providing guidance on the measurement of R&D, innovation, intangibles, MNE activity, the informal economy, and other concepts within an industrial context; 

- Strengthening methodological guidance on the use of administrative and other data sources, the role of the SBR, and integration of industrial statistics with labour, innovation, trade, and environmental data; 

- Updating the list of industrial performance indicators to better reflect contemporary policy priorities and data needs. 

This would result in a new generation of international standards for industrial statistics, replacing the existing manuals. Importantly, this should not be seen as an isolated technical exercise, but as part of a broader global effort to adapt official statistics so that they remain relevant, coherent, and fit for purpose amid accelerating economic, technological, and environmental change. 

The transformations described in this chapter will continue to evolve, and statistical systems will need to remain flexible and forward-looking while at the same time maintaining consistency over time. By building on the strengths of current standards while addressing emerging demands in a pragmatic manner, the forthcoming revision can help ensure that industrial statistics remain a solid analytical foundation for evidence-based policies in support of an inclusive, resilient, and sustainable industrial future.

## **B Explanatory notes** 

Unless otherwise indicated, _manufacturing_ refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section C, while the combined _mining and utilities_ sector includes sections B, D, and E of ISIC Rev. 4 [5].[INFO-CIRCLE] 

ISIC code numbers are accompanied by a descriptive title. For example, the descriptive title of ISIC division 16 is “Manufacture of wood and of products of wood and cork, except furniture; manufacture of articles of straw and plaiting materials”. However, the description is sometimes shortened for space considerations. In this example, ISIC division 16 may be described simply as “Wood products, excluding furniture”. A list of ISIC codes and their corresponding descriptive titles is given in Annex E.1. 

In the presentation of statistical tables and visualizations, individual countries and areas are referred to as economies. They are listed alphabetically, unless another ranking is considered more appropriate. Economies are classified according to their stage of industrial development and their geographical regions. Additional country groupings may be used whenever necessary. For additional information on UNIDO’s classification system, see Annex C. The lists of economies according to the main country groups used in the _Yearbook_ are provided in Annexes E.3, E.4, and E.5. 

In some cases, data on economic activity and traded commodities are classified according to technological intensity. For more details on the sources of these classifications, as well as the lists of highertechnology industries and traded commodities, see Annex E.2. 

Unless otherwise specified, data for China do not include Hong Kong SAR of China, Macao SAR of China, and Taiwan Province of China, which are reported separately. References to Kosovo should be understood within the framework of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999). References to Kosovo and to Taiwan Province of China are included exclusively for statistical completeness and do not imply any opinion whatsoever by UNIDO regarding their legal status. 

INFO-CIRCLE ISIC provides a comprehensive framework for collecting and reporting economic data for purposes of economic analysis, decision-taking and policy-making. 

International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities (ISIC)

_B Explanatory notes 143_ 

References to dollars ($) are to dollars of the United States of America. National currencies have been converted into dollar equivalents by using period average exchange rates as published in [120] and other sources. Data converted into dollars by using current exchange rates may be influenced by exchange rate fluctuations. Annual variations in data converted in that manner may not reflect movements in national currency data. 

Growth rates and proportions are expressed as percentages. Periods indicated with a dash (e.g. 2010–2022) include both the initial and final years. Apparent arithmetic discrepancies, such as disaggregated figures that do not sum exactly to reported totals, may arise from the rounding of underlying data or from figures available at different levels of precision. 

**==> picture [123 x 116] intentionally omitted <==**

Throughout this publication, three dots (…) indicate that data are not available or are not separately reported. 

--- end of page.page_number=156 ---

## **C Overview of methodological aspects** 

One of the most important objectives of UNIDO’s statistical databases and regular publications, such as this _Yearbook_ , is providing statistical information that facilitate international comparisons related to the manufacturing sector and the combined mining and utilities sector. Bearing in mind the requirements of international comparability when maintaining a common platform for global industrial statistics, the data presented were compiled using the international recommendations and the standards endorsed by the UN. Concepts and definitions are drawn from [4; 5]. 

## INDUSTRY **ISIC** 

ISIC has provided guidance for developing national activity classifications since its adoption in 1948. It is an essential tool for international comparison of statistical data on economic activities. 

ISIC is the recommended international reference classification of productive activities. Since the adoption of the first version in 1948, the majority of countries around the world have used ISIC as their national activity classification or have developed national classifications derived from it. Besides, it has become an essential tool for comparing statistical data on economic activities at the regional and international levels. 

In this publication, information on industrial sectors and their groups are presented according to ISIC Rev. 4 [5], since this revision remains the most used classification of economic activities worldwide. Data reported in accordance with ISIC Rev. 3 [121] or other national/regional classifications of economic activities were converted to ISIC Rev. 4 using appropriate correspondence tables. A new version of the classification, ISIC Rev. 5, was endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission at its 54[th] session in 2023 [94]. All economies are encouraged to reflect this new classification in the coming years, as far as national requirements permit, in their industrial classification schemes. 

In some cases, UNIDO applies imputation methods when data are missing. The primary objective is extending the length of time series and enabling the calculation of country group aggregates. Minor discrepancies may occur due to data revisions or during the conversion and estimation processes. As a result, users may observe differences when 

UNIDO databases provide statistical indicators to facilitate long-term analysis of economic performance across economies

comparing data for the same reference year across various editions of the _Yearbook_ or when contrasting earlier and later data releases.

These official data compiled by UNIDO were originally collected by individual national authorities and NSOs through surveys and censuses conducted periodically, as well as from business registers and other administrative sources. The data collected were generally complemented with estimations made by national experts. 

UNIDO relies on appropriate statistical benchmarking techniques to combine statistical information from multiple data sources in order to produce estimates with the highest degree of accuracy, reliability, coherence, and detail possible [4].

## **National accounts and population** 

Industrial statistics based on the SNA provide a continuing flow of key information that is indispensable for the monitoring, analysis, and evaluation of an economy’s performance over time. The main economic indicators presented in the _Yearbook_ , including value added of the manufacturing sector (ISIC Rev. 4 section C) and those for the mining and utilities sectors (ISIC Rev. 4 sections B, D, and E), are obtained based on the SNA. They represent the net contribution of the respective sectors to GDP. Information on MVA and MUVA serve as significant benchmarks for measuring performance in those industrial sectors. In this publication, both MVA per capita at constant prices and the share of MVA in GDP are used as markers of a country’s level of industrialization and its progress towards structural transformation. 

UNIDO obtains data on GDP, MVA, and other national accounts aggregates mostly from the National Accounts Main Aggregates Database [122]. The database is compiled by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) from official national accounts submitted by NSOs, supplemented with estimates generated by UNSD experts, whenever appropriate. It includes information for more than 200 economies and is updated annually in December. Complete information on the estimation methodology is available in [123]. The base year of these data is currently 2015.
