It is well understood that individual national data compilation schemes vary, which could affect comparability across economies. Hence, national authorities are encouraged to adhere to UN’s concepts and definitions on industrial statistics, whenever possible. 

Production (output) is an essential economic indicators in industrial statistics. While some data are still reported using census concept covering only activities of industrial nature, current recommendations call for approximating the national accounts measurement by including revenue from activities of a non-industrial nature. 

Manufacturing output refers to the more refined or higher value merchandise for use or sale. It is the end-product of industrial processes that use labour, machines, tools, and chemical and biological processing or formulation 

Output cannot be directly observed from the accounting records of enterprises/establishments [4]. The value of output in the case of estimates compiled on a production basis comprises: 

- a) The value of the sale of all products of the establishment; 

- b) The net change between the beginning and end of the reference period in the value of work in progress and stocks of goods to be shipped in the same condition as received; 

- c) The value of industrial work performed or industrial services rendered to others; 

- d) The value of goods shipped in the same condition as received less the amount paid for these goods; and 

## INDUSTRY **Census and gross output** 

The difference between census output and gross output is the exclusion or inclusion of the output from the activities that are nonindustrial in nature. 

- e) The value of fixed assets produced during the period by the unit for its own use. 

In the case of estimates compiled on a shipment basis, the net change in the value of stocks of finished goods between the beginning and the end of the reference period is also included. Gross output is equivalent to census output plus the revenue from activities of a non-industrial nature. 

Valuation methods of output vary across countries/areas. The main difference is the inclusion or exclusion of taxes and subsidies on products and production (see Figure C.3). 

- _Values at factor costs_ exclude taxes on production (taxes that the producing units are liable to pay as a result of engaging in production) and includes subsidies on production (subsidies that resident enterprises may receive as a result of engaging in production, with the exception of direct subsidies on products). 

- _Values at basic prices_ equal values at factor costs including taxes on production and excluding subsidies on production. 

- Finally, _values at producers’ prices_ equal values at basic prices plus taxes on products (taxes payable per unit of a product, excluding value added tax (VAT)) minus subsidies on products 

Value at factor costs excludes taxes on production and includes subsidies on production 

Value at basic prices = Value at factor costs + taxes on production - subsidies on production 

Value at producers’ prices = Value at basic prices + taxes on products (excl. VAT) - subsidies on products

Another important economic measurement is value added. In SBS, the value added of manufacturing industries is a survey concept that refers to the given industries’ net output derived from the difference of gross output and intermediate consumption/input. Items covered in the latter include: 

- a) value of materials and supplies for production, including the cost of all fuels and electricity purchased; and 

- b) the cost of services received (mainly payments for contract and commission work and repair and maintenance work). 

If input estimates are compiled on a “received” rather than on a “consumed” basis, the result is adjusted for the net change between the beginning and the end of the period in the value of stocks of materials, fuel, and other supplies. The estimates of value added are gross of depreciation and other provisions for capital consumption, unless otherwise stated. Similar to output, the valuation of value added may be at factor costs, at basic prices, or at producers’ prices, depending on the treatment of indirect taxes and subsidies as described above and summarized in Figure C.3.

One more important statistical concept presented in UNIDO’s databases and in this publication is employment. This is one of the central elements in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Within the framework adopted at the 19[th] International Conference of Labour Statisticians in 2013, employment is defined as work performed in return for pay or profit [129]. It has long been recognized as a pathway to economic development, social inclusion, and well-being. Estimates on the number of employees include both full-time and part-time workers, excluding working proprietors, active business partners, unpaid family workers, and home workers. The figures reported usually refer to the average number of workers during the reference year, obtained as the sum of the “average number of employees” during the year or the total number of employees measured for a single period of the year.

## **Competitive industrial performance (CIP) Index** 

The CIP Index is a composite indicator that measures the capacity of countries/areas to increase their presence in international and domestic markets, while developing industrial sectors and activities with higher value added and higher technological level. It is constructed by combining eight variables across three dimensions: 

- a) _Capacity to produce and export manufactured goods._ This dimension captures a country’s ability to increase the presence of its manufactured goods in international and domestic markets. It covers comparable measures of the country’s manufacturing production and exports, namely MVA and manufacturing exports in per capita terms. These indicators allow for cross-country comparisons, independent of the differences in population or economy size. 

- b) _Technological deepening and upgrading._ The second dimension measures the technological complexity of manufacturing processes in a country by using two composite sub-indices. First, the degree of industrialization intensity that estimates the complexity of production processes. This indicator consists of the share of MVA originating from MHT industries and the share of MVA in GDP. Second, export quality, another composite indicator 

## Three dimensions of the CIP Index 

**==> picture [96 x 96] intentionally omitted <==**

--- end of page.page_number=166 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 154_ 

that measures the quality of the integration process of the country’s manufacturing sector. This indicator is estimated based on the share of MHT manufacturing exports in total manufacturing exports and the share of manufacturing exports in total exports. 

- c) _World impact._ The third dimension serves as a proxy of economies of agglomeration, scope, and scale present in a country’s manufacturing sector. It captures the world impact based on two indicators: the country’s share in world MVA and in world trade of manufactured goods. 

All variables are first standardized to a [0, 1] interval. Scores for each dimension are obtained by calculating the geometric mean of the underlying variables. Finally, the overall CIP score is calculated as the geometric mean of the scores for the three dimensions. The higher the score in any of the variables, the higher the country’s industrial competitiveness and its rank in the overall CIP Index. The detailed conceptual framework and methodology of the Index are described in [130]. The Index’s scores, ranks, and underlying indicators are available in the UNIDO Statistics Portal [34].

## **SDG 9 Industry Index** 

The SDG 9 Industry Index is a composite indicator that summarizes countries’ performance on the industry-related targets of SDG 9. It combines the information of the indicators for which UNIDO is the custodian agency and for which sufficient data are available (i.e. the two series of indicator 9.2.1, plus 9.2.2, 9.4.1, and 9.b.1). 

A short explanation of the Index’s calculation is presented below. A more complete description on the methodology can be found in [28; 134]. 

All indicators are first normalized through the min-max method to standardize the variables for further data aggregation, as they have different measurement units. The normalization is applied with three caveats: (i) the minimum and maximum values for normalizing each indicator are calculated over the entire sample of observations, which consists of all countries with available information over the period from 2000 to the latest year; (ii) to avoid the excessive influence of outliers in the transformation, the observed minimum and maximum values are capped at three standard deviations from the mean; (iii) an inverse normalization is applied to SDG indicator 9.4.1 ( _CO2 emission intensity of manufacturing_ ), so that all normalized indicators follow the same direction. 

SDG indicators on small manufacturing 

lack sufficient data coverage to be included in the SDG 9 Industry Index 

After these steps, normalized indicators have a range of [0, 1], with zero indicating the case with the lowest performance and one indicating the case with the best performance. All normalized indicators have the same direction: a higher value indicates a better performance. Finally, since the normalization is calculated using common parameters, the resulting indicators can be used for comparisons across countries and time. 

--- end of page.page_number=168 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 156_ 

The Index score is then calculated as the geometric mean of the five normalized indicators. Geometric aggregation allows to limit compensability among indicators. However, it has the disadvantage that a country with a value of zero in one normalized indicator (i.e. when it coincides with the minimum value observed in the sample) also has a composite Index equal to zero in that period. It is worth noting that all indicators are aggregated under an equal weighting scheme. This choice makes the Index transparent and facilitates interpretation [135]. Ranks are also calculated to facilitate country comparison. 

SDG 9 Industry Index is a summary measure of inclusive and sustainable industrial development as declared in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development 

As described in the methodology summary above, the construction of the Index requires available information for all indicators. The Index currently covers 138 countries for the period from 2000 to 2022. 

## **Country/area classifications** 

The main purpose of the UNIDO country classification is defining a relatively homogeneous set of country groups that have common features in terms of their stage of industrial development, determined by objective criteria derived from official indicators of industrial performance. It adheres to the basic principles of statistical classifications, as defined in [136]. The country groups are revised annually with the objective of reflecting countries’ current economic situation, while the classification methodology remains stable. More information on the classification methodology can be found in [38]. 

UNIDO country 

is based on a combination of income groups and industrialization indicators 

The main country classification proposed by UNIDO divides countries/areas according to a combination of their income level and their stage of industrial development. It therefore relies on two parameters: (i) per capita income levels, sourced from the World Bank’s 2025 income groups [137]; and (ii) structural transformation metrics (MVA per capita in constant USD, historical maximum of the share of manufacturing employment in total employment, and exports of MHT products per capita), calculated from UNIDO databases. This classification system allocates countries/areas among five groups: 

- _High-income industrial economies_ : Countries/areas that have achieved a high national income through a development path that resulted in highly industrialized economies. 

- _High-income industrializing economies_ : Countries/areas with a high income level but with relatively low levels of industrialization. 

- _Medium-income industrial economies_ : Countries/areas classified as medium-income economies that have already achieved positive outcomes in terms of structural transformation indicators. 

Five UNIDO country groups: two groups of industrial economies and three groups of industrializing economies 

--- end of page.page_number=169 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 157_ 

- _Medium-income industrializing economies_ : Countries/areas classified as medium-income but that still remain at comparatively low levels of industrialization; these are some of the economies that could benefit the most from prioritizing industrial development in their policy strategies. 

- _Low-income economies_ : Countries/areas that remain at low income levels and also underperform in industrial development indicators; these economies would greatly gain from an accelerated structural change process that could help them escape the development trap. 

Emerging industrial economies includes the most dynamic low- and middle-income economies in terms of industrial performance 

This classification has the objective of summarizing large amounts of country-level data into relevant insights and common trends observed in countries facing similar development challenges. The list of economies according to these five groups is included in Annex E.4. 

A special economic group proposed by UNIDO is that of emerging industrial economies (EIEs). These are the most dynamic low- and middle-income economies in terms of their industrial performance. It includes economies that have continuously registered positive spells of growth in MVA. This group includes 12 economies in 2025: three middle-income industrial economies, six middle-income industrializing economies, and three low-income economies. The list is given in Annex Table E.5.1. 

Countries/areas are also classified according to geographical region. UNIDO follows the UN Standard Country or Area Codes for Statistical Use (M49) [138]. According to this standard, all world economies are assigned to one main regions, which are then further divided into subregions. These regional groupings are, inter alia, the main classification system used for SDG indicators. The complete classification is given in Annex E.3.

## **D UNIDO Statistics and the International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics** 

## **D.1 UNIDO Statistics** 

Following the recommendations of the United Nations Statistical Commission, UNIDO has the mandate to compile and disseminate international statistics on the manufacturing, mining, and utilities sectors. This involves the regular collection, screening, and validation of industrial data from official sources and presenting them according to harmonized definitions and classifications. UNIDO generates analytical indicators based on official data, which can be used to monitor a country’s prevailing performance and progress in terms of ISID. 

The statistics are disseminated through various databases available at the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3], as well as publications such as this _Yearbook_ . These products offer statistical information to a wide range of users, including national governments, international development partners, academic and research institutions, as well as the business and statistical communities. Priority is given to quality assurance of statistics, especially in terms of international comparability and alignment with UN recommended concepts and classifications. 

As a custodian agency of six industry-related indicators under SDG 9, UNIDO has been actively involved in the process of developing and monitoring the global indicator framework for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. UNIDO contributes to the _UN SDG Global Database_ [133], reports to the IAEG-SDGs, and collaborates with countries on improving data availability and quality for better tracking their progress towards the 2030 Agenda. 

The organization cooperates closely with other international agencies, namely the ILO on employment; the International Energy Agency (IEA) on CO 2 emissions; and the World Bank on access to finance, to produce data and compile the corresponding SDG indicators. Furthermore, UNIDO publishes the _SDG 9 Industry Index_ , benchmarking countries’ performance towards achieving the industry-related targets of SDG 9 [134]. Industrial statistics are essential for formulating industrial development strategies and policies, analysing structural change and monitoring economic growth. UNIDO shares its expertise in industrial statistics with national and regional statistical offices by providing technical assistance and trainings on a wide range of topics. By implementing customized programmes to target countries’ specific needs, UNIDO assists in strengthening the institutional capacity of NSOs and line ministries to collect industrial data, maintain business registers, set up short-term statistical indicators and information systems, carry out data analyses of industrial performance, and track progress on SDGs. UNIDO furthermore provides capacity development activities on the usage of empirical data for economic analyses, which are relevant for promoting industrial development through evidence-based policymaking. 

## **D.2 The International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics** 

This _Yearbook_ presents a summary of the most recent data in industrial sectors. It outlines the current performance and latest developments, allowing the reader to analyse patterns of growth, business cycle fluctuations, and longer-term trends, including progress towards structural change, ISID and SDG 9. While the _Yearbook_ focuses on aggregate global trends observed in industrial sectors, it also highlights the main regional trends and sector-specific developments. More detailed information for specific regions and country groups are presented in Factsheets accompanying the _Yearbook_ . 

This publication relies on visualizations and short analytical texts to summarize the prevailing situation in global industry and to highlight key insights extracted from the data. It is essentially sourced from information that is available on UNIDO Statistics Portal [3]. Interested readers are invited to visit this resource to access the full datasets and related statistical products. 

All data presented in this _Yearbook_ were compiled bearing in mind the coherence of industrial statistics derived from various sources, the requirements of international comparability, and the standards of this work endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission. Concepts and definitions were drawn from international recommendations applicable to industrial statistics [4] and the classification of economic activities according to ISIC [5].

_D UNIDO Statistics and the International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics 160_ 

This is the thirty-first edition of the _International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics_ , published by UNIDO since 1995. For historical reference, this publication replaced two reports: the _Handbook of Industrial Statistics_ [140], which was published biennially by UNIDO until 1992, and the _United Nations Industrial Statistics Yearbook Volume I (General Industrial Statistics)_ [141], which was discontinued after its 1991 edition was published in 1993 by UNSD. These changes were introduced in line with the recommendations of the UN Statistical Commission at its 27[th] session. 

This four most recent editions of the _Yearbook_ feature several novelties compared to earlier editions. The current format represents an effort to modernize this long-standing publication, expanding its coverage to include all aspects of industrial statistics. It merges the contents of earlier editions of the _Yearbook_ (see [142] for the last edition under the previous format) and the biennial report _World Statistics on Mining and Utilities_ (see [143] for the last edition), at the same time expands its coverage to include the CIP Index, SDG 9 indicators, and other industrial performance indicators. 

International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics 2024

The _Yearbook_ will continue upgrading and expanding its coverage of ISID indicators in coming years, reaffirming UNIDO’s role as the international reference point on industrial statistics.

## **E.2 List of higher technology industries and traded commodities** 

Data on economic activity and traded commodities can be classified according to technological intensity. In the case of industries, the classification is based on R&D expenditure relative to value added, also known as R&D intensity, as calculated by the OECD [26; 27]. In this publication, “higher-technology” industries refer to the group of medium-high and high technology industries (MHT) given in Table E.2.1[*] . In the case of traded commodities, the classification is based on technological content as calculated in [42; 144]. In this publication, “higher-technology” commodities refer to the group of medium- and high-technology commodities, provided in Table E.2.2

## **Concepts and definitions** 

## **C | E | F | G | H | I | L | M | S | U | W** 

## **C** 

**CO2 emission intensity** Indicator computed as the ratio between CO2 emissions from fuel combustion and the value added of associated economic activities. It can be computed for the entire economy (total CO2 emissions per unit of GDP) or for specific sectors, notably the manufacturing sector (CO2 emissions from manufacturing per unit of MVA). 25 

## **E** 

**Economies of scale** In economics, this term refers to the reduced cost per unit that arises from a higher production level. 5 

**Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply** This sector refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section D. It includes the provision of electric power, natural gas, steam, hot water, air-conditioning supply and the like through a permanent infrastructure of lines, mains and pipes. This section also includes the operation of electric and gas utilities, which generate, control and distribute electric power or gas. 4, 18, 186 

## **F** 

**Factoryless goods production (FGP)** Factoryless goods production represents a distinctive organizational model within the broader landscape of global manufacturing arrangements. A principal controls the production of a good by undertaking the entrepreneurial steps and providing the technical specifications required to produce the good, but outsources all or most of the material transformation process required to produce the output [151]. x, 120 

## **G** 

**Gross domestic product (GDP)** GDP basically derives from the concept of gross value added. GDP is the sum of gross value added of all resident producer units plus the part (possibly the total) of taxes on products that is not included in the valuation of output, less subsidies on products [152, p. 34]. x, 5 

## **H** 

**Human Development Index (HDI)** Long-standing indicator measuring human development, defined as the process of expanding people’s freedoms and opportunities and improving their well-being. The HDI is a composite index of three dimensions: 1) the ability to lead a long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth; 2) the ability to acquire knowledge, measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling; and 3) the ability to achieve a decent standard of living, measured by gross national income per capita. A higher HDI value indicates a higher human development level. This indicator is calculated and maintained by UNDP [16]. x, 7 

## **I** 

**Index of industrial production (IIP)** Indicator that describes changes in the volume of goods produced in industrial sectors over time. Its main purpose is to provide a measure of short-term changes in value added over a given reference period. However, since it is difficult to collect high-frequency data to accurately measure value added, gross output measures such as the value of production or turnover data are more commonly used. The IIP, being a volume index, is not influenced by price fluctuations [99, p. 11]. x, 18, 146 

--- end of page.page_number=198 ---

- **Industrial statistics** Field of statistics related to the characteristics and economic activities of all resident units in the reporting country that are primarily active in the following productive activities: 

      - a. Mining and quarrying (ISIC Rev. 4 section B); 

      - b. Manufacturing (ISIC Rev. 4 section C); 

      - c. Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply (ISIC Rev. 4 section D); 

      - d. Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (ISIC Rev. 4 section E). 

   - Industrial statistics form part of the broader domain of structural and short-term business statistics [4, pp. 2 and 12]. 4, 5, 159, 160 

- **Industry** This term refers to the set of all production units engaged primarily in the same or similar kinds of productive activity [5, p. 9] The ISIC provides the international guidelines for cataloguing economic activity into specific industries, such as agriculture, mining, manufacturing or services. 4 

- **Industry value added (IVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of industrial sectors to GDP. x, 13 

- **Inter-agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators (IAEG-SDGs)** Working group tasked by the United Nations Statistical Commission to develop and implement the global indicator framework for the SDGs and the Targets of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It is composed of representatives from Member States from all regions, with custodian agencies participating as observers and experts. 23 

- **ISIC** The International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities, abbreviated as ISIC, is a standard classification of economic activities arranged so that entities can be classified according to the activity they carry out. Currently, the fourth revision of ISIC [5] is the most commonly used, and it is the reference used throughout this Yearbook. The hierarchically structured ISIC Rev. 4 classification contains sections, divisions, groups and classes. The ISIC classification is maintained by UNSD. x, 4, 121 

## **L** 

- **Large case unit (LCU)** A large case unit is a specialized unit within an NSO that focuses on ensuring the quality and consistency of data for large establishments, especially MNEs. x, 127 

- **Least developed country (LDC)** The LDC category was established by the United Nations (UN) General Assembly in 1971. The UN defines LDCs as countries that have low-income levels and face severe structural impediments to sustainable development. x 

## **M** 

- **Manufacturing** This industry refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section C. It includes activities related to the physical or chemical transformation of materials, substances or components into new products, although such a definition cannot be used as the single universal criterion for determining what constitutes manufacturing (see [5] for more details on activities included and not included in manufacturing). The materials, substances or components transformed are raw materials that are products of agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining or products of other manufacturing activities. Substantial alteration, renovation or reconstruction of goods is generally considered to be manufacturing. The output of a manufacturing process may be finished in the sense that it is ready for utilization or consumption, or it may be semi-finished in the sense that it is to become an input for further manufacturing. 4, 18, 93, 146, 186 

- **Manufacturing value added (MVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of manufacturing to GDP [153, p. 5]. xi, 6 

- **Mining and quarrying** This industry corresponds to ISIC Rev. 4 section B. It includes activities related to the extraction of minerals that occur naturally as solids (coal and ores), liquids (petroleum) or gases 

--- end of page.page_number=199 ---

   - (natural gas). Supplementary activities aimed at preparing the crude materials for marketing are also included, if they are undertaken in conjunction with mining, for example, crushing, grinding, cleaning, drying, sorting, concentrating ores, liquefaction of natural gas and agglomeration of solid fuels. 4, 18, 93, 146, 186 

- **Mining and utilities value added (MUVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of mining and utilities sectors to GDP. xi, 89 

- **Multinational enterprise (MNE)** A multinational enterprise, sometimes also called multinational corporation (MNC), just multinational, or international corporation, is an enterprise producing goods or delivering services in more than one country. It has its management headquarters in one (or rarely more than one) country, the home country, while also operating in other countries, the host countries [154]. xi, 120 

## **S** 

- **Short-term statistics (STS)** Infra-annual production-related statistics collected to monitor the business cycle. They are suitable for the short-term evaluation of supply, demand and production factors [4, p. 3]. Although available more frequently and in a timelier manner, they usually cover only some variables of interest and are published with a limited level of detail. 146 

- **Statistical confidentiality** Principle 6 of the _Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics_ [155] stresses that data collected by national statistical agencies are to be strictly confidential and used exclusively for statistical purposes. Many NSOs therefore implement national rules on statistical confidentiality. The two main reasons for declaring data to be of primary confidentiality are: 

   - a. too few units in a cell; 

   - b. dominance of one or two units in a cell. 

The limits of what constitutes ”too few” or ”dominance” vary between statistical domains. Statistical confidentiality is ensured through appropriate methods: 

- **Physical protection:** data is securely stored and not accessible to anyone without explicit authorization. 

- **Statistical disclosure control (SDC):** methods for reducing the risk that statistical units are identified when the statistical data is being published, including: 

   - **Tabular data protection:** for aggregate information on respondents presented in tables (using suppression, rounding, combinations and interval publication). 

   - **Microdata protection:** for information on statistical units (using local suppression, sampling, recoding, top and bottom coding, rounding, rank swapping and microaggregation). 

xi, 89, 187 

- **Structural business statistics (SBS)** These are production-related statistics that are collected and compiled to determine the structure, activity, competitiveness and performance of enterprises at national, regional and international levels. They generally provide annual information with respect to a reference year [4, p. 3]. Although available only annually and published with some delay, they usually cover a large number of variables at a highly granular level. Other common abbreviations used by NSOs are ABS (annual business statistics/survey) or AIS (annual industrial survey). xi, 96, 149 

- **Sub-annual Manufacturing Trade Data** Manufacturing trade is a key component of global trade, accounting for the majority of traded goods and offering valuable, timely insights into a country’s productive structure and the competitiveness of its manufacturing sector. xi 

- **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development [17], adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, provides a shared blueprint for peace and prosperity 

--- end of page.page_number=200 ---

for people and the planet, now and into the future. At its core are the 17 SDGs, which are an urgent call for action by all countries in a global partnership. They recognize that ending poverty and other deprivations must go hand-in-hand with strategies that improve health and education, reduce inequality and spur economic growth—all while tackling climate change and working to preserve our oceans and forests. xi, 3, 154 **Goal 9** Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation. 3, 9, 13, 20, 29–31, 44, 54, 82, 130, 154, 155, 158, 159. 

- **System of environmental-economic accounting (SEEA)** An international statistical framework that organizes data to show the interrelationships between the economy and the environment, as well as the stocks and changes in stocks of environmental assets as they bring benefits to humanity. It provides a standardized approach with consistent definitions and classifications, similar to the system of national accounts (SNA), to measure environmental assets and their contributions to the economy [74]. xi, 114, 119 

- **System of national accounts (SNA)** A coherent, consistent and integrated set of macroeconomic accounts, balance sheets and tables based on a set of internationally agreed concepts, definitions, classifications and accounting rules [156]. xi, 119, 188 

## **U** 

**UNIDO industrial statistics databases** UNIDO Statistics currently maintains a variety of databases, as described below. These can be accessed at the UNIDO Statistics Portal. 158 The **Annual Manufacturing Trade Database** [40] contains aggregate data at the country, region and group level for variables related to the trade of manufactured goods. The database provides historical time series in current United States dollar (USD). The data are collected primarily from the United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD); other sources of official data may be used when appropriate. 61, 158. The **Competitive Industrial Performance (CIP) index** benchmarks the ability of countries to produce and export manufactured goods competitively. 158. The **Industrial Demand-Supply Balance Databases (IDSB)** [139] contain disaggregated data on the manufacturing sector, including a correspondence to international trade data. 158. The **IIP Database** [19] contains monthly, quarterly and annual data on the index of industrial production for the manufacturing as well as mining and utilities sectors. 146, 158. The **Industrial Statistics Databases (INDSTAT)** [35; 36] contain disaggregated data for selected variables on the manufacturing, mining and utilities sectors. 52, 158. The **Monthly Manufacturing Trade Database** [41] contains monthly data on manufacturing trade with special emphasis on higher-technology goods. 61, 158. The **National Accounts Database** [9] contains aggregate data at the country, region and group level for several national accounts indicators related to industrial economic activity. 158. The **SDG 9 Database** [20] contains the industry-related indicators of SDG 9. 158. 

## **W** 

**Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities** This industry, corresponding to ISIC Rev. 4 section E, includes activities related to the management (including collection, treatment and disposal) of various forms of waste, such as solid or non-solid industrial or household waste, as well as contaminated sites. Activities of water supply are also grouped in this section, since they are often carried out in connection with, or by units also engaged in, the treatment of sewage. 4, 18, 186

## **Foreword** 

The global industrial landscape continues to evolve and 2025 was a noteworthy year. Countries around the world had to steer their economies through a challenging environment marked by geopolitical tensions, the restructuring of supply chains, a rise in protectionist measures, and the need to transition towards more sustainability. Amid these uncertainties, industry remains a central driver of economic growth and resilience, as evidenced by the worldwide return of industrial policy to the centre of economic agendas. This latest edition of the _International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics_ offers an authoritative, data-based overview of these shifting dynamics and their implications for inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Recent trends confirm that the manufacturing sector continues to play a decisive role in global economic performance, with multiplier effects that generates additional output, income, and jobs elsewhere in the economy. Manufacturing activity continues to expand at a moderate pace worldwide, reaching a growth rate of 2.9 per cent in 2024. Although this confirms the sector’s resilience, it remains below the momentum observed before the pandemic. Middle-income economies again showed the strongest results, as many of them expand their participation in global value chains and invest in technological capabilities that enable a gradual shift toward higher-value and innovationintensive industries. The results here also show that while manufacturing value added has continued to grow, this has not consistently translated into broad gains in employment, especially for women and youth. Automation, digitalization, and the emergence of artificial intelligence are reshaping production, demanding new ways to provide people with the skills and opportunities needed for the future of work. Ensuring that technology supports decent jobs instead of displacing them is essential for maintaining trust in the current industrial transformation. In terms of environmental sustainability, the evidence encouragingly shows that most economies have begun to decouple industrial growth from carbon emissions. Technological upgrading, greater energy efficiency, and an expanding market for low-carbon products demonstrate that greener industry is not only possible, but increasingly economically viable. However, the pace of change is uneven. Many low-income economies still face barriers to adopting cleaner production methods due to limited financing, technical capacity, or a lack of access to affordable technologies. Strengthening international cooperation, 

--- end of page.page_number=12 ---

technology transfer, and climate finance is absolutely critical in the years ahead. The need for reliable and up-to-date industrial statistics has never been greater. Amid the rapid transformation and the volatile international environment, policymakers require accurate data to identify opportunities, measure progress, and ensure that industrialization leads to lasting impact and shared prosperity. UNIDO’s statistical work, including this _Yearbook_ and the open-access UNIDO Statistics Portal, is a core contribution to global evidence-based decision-making. The _Yearbook_ offers a clear and objective picture of global industrial performance and long-term structural trends. Looking ahead, we must ensure that industrialization allows opportunities for all, advances climate and environmental goals, and serves as a force for human well-being. The evidence presented in this _Yearbook_ affirms that progress is possible and that there are important lessons to be learned from economies that have transitioned to innovationbased industrial sectors. Strategic investments, strong partnerships, and sound policies are all essential and should be prioritized. I encourage policymakers, researchers, and all those driving industrial change to draw on the insights of this _Yearbook_ to turn plans into action as we build a more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable future where no one is left behind. **==> picture [136 x 136] intentionally omitted <==**

## **1.1 Preface** 

According to the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index and the World Uncertainty Index, two widely cited measures in the literature [1; 2], global economic uncertainty is at its highest level in at least three decades, since the beginning of the indices’ historical records. The current landscape, characterized by persistent geopolitical tensions, prolonged disruptions in production chains, rising trade protectionism, environmental pressures, and rapid technological change, has resulted in economic volatility and uncertainty exceeding even the levels observed during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic. In this volatile context, the ability to rely on consistent, comparable data is more essential than ever.


Final chunk number 280, content : 
Industrial statistics play a vital role in understanding global industrial developments, identifying industries and groups that are advancing or lagging behind, and formulating effective strategies for inclusive and sustainable industrialization. Industrial sectors are closely linked to productivity improvements, employment creation, innovation, and technological upgrading. Their evolution therefore has direct implications for broader development outcomes, including human development, food security, equity, and environmental sustainability. However, manufacturing has not been immune to the current uncertainty. As countries work towards achieving the industry-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets in this challenging context, statistics remain indispensable for monitoring progress, diagnosing structural constraints and growth opportunities, guiding investment in infrastructure and innovation, and crafting effective industrial policy. The _International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics_ is UNIDO’s flagship statistical publication. It provides a concise and accessible overview of recent global trends in industrial sectors, including the impact of ongoing uncertainty, based on authoritative indicators that allow for meaningful comparisons across countries, regions, and over time. This edition presents a snapshot of the latest data available as of October 2025. This introductory chapter outlines the definition and significance of industry in sustainable development. Chapter 2 then provides a global overview of industrial performance, examining recent developments across all industrial sectors (including mining, manufacturing, and utilities). It also reviews progress towards SDG 9 industry targets and summarizes the latest results of the UNIDO competitive industrial performance (CIP) Index. Thereafter, Chapter 3 focuses on the manufacturing sector, analysing recent global and regional production trends, structural patterns across industries, and key indicators related to international trade, employment, productivity, gender equality, and environmental impact. Chapter 4 turns to mining and utilities, discussing their role in regional industrial structures and their linkages with energy systems and resource use. Finally, Chapter 5 is a thematic chapter that discusses the ongoing evolution and future transformation required for industrial statistics to remain responsive to policy needs in a world shaped by globalization, environmental pressures, technological change, and deepening inequalities. All indicators featured in the _Yearbook_ are based on official national and international statistics. The vast majority are drawn from UNIDO’s own industrial statistics databases, developed in close collaboration with national statistical offices and international partners. Reflecting UNIDO’s commitment to transparency and open data, all data featured in this publication are freely accessible through the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3], where users can explore, visualize, download, and reuse the information. --- end of page.page_number=16 ---

## **1.2 What are industrial statistics?** 

In statistics, having a clear and unambiguous definition is the essential first step before measuring or describing any concept. This ensures the production of consistent, harmonized, and internationally comparable data across statistical sources. According to current international standards, _industrial statistics_ are defined in relation to a specific set of productive activities, as determined by the International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities (ISIC) [4]. These encompass four broad economic sectors, as outlined in the box below. ## **Definition of industrial statistics** 

Industrial statistics cover the characteristics and economic activities of all resident units in the reporting country that are primarily engaged in the following productive activities, as defined by the ISIC [4, p. 12; 5, pp. 79–172]: 

- _Mining and quarrying_ (ISIC Rev.


Final chunk number 281, content : 
4 section B): The extraction of minerals that occur naturally as solids (e.g. coal and ores), liquids (e.g. petroleum), or gases (e.g. natural gas). - _Manufacturing_ (ISIC Rev. 4 section C): The physical or chemical transformation of materials, substances, or components into new products. - _Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply_ (ISIC Rev. 4 section D): The provision of electric power, natural gas, steam, hot water, and the like through a permanent infrastructure of lines, mains, and pipes. - _Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities_ (ISIC Rev. 4 section E): Activities related to the management (including collection, treatment, and disposal) of various forms of waste; water supply activities are also included in this section, as they are often carried out by the same establishments that provide sewage management. Sections D and E are usually combined under the _utilities_ sector. Given manufacturing’s greater data availability and economic weight, separate statistical information for this sector is typically compiled, while data for the other three sectors are frequently grouped together under _mining and utilities_ . UNIDO’s statistical products, including this _Yearbook_ , adhere closely to this definition and the associated terminology. ## Mining and quarrying

It is important to note that the everyday or specialized use of the term _industry_ may deviate from this statistical definition. For instance, the term is often used narrowly to refer only to manufacturing activities, whereas in official statistics, manufacturing represents just one sector 

--- end of page.page_number=17 ---

_1 Introduction 5_ 

within industry. This narrower interpretation is common in economics and in the literature on industrialization and structural transformation, including in UNIDO. In the current version of the _Classification of Industrial Activities_ [6], the term _industrial statistics_ is not explicitly mentioned but falls under Domain 2 (economic statistics), Subdomain 2.3 (sectoral statistics). Within this framework, the four sectors listed in the box above partially overlap with Activities 20302 (energy), 20303 (mining, manufacturing, and construction), and 20399 (sectoral statistics not elsewhere classified). In official statistics, manufacturing is only one of four industrial sectors 

Given these variations, some fluidity in the use of the term _industry_ and related concepts should be expected. Finally, it is worth noting that construction (ISIC Rev. 4 section F) is not considered part of _industry_ as defined in official statistics. The definitions used here are based on the fourth revision of the ISIC, issued in 2008 [5]. A fifth revision, together with its implementation plan, has been endorsed by the United Nations (UN) Statistical Commission [7; 8]. While the new revision does not alter the scope of industrial statistics, it enhances the classification’s relevance by better reflecting the structure of the contemporary global economy, including at a more detailed activity level. Relevant updates for industrial statistics will be reflected in future UNIDO statistical products, in line with their implementation by NSOs worldwide. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**

The fifth revision of the ISIC was globally endorsed in 2023–2024 

## **1.3 Why is industry important?** 

In 2024, industry accounted for 20.9 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) globally, reflecting its central role in the world economy. Within industry, manufacturing remained the dominant sector, generating 78.7 per cent of total industrial value added, while the combined mining and utilities sector contributed the remaining share [9]. Manufacturing continues to stand out as one of the most dynamic components of economic activity, both because of its scale and its strong linkages with other sectors.


Final chunk number 282, content : 
Historically, industrialization has been the engine of economic progress, driven by manufacturing’s unique capacity to foster technological advancement, productivity growth, and innovation. Economies of scale are typically easier to achieve in manufacturing than in other sectors, allowing productivity gains to spread more broadly. As manufacturing expands, its cross-sectoral linkages stimulate activity in services, infrastructure, and agriculture, helping to lift the entire economy. Structural change towards higher value-added manufacturing has

long been recognized as the main pathway to higher income levels and sustainable livelihoods [10; 11]. The role of industry extends far beyond economic growth and productivity. Industrialization contributes directly and indirectly to the economic, social, and environmental pillars of the SDGs. By generating employment, improving living standards, and driving technological innovation, including advances in green production and circular economy practices, industry supports progress across multiple Goals (Figure 1.1). Research shows that manufacturing has accounted for roughly two-thirds of all country-level growth episodes over the past five decades, has led patenting activity related to frontier technologies and green innovation, and exhibits one of the strongest employment multiplier effects across sectors [10]. Given these broad spillover effects, the contribution of industry to sustainable development must be assessed beyond economic growth alone. Policies should capture industry’s wider impacts on social inclusion, innovation, and environmental sustainability, to fully realize its potential contribution to these areas [12; 13]. ## **2.1 Recent trends in industrial sectors** 

This chapter examines the latest global developments shaping the industrial landscape. As outlined in Section 1.2, the term _industry_ encompasses mining, manufacturing, and utilities activities. The following analysis offers a comprehensive overview of recent trends across these sectors from a comparative perspective and presents UNIDO’s 2025 global growth forecasts. In addition, it reviews progress in key indicators related to SDG 9 and industrial competitiveness, highlighting how countries and regions are adapting to shifting economic and technological conditions. A more detailed analysis of manufacturing performance is provided in Chapter 3, while Chapter 4 explores the dynamics of the mining and utilities sectors. ## **2.1.1 Annual industrial production** 

Industrial sectors accounted for 20.9 per cent of world GDP in 2024, equivalent to 20.1 trillion USD at constant 2015 prices. Manufacturing was the largest industrial sector, representing 78.7 per cent of total industry in 2024, while the combined mining and utilities sector was responsible for the remaining 21.3 per cent. **==> picture [64 x 64] intentionally omitted <==**

In 2024, manufacturing and mining and utilities together accounted for more than one fifth of global economic activity 

The predominance of manufacturing is evident across most regions, though with significant variation. As illustrated in Figure 2.1, in terms of value added, manufacturing was the main industrial sector in Europe (with 82.8 per cent of industry value added in 2024), Asia (81.1 per cent), Northern America (75.1 per cent), Latin America and the Caribbean (71.4 per cent), Sub-Saharan Africa (56.0 per cent), and Northern Africa (55.8 per cent). Oceania was the only region where mining and utilities prevailed, with manufacturing accounting for just 42.4 per cent of industry value added. While industrial activity rebounded strongly following the COVID-19 crisis, growth has remained moderate. Figure 2.2 shows that industry has consistently grown at a slower pace than GDP since 2022. In 2024, global industry value added (IVA) rose by 2.5 per cent, below the 2.8 per cent increase in global GDP. This gap is expected to persist, though to narrow, in 2025. Middle-income industrial economies were the most dynamic country group in 2024, recording an annual industrial growth rate approaching 4 per cent, followed by middle-income industrializing economies with growth of 3.5 per cent. In contrast, industrial growth in high-income economies remained close to 1 per cent in 2024 and is expected to continue at this subdued pace in 2025. Globally, industry value added grew by **2.5%** in 2024

## **2.1.2 Quarterly industrial production** 

In addition to the information based on annual national accounts data described above, UNIDO also compiles sub-annual IIPs covering all industrial sectors: mining and quarrying; manufacturing; electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply; and water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities. Owing to their higher frequency, the IIPs enable a more detailed and timely analysis of sectoral trends and current performance. Annex C summarizes the main characteristics and methodological aspects of these indices.

## **2.2 SDG 9** 

Industrialization is central to SDG 9, which seeks to build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization, and foster innovation. Its role and outcomes, however, vary across development stages. In lower-income economies, industrialization marks a structural shift from traditional agriculture or low-value-added activities toward higher productivity in modern industry.


Final chunk number 315, content : 
In higher-income economies, it involves diversification, technological upgrading, and specialization in innovation-driven sectors. A unifying feature across all contexts is the transition toward environmentally sustainable manufacturing practices. Industrialization drives productivity growth, job creation, and improved living standards, thereby contributing to poverty reduction and overall economic resilience [11]. Moreover, it supports broader SDG objectives by promoting innovation, technological progress, and green production and consumption. Evidence shows that, over the past five decades, the manufacturing sector has accounted for about two-thirds of global growth episodes, stimulated frontier and green technology development, and generated strong employment multipliers [10]. Given these wide-ranging impacts, assessing industrial performance requires going beyond traditional measures of economic growth to include broader dimensions of sustainable development when designing effective industrial policies. The industry-related targets of SDG 9 aim to capture these different dimensions and measure progress through internationally–agreed indicators. ## **2.2.1 SDG 9.2** 

Global manufacturing has maintained a steady growth in recent decades, only interrupted by the global financial crisis in 2008–2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The left-side panel of Figure 2.7 shows that global MVA per capita reached an all-time high in 2024, at 1,937 USD in constant 2015 prices. This represents an increase of 17.4 per cent with respect to 2015. However, as shown in the right-hand panel of Figure 2.7, the contribution of manufacturing to total economic activity has slowed in recent years. After declining to 15.1 per cent in 2009, the share of MVA in GDP gradually recovered, peaking at 16.8 per cent in 2021. However, it has slightly declined since then, reaching 16.5 per cent in 2023, where it is projected to remain in 2024 according to UNIDO estimates. Despite some gains, the dynamism seen before the global financial crisis has not been regained, and the current trajectory reflects a period of relative stagnation. **==> picture [109 x 109] intentionally omitted <==**

In addition to value added, SDG target 9.2 also emphasizes employment. The second panel of Figure 2.7 presents the share of manufacturing in total global employment. After peaking at 14.6 per cent in 2012, manufacturing employment has followed a steadily declining trend, falling to 14.1 per cent in 2023, the latest year with complete data. This pattern of output growth without commensurate job creation raises concerns regarding the sustained capacity of manufacturing to generate employment and support livelihoods. Regionally, trends in the proportion of manufacturing in GDP (9.2.1a) and in total employment (9.2.2) since the start of the century have varied considerably, as shown in Figure 2.8. Among all regions, only Asia and Oceania shows simultaneous growth in both indicators, suggesting a sustained path of industrialization. By 2023, this region achieved the world’s highest shares in both value added and employment, positioning it as a leader in industrial development. In contrast, Latin America and the Caribbean as well as Northern America and Europe are experiencing deindustrialization, reflected in declining shares of manufacturing in both GDP and employment. Africa presents a more nuanced picture: while the manufacturing share in GDP is falling, the share in employment is rising, indicating shifts in production and labour dynamics in this region. SDG target 9.3 underscores the importance of small-scale enterprises, particularly those operating in the manufacturing sector, and their crucial role in fostering inclusive economic development. These enterprises typically operate with limited capital, rely heavily on local resources, and are a major source of employment in low- and middleincome economies. They also play a pivotal role in promoting entrepreneurship and creating job opportunities for women, youth, and vulnerable groups, helping to reduce socioeconomic disparities. SDG target 9.3 includes two indicators: one measuring the share of MVA generated by small-scale enterprises (9.3.1), and another tracking their access to financial services (9.3.2). Due to a lack of consistent official data for indicator 9.3.2, results from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys are currently used as proxy values. For indicator 9.3.1, UNIDO compiles official data on MVA by firm size. A key challenge in producing internationally comparable data lies in the wide variation of national size classifications. Countries differ not only in the thresholds they apply, such as number of employees, turnover, or assets, but also in how these categories are defined and integrated into national legal and policy frameworks. These classifications often determine business

Since few economies report data following the international definition of small-scale enterprises, fewer than 20 employees, as per international guidelines [4], the indicator remains geographically and temporally limited. To address this, starting in 2025, UNIDO began collecting two separate series for indicator 9.3.1, as described in the box below. ## **Dual reporting of SDG 9.3.1** 

With the aim of increasing data availability, UNIDO started collecting two separate data series for indicator 9.3.1 in 2025. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Small firms play a pivotal role in creating job opportunities for woman, youth, and vulnerable groups 

- **9.3.1a** : Indicator based on UNIDO’s standardized international classification of small-scale enterprises, ensuring crosscountry comparability and maintaining continuity with previously reported data. - **9.3.1b** : Indicator based on national definitions of small-scale enterprises to broaden country coverage, but with limited comparability across countries. This dual-reporting approach was endorsed by the Inter-agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators (IAEG-SDGs) and the UN Statistical Commission as part of the 2025 Comprehensive Review. Despite the option to use national classifications, only seven additional countries were included under the expanded reporting framework (i.e. 9.3.1b) in 2025. However, as this is the first year of implementation, it is expected that adoption will gain momentum over time. Figure 2.9 presents recent trends for indicator 9.3.1a among economies with available data for both 2015 and 2022. It conveys a rather sobering picture: from 2015 to 2022, the share of small-scale industries in total MVA has either stagnated or declined in most economies. Malta recorded the most significant drop, with a decrease of 18.3 percentage points. Only Georgia and Romania registered increases above 2 percentage points in the same period, rising by 5.1 and 2.4 percentage points, respectively. Overall, the share of small-scale industries in manufacturing remains under 20 per cent across all countries, with the sole exception of Cyprus, where it reached 32.2 per cent in 2022, despite declining by 2.2 percentage points since 2015.

After maintaining CO2 emissions from fuel combustion below 6 gigatonnes (Gt) for five consecutive years, the manufacturing sector surpassed this threshold in 2021, largely due to the post-pandemic rebound. However, emissions declined again in 2022, falling just slightly below the 6 Gt mark to 5.98 Gt. Thereby, manufacturing accounted for 17.5 per cent of total CO2 emissions from fuel combustion in 2022, a decrease of 0.35 percentage points from the previous year. The CO2 emission intensity of global manufacturing declined from 0.49 kg per USD in 2015 to 0.39 kg per USD in 2022, marking the first time it has fallen below the 0.40 threshold. The statistical evidence therefore corroborates that global progress towards SDG target 9.4 has taken place. Figure 2.11 disaggregates the trends in indicator 9.4.1, the CO2 emission intensity of manufacturing, since the adoption of the SDGs in 2015. It shows that all country groups have achieved reductions, albeit to varying degrees. China recorded the largest decline, with a 36.6 per cent drop from 0.90 kg per USD in 2015 to 0.57 kg per USD in 2022. This substantial reduction is largely attributable to a shift toward renewable energy sources, particularly wind and solar photovoltaics, as well as energy efficiency improvements across its manufacturing sector. Furthermore, China’s major investments in clean energy technologies have contributed to lowering global costs, thereby accelerating the global transition to

## **2.2.4 SDG 9.b** 

Structural change entails not only a redistribution of economic activity from agriculture to industry, but also a shift towards higher-value added, higher-productivity sectors. In manufacturing, this is generally associated with an increasing share of innovation-focused industries that rely on advanced technologies and that operate with sophisticated digital production processes. A transition towards these sectors would lead to a more diversified, resilient, and stable economy [23], a continuous support for innovation and knowledge creation, an upgrade in skills and jobs, and a progression to green growth, as these activities are generally less energy and emissions intensive [24]. Given manufacturing’s potential for knowledge transmission and economic spillover, the reliance on technology and innovation in manufacturing could have significant benefits throughout the economy [25]. This is the subject of SDG target 9.b, which highlights the role of technology development, research, and innovation, and their relevance for promoting industrial diversification and boosting value addition. The target is monitored through indicator 9.b.1, which measures the contribution of medium-high and high technology (MHT) industries to total MVA. Manufacturing industries are grouped by their level of technological intensity according to a taxonomy developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which is based on average research and development (R&D) expenditure by sector [26; 27]. The classification is presented in Annex C. Globally, the share of MHT industries in total manufacturing has remained relatively stable in recent years, fluctuating within a narrow range. As shown in Figure 2.12, the share declined steadily between 2000 and 2009, reaching a low of 43.9 per cent.[INFO-CIRCLE] This trend reversed after 2009, with the indicator rising to 45.1 per cent by 2018. It then dipped slightly to 44.7 per cent in 2019 and remained at that level during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the sector’s resilience. In 2021, however, the share dropped to 43.8 per cent, its second-lowest level since the start of the century, before quickly recovering to 44.5 per cent in 2022. Nonetheless, this still represents a decline of 0.49 percentage points compared to 2015. Figure 2.13 shows that only high-income industrial economies registered an increase in the share of MHT industries in total manufacturing, albeit a modest rise of 0.54 percentage points. This group also maintains the highest overall share, fluctuating around 50 per cent, significantly ahead of other country groups. They are followed by middle-income industrial economies, which have largely stagnated since 2015. In contrast, high-income industrializing economies experienced the most substantial decline, with a drop

Middle-income industrializing and low-income economies saw similar levels of decline over the same period, though the latter continued to lag significantly behind all other groups in this indicator. ## **2.2.5 Overall performance towards SDG 9 industry targets** 

The UNIDO SDG 9 Industry Index is a composite measure of the industryrelated indicators considered in SDG 9. It was introduced as a tool for supporting policymakers and other users in measuring a country’s overall progress towards industrialization and evaluating performance along the different dimensions of industrial development, as defined in the 2030 Agenda. The Index encompasses the SDG 9 targets directly related to industrialization. These targets are monitored through eight indicators, referring to all three dimensions of inclusive and sustainable industrial development: economic (9.2.1a, 9.2.1b, 9.3.1a, 9.3.1b, 9.3.2, and 9.b.1), social (9.2.2), and environmental (9.4.1). However, due to insufficient data coverage across countries and time, SDG indicators 9.3.1 and 9.3.2 ( _Proportion of small-scale industries in total industry value added_ and _Proportion of small-scale industries with a loan or line of credit_ ) are excluded. The Index is therefore constructed from the other five indicators. Future editions may include these omitted indicators if data availability improves, offering a more comprehensive assessment of inclusive industrial development. The Index ranges from zero to one, with higher values reflecting better performance. A brief explanation of the Index and its methodological background can be found in Annex C, while a comprehensive coverage is provided in [28; 29]. The current edition of the SDG 9 Industry Index benchmarks 138 economies based on 2022 data. Although some indicators are available for more recent years, the Index requires data for all five indicators, which is only possible up to 2022. Figure 2.14 presents the ranking of the top ten economies based on the SDG 9 Industry Index. Compared to 2021, the ranking in 2022 is marked by a position exchange between Ireland and the Republic of Korea, as well as between Japan and Czechia. The Republic of Korea climbed from the third position to the second, while Ireland fell from the second to the third position. Japan dropped from the seventh to the eighth position, while Czechia moved from the eighth to the seventh. China entered the top ten for the first time, climbing from 11[th] to 10[th] place. Since the launch of the SDGs in 2015, the top four economies have remained consistent, comprising Taiwan Province of China, the Republic of Korea, Ireland, and Germany. ## **2.3 Competitive industrial performance** 

UNIDO has tracked industrial competitiveness through the CIP Index for more than two decades. This Index assesses how effectively an economy’s manufacturing sector produces and sells goods in domestic and international markets while advancing technologically. A core feature of the CIP Index is its comparative nature: each economy’s performance is evaluated relative to all other economies, thereby embedding a true measure of global industrial competitiveness.[INFO-CIRCLE] 

INFO-CIRCLE See [30; 31; 32; 33] for a detailed description of the CIP Index’s methodology and historical results.


Final chunk number 317, content : 
A brief overview of the Index’s dimensions and the calculation of the composite index is presented in Annex C. The complete dataset is available in [34]. The Index enables cross-country comparisons of industrial competitiveness and highlights key industrial development challenges. It is important to note, however, that the CIP Index focuses exclusively on economic competitiveness. The CIP Index is constructed using statistical indicators across three dimensions: 

1. Capacity to produce and export manufactured goods; 

2. Technological deepening and upgrading; 

3. World impact. In its latest update, the Index covers 153 economies from 1990 to 2023. The overall CIP Index score ranges from zero to one, with higher scores indicating stronger industrial competitiveness. In practice, the observed range is narrower, as no country excels simultaneously across all dimensions. This section presents key findings from the most recent update of the CIP Index. The latest scores and global rankings for all economies are presented in Annex A. ## Three dimensions of the CIP Index

## **2.3.1 Global results** 

Figure 2.16 presents the economies with the most competitive manufacturing sector according to the CIP Index. Germany, China, and Ireland currently hold the top three positions. These economies have ranked among the three global leaders since 1990, 2014, and 2020, respectively. While the composition of the top 10 remained unchanged between 2022 and 2023, slight shifts occurred in the relative rankings. China, Taiwan Province fell one position to sixth place, exchanging ranks with the United States of America, which moved up to fifth place. Japan likewise dropped one position to eighth, continuing its gradual decline since it ranked as the world’s most competitive industrial economy in 1994. Switzerland, by contrast, improved its position, rising from eighth to seventh rank. The full results reveal a strong correlation between income level and industrial competitiveness. The top ten economies in the CIP Index ranking are almost exclusively high-income economies. China, a

## **2.3.3 Regional competitiveness** 

Industrial competitiveness also varies considerably across regions. Figure 2.20 presents the average CIP Index ranking by geographical region. The joint region of Northern America and Europe records the highest level of competitiveness, with an average rank of tenth in 2023. Notably, 14 economies from this region appear among the top 20 of the global CIP ranking. Close behind, Asia and Oceania achieves an average position of 12[th] , led by China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Taiwan Province of China. Since 2010, this region has climbed three positions on average and now places five economies among the world’s top 20. By contrast, Latin America and the Caribbean recorded an average rank of 43[rd] in 2023, four positions lower than in 2010. Africa shows the steepest decline, dropping nine positions over the same period and currently averaging 88[th] place. The results by CIP dimensions are summarized in Figure 2.21. Asia and Oceania leads in the second and third pillars of the Index, closely followed by Northern America and Europe. However, the latter is the world’s best performing region in the first dimension. Latin America and the Caribbean is relatively well placed in the _World impact_ dimension, driven by the presence of major manufacturers, such as Brazil and Mexico, but remains at a considerable distance from the two leading regions in the other two dimensions. Africa faces the greatest challenges, ranking last among world regions across all three dimensions of industrial competitiveness. **==> picture [136 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Figure 2.22 provides a more granular overview of industrial competitiveness, enabling a detailed assessment of current performance and long-term trends across subregions. Within Africa, Southern and Northern Africa are the strongest performers, although both have slipped in the global ranking in recent years, particularly the former subregion. Central Africa is the only African subregion that registered an improvement between 2010 and 2023, though the gain was marginal and from a low starting point. In Asia and Oceania, Eastern Asia is not only the highest-performing subregion within the region but also the strongest worldwide. It currently holds an average rank of third, driven by the robust competitiveness of China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Taiwan Province of China. South-Eastern Asia follows, reaching an average of 32[nd] in 2023 and benefiting from solid results in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Viet Nam, and others. With the exception of Oceania, all subregions in Asia and Oceania improved their ranking between 2010 and 2023. In Latin America and the Caribbean, two of the three subregions experienced declines in the CIP ranking. South America fell by 10 positions between 2010 and 2023, reaching a rank of 54[th] , while the Caribbean dropped from 88[th] to 100[th] over the same period. Central America is the best-performing subregion, although its progress has stalled; it gained only one position between 2010 and 2023, reaching a rank of 25[th] . Taken together, these trends suggest that Latin America and the Caribbean may be undergoing a deindustrialization process. **==> picture [136 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

The CIP Index has served as a global benchmark for measuring countries’ industrial competitiveness for over two decades. However, evolving industrial paradigms and the growing need to integrate inclusiveness and sustainability have prompted a comprehensive revision of the Index. UNIDO is currently developing a revamped CIP Index grounded in an enhanced conceptual framework, stronger statistical robustness, and greater policy relevance. The updated Index, scheduled for launch in mid-2026, will provide policymakers with a broader and more actionable tool for evaluating and advancing sustainable industrial competitiveness. **==> picture [136 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

## **3.1 Current trends and distribution of world manufacturing** 

This chapter examines both the short- and long-term developments shaping the manufacturing sector, with particular attention to their potential influence on the global distribution and evolution of manufacturing activity. It explores how recent shifts in production patterns, technology adoption, and market integration may redefine the geography of industrial output worldwide. A more granular breakdown of production across individual industries is presented in Section 3.2, providing deeper insight into sectoral dynamics. The subsequent four sections expand the analysis to encompass a range of complementary indicators, such as international trade performance, employment trends, productivity levels, gender equality dimensions and environmental implications, offering a broader view of the sector’s overall transformation. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**

Global manufacturing value added increased by **2.9%** in 2024 

## **3.1.1 Annual manufacturing production** 

Globally, the manufacturing sector grew by 2.9 per cent in terms of value added in 2024. Although this marks a gradual acceleration compared with the 1.6 per cent recorded in 2023, it continues the pattern of subdued expansion in the sector, remaining below pre-pandemic growth levels. This outcome reflects the impact of moderating global economic growth and persistent headwinds, including armed conflicts, geopolitical instability, and elevated energy and commodity prices. The effects of recent trade restrictions and tariff disputes are not yet captured in these annual figures but will be discussed later in this section based on quarterly IIP data. Table 3.1 presents the latest MVA growth rates for selected country groups and regions, illustrating that manufacturing performance varied considerably across the world. Among the UNIDO groups by industrial development, middle-income industrial economies recorded the strongest performance in 2024. This was partly driven by China’s robust growth rate of 4.9 per cent, while the remaining economies in this group expanded at a combined rate closer to the world average, around 3.2 per cent. This solid performance is expected to continue in 2025. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**

Manufacturing in middle-income economies achieved higher growth relative to other groups 

By contrast, manufacturing in low-income economies has grown at a more modest pace in recent years, reaching only 2.0 per cent in 2024, though it is projected to accelerate significantly in 2025. High-income industrial economies, meanwhile, recovered from the decline in MVA observed in 2023 but registered only 1.2 per cent growth in 2024, the

_3 Spotlight on manufacturing 47_ 

## **3.1.2 Quarterly manufacturing production** 

In addition to the yearly statistics presented above, the remainder of this section draws on seasonally-adjusted IIPs on a quarterly basis to provide a more up-to-date view of trends in the manufacturing sector. The IIP is a key indicator for monitoring economic activity in a timely and consistent manner, given its broad availability across countries. The main features of this index are summarized in Annex C. Figure 3.4 traces the long-term evolution of global manufacturing production. Beyond major setbacks during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020–2021, the sector experienced only temporary slowdowns followed by strong recoveries, underscoring its overall resilience. The latest data indicate a solid quarter-on-quarter increase of 1.0 per cent in the second quarter of 2025, maintaining the positive quarterly growth trend since mid-2022. This steady improvement, particularly in recent periods, can be partly explained by increased defence spending and military equipment production across major economies. Overall, global manufacturing has demonstrated remarkable momentum despite tariff escalation, inflation, supply chain disruptions, and geopolitical instability. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**
