## **Methodological explanation** 

This section focuses on the contribution of different industrial activities to total manufacturing. It presents industry-level information according to technological intensity and more detailed ISIC Rev. 4 levels. It also highlights evolving trends among leading manufacturers within selected country groups, alongside the transformations observed over the past two decades. The growing importance of MHT industries,[INFO-CIRCLE] already highlighted in previous editions of this _Yearbook_ , persisted in 2023, according to the most recent UNIDO estimations at constant prices. The trend observed in industrial economies has played a pivotal role in reinforcing the global dominance of MHT sectors. In these economies, MHT industries have consistently outpaced other manufacturing sectors in terms of their share in MVA, as illustrated in Figure 3.8. Their share rose from 42.5 per cent in 2000 to 53.9 per cent in 2023, corresponding to a compound average annual growth rate of approximately 1.0 percentage point over the full period. Notably, the pace of growth has intensified in recent years: between 2020 and 2023, the share increased from 51.1 per cent to 53.9 per cent, implying an average annual growth rate of 1.8 percentage points, nearly double the long-term average. This acceleration highlights the faster recovery of MHT industries following the COVID-19 pandemic, benefitting from resilient global demand in health-related products, strong investment in innovation, and the 

The figures presented throughout Section 3.2 are based on value added, compiled using base weights for the reference year 2015. These are mainly calculated using data from UNIDO’s Industrial Statistics Databases (INDSTAT). However, value-added figures are only available in current prices. The annual IIP is used to present trends over time, free from currency and price variations. INFO-CIRCLE The composition of these categories in the sense of the ISIC classification of economic activities is presented in the Annex E.2. --- end of page.page_number=65 ---

Industries such as pharmaceuticals, electronics and machinery have increasingly displaced traditional manufacturing activities and reinforced their upward trajectory within industrial countries. In comparison, the picture for industrializing economies remains markedly different. Despite some growth in MHT industries reflecting an increase in the proportion from 25.9 per cent in 2000 to 29.3 per cent in 2010, their share has remained relatively modest and stagnant from 2011 onward. In 2023, other manufacturing industries still dominate, accounting for nearly 70 per cent of MVA. This reflects earlier stages of structural transformation, with continued reliance on labour-intensive and resource-based manufacturing. Factors such as limited access to advanced technologies, lower R&D capacity, and dependence on global value chains for intermediate goods may be constraining the expansion of MHT sectors. This divergence is not unexpected, given that UNIDO‘s classification of countries as ’industrial’ or ‘industrializing’ is partly based on the share of MHT industries in their manufacturing structure [38]. In essence, economies are considered ‘industrial’ because they have successfully transitioned towards more technology-intensive production. When analysed by income group, the pattern remains consistent and reinforces the structural narrative. High-income economies had already achieved MHT predominance around 2015, with MHT industries accounting for 53.6 per cent of MVA in 2023. Middle-income economies are converging rapidly,

4 division 21), and motor vehicles (ISIC Rev. 4 division 29) dominate its profile, as shown in Figure 3.13, each commanding significant shares of global output and reflecting decades of investment in innovation and advanced production systems. The EU’s technological depth, combined with a large and affluent internal market of approximately 450 million people, positions it at the forefront of global value chains. 4 division 11), leather goods (ISIC Rev. 4 division 15), and paper products (ISIC Rev. 4 division 17) remain central pillars, while MHT industries occupy only a modest share of its manufacturing structure. Although chemicals (ISIC Rev. 4 division 20) and motor vehicles (ISIC Rev. 4 division 29) show some presence, their global footprint is limited, underscoring the scope for structural upgrading. With a population of around 300 million, MERCOSUR offers scale and resource advantages (see also Section 4.2), yet its per-capita industrial output lags far behind that of the EU, particularly in technology-driven sectors. **==> picture [136 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

The EU and MERCOSUR together represent 18.6% of the world’s population, and account for 17.4% of global MVA in 2023 

The proposed EU–MERCOSUR partnership agreement may serve as a catalyst for a deeper industrial transformation. If ratified, the agreement could reduce tariffs, harmonize standards, and facilitate technology transfer, thereby creating opportunities for MERCOSUR to diversify beyond resource-based production and integrate more deeply into global supply chains. Brazil, as the largest economy in MERCOSUR and a key member of the BRICS grouping, appears uniquely positioned to leverage its dual connectivity by drawing on both its regional leadership and global partnerships to attract investment and promote industrial upgrading. In a global context increasingly shaped by shifting trade alliances and rising protectionism, enhanced cooperation between MERCOSUR and the EU holds the potential to play a transformative role in reshaping industrial dynamics across the Atlantic. Such collaboration could accelerate the transition towards more inclusive, innovation-led, and technology-intensive models of growth.

_3 Spotlight on manufacturing 61_ 

## **3.3 The manufacturing sector trade** 

This section examines various aspects of manufacturing trade. While both exports and imports will be analysed, the focus will remain on exports to maintain consistency with earlier discussions on manufacturing production, as domestic manufacturing output is closely linked to export performance. The first part of this section presents the latest developments on global manufacturing trade, drawing from both annual and quarterly data. Thereafter, an analysis of the structure of global manufacturing trade and the trade balance across country groups and regions will be presented. Annex C summarizes the key features of both annual and sub-annual manufacturing trade data. ## INDUSTRY **Manufacturing trade data** 

Annual trade data with full country coverage can be found in the Annual Manufacturing Trade Database [40], while sub-annual trade data with higher frequency, but lower data coverage, can be found in the Monthly Manufacturing Trade Database [41], both accessible from the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3]. ## **3.3.1 Global, regional, and country-level performance** 

The latest annual growth rates of exports of manufactured and nonmanufactured goods are presented in Figure 3.14.[INFO-CIRCLE] Overall, nonmanufactured goods have exhibited greater volatility compared to manufactured goods. In 2024, both categories posted modest growth, following declines of varying magnitude in the previous year that offset the exceptional gains seen in previous years. Although the downturn and subsequent recovery of exports during the COVID-19 pandemic were smoother than, for instance, the trends observed in manufacturing production (see Section 3.1.2), it is worth noting that global exports had already begun to decline since 2019. Seasonally adjusted sub-annual manufacturing trade data provide a more up-to-date and granular view of trade dynamics but entail a trade-off in terms of country and time coverage. Multiple factors have contributed to the growing uncertainty in global trade since early 2025. The data available at the time of writing this _Yearbook_ extend up to June 2025 and already capture some of the initial effects of this uncertainty on manufacturing trade. In April 2025, the United States of America announced a series of protectionist measures targeting most countries, prompting retaliatory actions, renewed negotiations, delays in investment decisions, measures to promote diversification in products and trade partners, and shifts in ongoing trade dynamics. At the same time, a depreciation of the United States dollar against other major currencies altered relative export competitiveness, strengthening that of the United States of America while weakening that of many other economies. These developments have compounded preexisting challenges to global trade, including rising geopolitical tensions, vulnerabilities in global shipping, rapid technological change, and environmental pressures. Figure 3.16 illustrates the quarterly trajectory of world manufacturing exports since early 2022. In the second quarter of 2025, exports expanded robustly by 4.1 per cent, following a 1.3 per cent increase in the previous quarter. The strong expansion observed in the first half of the year may partly reflect trade diversion and front-loading of shipments in anticipation of expected trade measures. In the second quarter of 2025, higher-technology exports rose by 4.4 per cent, while other manufactured goods grew by 3.0 per cent relative to the previous quarter. Since mid-2022, higher-technology exports have outperformed lower-technology goods, which saw subdued activity until early 2025. The sharp contraction at the end of 2022 mainly reflected China’s export downturn resulting from COVID-19 measures, an effect also visible in the production data (see Figure 3.4). Figure 3.17 provides further insights into the most recent quarterly developments, highlighting the effects of the newly introduced or announced tariff measures. China) recorded steadily rising manufacturing exports and imports, resulting in a largely balanced trade position over time, with high-income industrial economies gradually shifting towards a deficit in recent years. China’s manufacturing exports, by contrast, have grown far more rapidly than its imports, leading to a substantial and expanding manufacturing trade surplus. High‑income industrializing economies exhibited trade deficits of varying magnitude. Middle‑income industrializing and low‑income economies showed the largest manufacturing trade deficits relative to their overall trade values, with an increasing share attributable to higher-technology imports. Notably, the deficit of the low-income economies has widened significantly in recent years. Because of the large differences in the scale across country groups, Figure 3.23 applies different axis limits. For higher‑technology goods, the right-side panel of Figure 3.24 shows more balanced trade patterns across regions. ## **3.5 Gender and manufacturing** 

Women’s participation in manufacturing is a critical factor in advancing inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Despite progress in education and growing commitment to gender equality, structural barriers, unequal access to opportunities, and persistent gender norms continue to constrain women’s role in industry. Four out of ten people employed in the manufacturing sector worldwide are women.


Final chunk number 398, content : 
A share that has largely remained stable in recent years, underscoring persistent structural imbalances and limited progress towards gender inclusivity in the sector. Despite this relative stability at the global level, growth trends in female and male manufacturing employment have not always converged. Figure 3.31 highlights that during the 2010s, female employment growth generally lagged behind that of men. Both groups were equally affected by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, but female employment rebounded more strongly in 2021, rising by 3.5 per cent compared to 2.5 per cent for men. This momentum continued in 2022, before moderating in 2023, when male employment grew by 2.2 per cent, slightly outpacing the 2.0 per cent recorded for women. In addition, a more detailed analysis reveals heterogeneous trends across country groups. Figure 3.32 shows that the proportion of women in manufacturing employment has declined in both high-income and middle-income industrial economies. Notably, middle-income industrial economies remains the only country group where women form the majority of manufacturing employment, although their share fell from 53.4 per cent in 2000 to 50.3 in 2023. By contrast, women’s participation has increased in both middle-income industrializing and low-income economies, with the latter now exceeding the world average. Finally, in high-income industrializing economies, manufacturing employment is dominated by men, with women accounting for only one in ten positions. While recent years have seen a modest rebound in women’s manufacturing employment growth, this has not translated into improvements in the types of industries where they work. Women remain disproportionately concentrated in lower-productivity sectors, limiting the potential impact of any increase in participation. Figure 3.33 illustrates employment distribution across MHT and other manufacturing industries by sex, showing that women’s share in MHT industries lags behind that of men. In 2023, 23.1 per cent of men employed in manufacturing worked in an MHT industry, compared to only 15.6 per cent of women. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

## **3.6 Environmental impact of manufacturing** 

The manufacturing sector plays a major role in shaping the environmental footprint of economic activity. This is a critical consideration: although manufacturing is one of the key engines of sustained growth and a central pillar of many development strategies, it can also generate significant environmental pressures if adequate policies and safeguards are not in place. These impacts include direct and indirect greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from energy use; air and water pollution; intensive use of materials, particularly minerals, metals, and other natural resources; waste generation; and land-use pressures. This section provides a brief, non-exhaustive overview of some of these environmental effects. Previous editions of the _Yearbook_ have examined additional dimensions. As will be discussed later, however, the ability to undertake a comprehensive assessment remains limited by persistent data gaps and insufficiently harmonized environmental reporting. **==> picture [55 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Manufacturing plays a critical role in mitigating the environmental impact of overall economic activity 

Manufacturing is a significant contributor to global GHG emissions. This section presents recent data on CO2 emissions, the largest component of GHGs and explicitly referenced under SDG 9. As noted in Section 2.2, manufacturing accounted for about 17.5 per cent of global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion, about 6.0 Gt, in 2022, the latest year with data available. Although absolute emissions have remained relatively constant in recent years, they remain at or near historical peak levels. Three industries together were responsible for 67.3 per cent of manufacturing’s CO2 emissions in 2022: iron and steel, non-metallic minerals, and chemicals and petrochemicals. Their combined contribution to the sector’s total has increased over time, rising from 57.9 per cent in 2000. Figure 3.36 shows both the long-term trajectory of manufacturing CO2 emissions and the evolving distribution of emissions across these sectors. The iron and steel industry (ISIC Rev. 4 group 241 and class 2431), critical for infrastructure, construction, and automotive production, is the largest CO2 emitter in manufacturing. It accounted for 35.9 per cent of the sector’s total emissions in 2022, generating 2.1 Gt of CO2, a 1.0 per cent increase compared with 2021. While this section focuses primarily on CO2 emissions due to data availability, it is important to acknowledge the substantial role of other GHG, such as methane and nitrous oxide, both of which have far higher global warming potential. Methane, for instance, is 27-30 times more potent than CO2 over a 100-year timescale, while nitrous oxide is 273 times more potent [53]. These gases are often released during industrial processes and the production of chemicals, meaning that exclusive attention to CO2 provides only a partial view of manufacturing’s climate impact. Moreover, the environmental effects of manufacturing extend beyond GHG emissions. They include resource-intensive practices, such as excessive water use, pollution from industrial wastewater, large-scale extraction of materials, and significant land use. For example, the textile industry is a major consumer of water and chemicals, whereas the paper industry (ISIC Rev. 4 divisions 17 and 18) contributes to deforestation and water pollution. Transporting manufactured goods also contributes to the sector’s broader footprint, adding to GHG emissions and resource depletion. ## **4.1 Current trends and distribution of world mining and utilities** 

Although the mining and utilities sectors together account for only 4.5 per cent of global GDP, they exert an outsized influence on many areas of the economy that are strategically important or essential for daily life. For instance, these sectors encompass: 

- The extraction of minerals and metals, including critical minerals, that form the foundation of many manufacturing products; 

Mining and utilities are strategic sectors for economic growth, energy security, and social well-being 

- The extraction of oil, gas, and other energy-related resources; 

- The production and distribution of electricity and water, as well as the treatment of wastewater, relied upon daily by households and businesses; 

- Recycling and material recovery, which play a key role in mitigating the environmental impacts of production and consumption. Despite their strategic significance, statistical information on these sectors remains relatively limited. This is partly due to the fact that activity in each sector is typically concentrated among a small number of firms, which restricts data dissemination under statistical disclosure control (SDC) rules. As a result, substantial data gaps persist, and information is often available only in aggregated form rather than by individual sector. This chapter therefore draws on available information from national accounts, IIPs, and novel data sources to present an overview of the combined mining and utilities sectors. The first section examines the short- and long-term trends in global production, followed by a detailed analysis of the global output of mining commodities in Section 4.2. The final section discusses the main environmental challenges associated with these sectors. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Statistical disclosure control may pose challenges to the dissemination of disaggregated mining and utilities data

Figure 2.3 already compared the trajectories of broad industrial sectors, highlighting the generally weaker performance of the mining and utilities sectors relative to manufacturing in most, though not all, regions. Overall, the combined mining and utilities sector grew moderately by 1.0 per cent in 2024, marking a significant slowdown compared with 2023 and a return to the subdued trend observed in previous years. According to UNIDO estimates, output in this sector is expected to decelerate further to 0.82 per cent in 2025. ## **4.1.2 Quarterly production in mining and utilities** 

As noted earlier, UNIDO also compiles and publishes sub-annual IIP data, which enable a more detailed and timely analyses than those based on annual national accounts. These data encompass four industrial sectors: mining and quarrying (ISIC Rev. 4 section B), manufacturing (section C), electricity and related industries (section D), and water supply and related sectors (section E). Mining and electricity production indices are available for more than 100 economies, representing about 80 per cent of global mining and utilities value added, while data on water supply and other sectors included in ISIC Rev. 4 section E cover around 60 economies. Due to this limited availability of quarterly data as well as insufficient coverage for calculating country group and regional aggregates, this section is excluded from the analysis. Annex C summarizes the main characteristics and methodological aspects of these indices. Recent developments in the mining and electricity sectors are illustrated in Figure 4.3. Global mining and quarrying activities have followed a volatile trajectory, registering only a modest production increase of 2.4 per cent in cumulative terms since the first quarter of 2022, the first year free from most pandemic-related disruptions. Production levels in this sector have remained relatively flat across both industrial and industrializing economies. Recent quarterly data indicate moderate growth of 0.73 per cent in industrial economies, while output in industrializing economies recorded a slight short-term decline. Given the dominant share of industrial economies in global mining output, the global growth rate largely reflects their recent performance and longer-term growth trends. Global initiatives aimed at reducing the environmental impact of mining activities, as discussed in Section 4.3, will likely contribute to increased instability in the sector’s prospects. At the same time, advances in technologies related to energy, batteries, machinery, and transportation may stimulate demand for minerals and metals, potentially leading to higher production levels in the sector. In contrast, the production of electricity and other utilities classified under ISIC Rev. 4 section D exhibited stronger global momentum, increasing by 6.5 per cent in cumulative terms since early 2022. When disaggregated by country group, industrializing economies recorded a steady and sustained expansion, with electricity rising by more than 17 per cent over the past ten quarters. Conversely, industrial economies experienced a pronounced slowdown in recent years. In the most recent quarter, electricity output in industrializing economies continued to expand robustly by 1.1 per cent, while it declined by 0.81 per cent in industrial economies. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**

## **4.2 Structure and transformation of mining and utilities industries** 

In previous editions of this Yearbook [37; 56; 15], the transformation of mining and utilities sectors has been analysed through the lens of structural business statistics (SBS), focusing on value added, employment, and investment by activity classification according to ISIC (e.g. ISIC Rev. 4 sections B, D, and E).


Final chunk number 434, content : 
While this approach provides essential insights into the economic structure, performance and transformation of these sectors, it often cannot reveal the underlying dynamics of specific mineral commodities that are increasingly shaping global industrial development. In response to the growing importance of critical raw materials, strategic resource dependencies, and increasing energy demand, this section introduces a product-level perspective. Drawing on information published by World Mining Data (WMD) [54], the analysis shifts focus from aggregated industry indicators to monetary values and physical production volumes of individual mineral commodities. This approach enables a more granular understanding of global mining trends and a better alignment with resource security and sustainability topics. The emphasis on product-level data complements previous analysis based on industrial activities, offering a multidimensional view of the transformation underway in the combined mining and utilities sector. Global production of mineral raw materials nearly doubled over the last four decades, underscoring the intensification of industrialization and the broadening of resource demand across sectors. According to WMD 2025 data [57], total world mining production (excluding bauxite)[INFO-CIRCLE] surged from 9.6 billion metric tons in 1985 to 19.2 billion metric tons in 2023, a 99.0 per cent increase. This represents a compound average annual growth rate of approximately 1.8 per cent, underscoring the resilience of extractive industries. Sustained expansion led to the highest recorded level of production in 2023, reaffirming the pivotal role of mineral commodities in the global economy. ## **Global production of mineral raw materials: regional shifts and emerging leaders (1985–2023)** 

In the past forty years, global minerals production has experienced significant regional shifts, as illustrated in Figure 4.6. Asia has emerged as the leading contributor, tripling its output to surpass 12.0 billion metric tons in 2023, which accounts for more than 60 per cent of global production. Concurrently, Northern America, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Oceania have overtaken Europe, indicating a notable reconfiguration of the global mining landscape. Indeed, Northern 

## **World Mining Data (WMD)** 

World Mining Data [54] is an internationally recognised annual statistical publication issued by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance. It provides comprehensive mineral production data from more than 160 countries, dating back to 1984, presented in both physical quantities and monetary terms. The data serves as a key resource for raw material policy analysis and commodity forecasting. The World Mining Congress (WMC) [55], founded in 1958 under UN auspices, plays a pivotal role in supporting data collection through dedicated questionnaires. National Committees of WMC member countries are among the primary contributors to the dataset, alongside other entities such as embassies and foreign trade representatives. Publicly accessible mining statistics from reputable sources, including the United States Geological Survey, are utilised for validation and

The composition of global minerals production can be broadly categorized into two groups: first, _mineral fuels_ , which include coal, petroleum (incl. natural gas liquids), and natural gas, and second, _non-fuel minerals_ . Although the term ‘non-fuel minerals’ is not used in the current version of WMD, it is nonetheless useful to employ such a category in further analysis to streamline findings. It encompasses iron and ferro-alloy metals like cobalt, nickel and titanium, non-ferrous metals such as aluminium, lithium, and rare earths, industrial minerals including phosphate rock and kaolin, and precious metals like gold and silver. **==> picture [62 x 44] intentionally omitted <==**

_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 99_ 

In terms of volume, production is overwhelmingly dominated by mineral fuels, as shown in figure 4.7. In 2023, these amounted to approximately 16.6 billion metric tons, exceeding the volume of non-fuel minerals, which were estimated at 2.6 billion tons, by more than sixfold. Over the past four decades, mineral fuels production has generally followed an upward trajectory, with occasional declines in specific years such as 1991–1993 , 1999, 2009, 2016, and 2020. These fluctuations are likely attributable to geopolitical developments, global economic downturns, or shifts in energy policy. By contrast, non-fuel minerals have shown more gradual growth, yet their production has more than doubled since the mid-1980s, reflecting sustained demand for raw materials essential to industrial production, infrastructure, and technological advancement. Although petroleum, among other products, is classified as fuel, it also serves as a feedstock for a wide array of manufactured products. However, the available data do not differentiate between its use as a fuel for energy generation and its use as a material input. A further methodological consideration of significance pertains to the standardization of units within the data illustrated. To present all production figures in metric tons, data compilers, such as the contributors to WMD, have applied conversion factors to harmonise disparate mineral raw materials [57, pp. 10–11]. This practice enhances comparability across commodities, yet it also introduces interpretative nuances, particularly when analysing energy-related materials. **==> picture [55 x 54] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Mineral fuels from 1985 to 2023** 

A comparison of mineral fuels over time makes it essential to distinguish between their physical volume—measured in metric tons after harmonisation—and their energy content, expressed in tons of coal equivalent (TCE). This dual metric reveals important shifts in the global energy landscape between 1985 and 2023, as shown in Figure 4.8. In 2023, steam coal was the dominant fuel by mass, with a production volume of approximately 7.0 billion metric tons, contributing 41.7 per cent to the global mineral fuels production. However, its energy content was significantly lower, amounting to 5.2 billion TCE or a share of 27.7 per cent. This discrepancy underscores steam coal’s relatively low energy density. Nonetheless, its share in both mass and energy terms increased compared to 1985, indicating a strong expansion in absolute output and a growing reliance on steam coal in certain regions. By contrast, petroleum, with a lower production volume in 2023 of 4.5 billion metric tons, yielded a much greater energy output of 6.5 billion TCE, thereby overtaking steam coal as the leading energy source when measured by calorific value. Interestingly, petroleum’s share in the fuel mix declined between 1985 and 2023 from 32.3 per cent to 27.0 per cent by mass and from 40.6 per cent to 34.9 per cent

Lithium, a non-ferrous metal among the highly concentrated commodities and known for its decisive role in energy storage solutions, has recorded the most pronounced production dynamics in most recent years with a growth rate of 160.2 per cent between 2019 and 2023. Australia led global production in 2023 with a share of 40.8 per cent, followed by Chile, which also anchors the strategically significant Lithium Triangle, a region comprising Chile, Argentina, and the Plurinational State of Bolivia. This dominance also raises broader questions about strategic dependencies and development opportunities—issues explored in greater depth by the United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD)’s recent analysis of critical minerals and their role in sustainable industrial transformation [59]. The global reliance on a few key producers poses risks for countries seeking secure access to essential inputs for clean energy and digital technologies. UNCTAD emphasizes the need for resource-rich developing economies, particularly in Africa, to move beyond raw material extraction by investing in domestic refining and processing capabilities. Such investments can drive industrial development and enable these countries to capture greater value from their mineral wealth. The current boom in critical minerals presents a unique opportunity for sustainable transformation, provided it is supported by inclusive governance, transparent contracting, and equitable benefit-sharing. _4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 108_ 

## **4.3 Environmental impact of mining and utilities** 

Mining and utilities generate significant environmental pressures, including land degradation, water and air pollution, and GHG emissions. As a result, environmental considerations have become increasingly central to policy discussions in these sectors. Similar to the environmental analysis of the manufacturing sector in Section 3.6, this section offers a non-exhaustive overview of the main environmental challenges linked to mining and utilities. The use of examples and isolated figures throughout reflects the limited availability of consistent, comprehensive data on these topics. Mining activities are a major driver of land degradation, contributing to deforestation, soil erosion, and water depletion. Gold and coal extraction together account for most mining-related forest loss globally, responsible for 36 per cent and 34 per cent, respectively. While the impacts of gold mining are distributed across several countries, coal-related deforestation is heavily concentrated in Indonesia, which accounted for 57 per cent of global tree-cover loss linked to coal extraction between 2000 and 2019 [60]. In Mongolia, an estimated 72 per cent of land is degraded due to desertification and mining activity, among other factors, with coal and gold extraction playing a significant role [61]. Moreover, mining frequently takes place in ecologically sensitive, biodiversity-rich areas, contributing to habitat fragmentation and species loss [62]. Mining operations also pose substantial risks of water and air pollution. Toxic by-products, waste rock, and tailings may contaminate water bodies for decades after mine closure. One study estimates that 23 million people globally live on floodplains contaminated with potentially harmful levels of toxic waste from current and historical metal-mining activities [63]. Air quality is also affected, as blasting, excavation, and ore transport release dust and fine particles containing heavy metals, which could increase the risk of respiratory and other health risks. As expected, electricity generation accounts for a significant share of global CO2 emissions, as it produces the energy required to power households and all other economic activities [64; 65]. But mining and water provision are also highly energy-intensive sectors. For example, examinations of drinking-water utilities have shown consistently high and rising energy intensity over time [66]. Mining also requires substantial energy, particularly during comminution and through the fuel used for mining and transport equipment. As easily accessible, high-quality mineral deposits become depleted and global demand for mining products grows, the sector’s overall energy consumption is expected to rise further [67; 68]. Mining and utilities have significant environmental impacts though comprehensive data remain limited 

Mining operations could exacerbate deforestation and land degradation including in ecologically sensitive areas 

Toxic waste contaminates air and water and poses health risks over decades 

Mining comprises energy-intensive activities and drives CO 2 emissions 

--- end of page.page_number=121 ---

_4 Mining and utilities in the spotlight 109_ 

Despite this high energy use, mining accounts for a relatively small share of global GHG emissions, between 4 and 7 per cent, because of its limited weight in the global economy.[INFO-CIRCLE] Moreover, only a small portion of these emissions results from electricity use; the majority stems from fugitive methane released during the extraction and handling of coal, oil, and natural gas [69]. These environmental pressures are likely to be intensified by climate change, including through greater water scarcity and more frequent extreme weather events. Addressing them will require improved land rehabilitation, decarbonization of operations, stronger watermanagement systems, and enhanced engagement with affected communities. Global policy frameworks increasingly target environmental sustainability in mining and utilities. Common instruments include environmental impact assessments, environmental taxes, green-finance incentives, and international cooperation to strengthen responsible practices. These measures seek to reduce habitat destruction, pollution, and emissions while advancing circular-economy approaches, technical capacity, and the transition to low-carbon energy sources. Countries are increasingly adopting policies that aim to balance economic priorities with environmental sustainability by setting carbonneutrality targets, promoting cleaner technologies, and reinforcing regulatory frameworks. However, gaps in implementation and enforcement remain widespread, including limited monitoring capacity. Expanded global data collection and strengthened statistical systems would further support these efforts, by enabling more robust assessment and monitoring of the ecological and health impacts associated with mining and utilities. _5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 111_ 

Industry remains central to development strategies around the world, but the context in which it operates is changing rapidly. As documented in the earlier chapters of the _Yearbook_ , global manufacturing continues to expand, but trends in output, trade, productivity, and emissions have become increasingly uneven across regions and country groups. Progress towards the industry-related SDG 9 targets is generally offtrack and unlikely to be achieved without a significant acceleration in the years remaining until 2030. At the same time, the sector is being reshaped by decarbonization pressures, digital technologies, shifting trade patterns, and changing labour markets. The thematic chapter of the _Yearbook 2024_ [37] reviewed the last three decades of industrial development, summarizing major trends observed globally and across regions and industries, and documenting the scale of the sector’s transformation. In contrast, this thematic chapter of the _Yearbook 2025_ takes a forwardlooking perspective instead. It focuses on the main changes expected to shape industrial development in the coming years, including the shift towards production that is greener, more digital, more globalized, but also increasingly exposed to shocks. On this basis, the chapter considers strategic responses aimed at ensuring that industrial statistics continue to support evidence-based policymaking for a sustainable industrial future. Furthermore, it critically assesses existing gaps and challenges in this area of official statistics, outlining how standards and frameworks may need to evolve to meet the broader and more complex data needs in the years ahead. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Industrial statistics are at a turning point, requiring modernization to remain fit for purpose 

Increasing demand for information that explains ongoing changes and not just historical performance 

Advancing the modernization of this field has become increasingly urgent. First, the rapid transformation of industrial activity risks rendering existing statistical standards obsolete or insufficient for future policy needs. Second, major international statistical frameworks have recently been revised, already incorporating many of the changes needed to better capture current and future economic structures. Together, these developments create a window of opportunity for developing the next generation of industrial statistics. The objective of the chapter is therefore to identify the key emerging policy themes and structural transformations that will shape future demand for industrial statistics, outlining the response required to ensure they remain relevant, consistent, and fit for purpose. This analysis is framed within the broader context of recent changes to international statistical frameworks and the expected areas of methodological work in the coming years. The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. The next section presents the major transformations reshaping industrial development and industrial policy, and examines how these shifts alter the demand for industrial statistics. Section 5.2 then discusses the statistical implications of these changes and discusses how existing and emerging

Section 5.3 turns to cross-cutting challenges in the compilation and production of industrial statistics, including response burden, data integration, data quality, and timeliness, and explores how future frameworks may mitigate these issues. The final section concludes by outlining the rationale and main directions for the forthcoming updates to the international industrial statistics standards, highlighting how these revisions can support the development of future-ready industrial statistics. ## **5.1 Transformations shaping the industrial landscape** 

A set of structural changes, operating on both the short- and long-term, are reshaping the trajectory of industrial development worldwide. Recent UNIDO publications have highlighted several cross-cutting, interrelated megatrends: the green and energy transition, digitalization and AI, reconfigured global value chains, demographic and labour market shifts, the growing importance of innovation and intangible assets, and an increasing emphasis on resilience to shocks [10; 70; 71]. Each of these transformations changes what needs to be measured and therefore has significant implications for industrial statistics. Three features are especially relevant from a statistical perspective. First, these changes are multidimensional and require information from domains that extend well beyond the traditional scope of industrial statistics. Second, they are interdependent, which calls for an integrated statistical system capable of linking information from multiple sources and domains. Third, they evolve over long periods but can shift abruptly in response to shocks. Monitoring them effectively therefore requires a combination of high-frequency indicators and long-term structural measures. The main megatrends are discussed below, with an emphasis on their implications for industrial statistics. ## **The green and energy transition: decarbonization, circularity, and resource efficiency** 

As discussed in Sections 2.2 and 3.6, manufacturing is a major source of global GHG emissions and resource use, accounting for 17.5 per cent of global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion. If emissions from industrial processes are added, this share increases further. Energyintensive industries, such as steel, cement, and chemicals, make particularly large contributions. A consistent identification of “green” manufacturing activities and products in industrial statistics has also become essential, including activities related to material recycling and product repurposing. Finally, the green transition requires statistical systems capable of linking industrial performance to broader environmental and social outcomes. This requires greater integration of industrial statistics with other sources such as energy balances, emission inventories, labour and household surveys, agricultural statistics, and land registers. ## **Digitalization and AI** 

Advanced digital production technologies, many of them powered by AI, are enabling new forms of smart, connected production, often referred to as Industry 4.0. These technologies are transforming how industrial firms produce, organize, and compete [25]. Evidence from recent research indicates that the adoption of digital technologies is associated with substantial productivity gains, and that investments in these technologies can help lagging firms catch up with the productivity frontier. However, the extent of those benefits depends heavily on the presence of key enabling conditions, particularly access to the required skills [75; 76; 77]. Digitalization and AI are not limited to production processes. They also change how industrial value is created and captured. A growing share of manufacturing companies derive income from the provision of digital services related to their products. At the same time, digitalization raises new challenges. The diffusion of AI and automation is reshaping the organization of work, skill requirements, and the distribution of employment within and across

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face particular constraints: many continue to lack adequate digital connectivity, relevant skills, or access to advanced digital tools, reinforcing a widening digital divide [78]. Policies aiming at supporting the adoption of advanced digital production technologies should also consider critical enabling factors, such as digital infrastructure, governance systems, data security, access to finance, and skill development. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

From the point of view of statistics, these transformations have several implications. First, there is a growing demand for systematic information on the adoption and use of digital technologies in manufacturing and related industries. This includes granular information disaggregated by industry, firm size, ownership, and region. Meeting this demand requires integrating questions on digital technologies into business and industrial surveys, and linking them with other sources of information on digital readiness, such as indicators on connectivity, cybersecurity, and digital skills. Second, digitalization increasingly blurs traditional boundaries in industrial statistics, particularly between manufacturing and services and between tangible and intangible assets. As manufacturers expand their service-based activities, it becomes more difficult to capture their full value creation using concepts and classifications focused primarily on physical goods. This raises questions about how industrial statistics should treat service activities carried out within (digitally-enabled) manufacturing firms, as well as how to account for non-manufacturing companies that provide production-related services to the manufacturing sector. Industrial statistics need to measure novel concepts related to digital technology adoption and impacts 

And third, understanding the impact of digital technologies on productivity, workforce dynamics, and inclusiveness requires closer integration between industrial statistics and other domains, including labour, education, and skills statistics. ## **Globalization, GVCs, and supply-chain reconfiguration** 

The expansion of global value chains (GVCs) has been one of the defining features of industrialization and trade over the past decades. Production processes have become increasingly fragmented across borders, with different stages of design, component manufacturing, assembly, logistics, and support services located where firms perceive comparative advantages. GVCs have supported export growth, productivity gains, and structural transformation in many economies, while also creating new forms of dependency and vulnerability [79]. **==> picture [69 x 42] intentionally omitted <==**

## GVCs 

remain engines of export growth, but also channels of vulnerability

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 116_ 

Recent crises, including the COVID-19 pandemic, regional conflicts, rising trade tariffs and climate-related disruptions, have exposed these interdependencies. They have revealed the extent to which industrial production in one country can be affected by events taking place in another. Disruptions can propagate rapidly through supply chains and severely impact globalized enterprises that rely on just-in-time delivery of key components, leading to production delays [23; 80; 81]. Partly in response to these developments, industrial policy has resurged worldwide, as countries seek to strengthen diversification, resilience, and economic security [10; 82]. The general policy challenge is therefore to deepen and upgrade GVCs participation as a channel for industrialization, technology diffusion, and job creation, while managing risks related to trade protectionism, logistical bottlenecks, climate shocks, and the concentration of critical inputs in a limited number of producers [83]. To support these policy objectives, timely and granular statistics are essential. Beyond measuring domestic production and trade flows separately, it is increasingly important to understand how firms and industries are integrated into cross-border production networks, what determines their participation, and where value added is generated along supply chains. Given the speed at which shocks circulate across production networks, developing high-frequency indicators of production and trade is also crucial. Comprehensive information on the activities of multinational enterprises, the extent of foreign ownership, and the degree to which domestic firms participate in exporting, importing, and supplying inputs to GVCs is equally important. This underscores the need to integrate statistical business registers (SBRs), SBS, and trade microdata, and to strengthen statistics on foreign affiliates and enterprise groups. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Demographic change, jobs, informality, and inclusion** 

Demographic trends are reshaping the global supply of labour and the composition of the industrial workforce. UN population projections indicate that the world will continue to grow in the coming decades, but with marked regional differences: populations are ageing rapidly in many countries, while a large and growing youth population is concentrated in others [84]. Urbanization and international migration further alter the geographical distribution and skills profile of workers.

These contrasting dynamics create very different policy challenges. In ageing economies, concerns focus on labour shortages, the sustainability of social protection systems, and the need to retain workers in productive employment. In younger economies, the priority is to 

Manufacturing’s share in global employment declined to **14.1%** in 2023, down from 14.6% in 2012 

--- end of page.page_number=129 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 117_ 

generate sufficient decent jobs for a growing working-age population and prevent underemployment and informality [85]. The manufacturing sector remains an important source of decent work, particularly in low- and middle-income economies. However, as shown in Sections 2.2 and 3.4, its sustained capacity to provide employment appears to be at a turning point: over the past decade, manufacturing’s share to global GDP has kept increasing, but its share in total employment has declined. Underutilization, labour market insecurity, limited access to social protection, and high rates of informality remain important concerns across regions [86]. In addition, industrial restructuring, globalization, digitalization, automation, and other factors affect different groups of workers unevenly, depending on their skills, gender, age, and location. Women, in particular, remain underrepresented in many industrial occupations, especially in higher-skilled, higher-paid jobs and in leadership roles, even as their overall participation in the manufacturing workforce has increased. Persistent wage gaps underscore these inequalities [39; 87]. Similar challenges apply to other groups, including youth, migrants, and persons with disabilities, who may face higher risks of exclusion or vulnerability during periods of rapid change. Industrial statistics must therefore go beyond aggregates of production and value added to capture who participates in industry, under what conditions, and with what outcomes. To design policies that promote quality job creation and address inequalities, policymakers require granular data, at minimum disaggregated by sex, age, disability status, type of employment, occupation, and other relevant characteristics. Moreover, the focus on inclusion requires analysing the entire distribution of employment outcomes, rather than relying only on averages that may obscure important disparities. Meeting these needs calls for stronger integration between establishmentbased industrial surveys, labour force and household surveys, and administrative records on employment and wages, supported by the use of common identifiers to facilitate data linkage. Where informality is widespread, SBRs and standard establishment surveys capture only part of industrial activity. Measuring informal industrial employment and output requires special approaches, including dedicated modules in labour force or household surveys, mixed survey designs, and methods to estimate non-observed activities. ## **Innovation, R&D, and the growing importance of intangibles**

In many sectors, competitive advantage now depends on the ability to develop new products and processes, protect and leverage intellectual property, and use digital technologies to organize production and supply chains more efficiently. These changes are mirrored in companies’ balance sheets and in national accounts, where investments in intangibles, such as R&D and innovation-related activities, constitute a rapidly growing share of GDP and are becoming stronger predictors of manufacturing performance than investment in physical assets [91; 92]. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Intangible assets are gaining predominance as drivers of industrial competitiveness and productivity 

The growing prominence of R&D and innovation is closely linked to the megatrends discussed above. Digitalization expands opportunities to embed intangibles in products and production systems. Participation in GVCs often relies on product design, process know-how, quality control, and relational assets. In this context, R&D and innovation form part of a broader set of industrial capabilities that encompass technological and non-technological elements. These trends have important implications for industrial statistics. First, they increase the need for robust and detailed statistics on R&D and innovation in industry, which remain limited or absent in many economies. Such information is necessary to understand which industries and firms invest in R&D, design, data, and other innovationrelated activities; how this investment is financed; and what outcomes it generates in terms of new products, processes, and intellectual property. Second, the growing importance of intangibles calls for a broader scope of investment and capital stock. Many traditional surveys remain rooted in outdated statistical frameworks and focus primarily on tangible assets such as machinery, equipment, and buildings, while treating intangibles as intermediate inputs, if they are captured at all. Aligning industrial statistics with the revised macroeconomic standards offers a pathway toward more comprehensive measurement of intangible assets. Third, intellectual property indicators, such as patents, trademarks, and industrial designs, offer valuable complementary information. When compatible classifications and identifiers are used, these data can be linked to traditional industrial statistics, enabling analysis of innovation dynamics. Finally, industrial statistics must be complemented by broader innovation surveys and by both qualitative and quantitative data on management practices and organizational change. This is especially crucial for SMEs, which often innovate without formal R&D expenditure or rely on non-technological forms of innovation. Capturing these activities is essential for understanding the full breadth of innovation across industrial systems. Not enough is known about firm-level R&D and business innovation, especially in SMEs

## **Industrial resilience and shocks** 

The past decade has underscored the vulnerability of industrial sectors when facing large and overlapping shocks. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, different regions have faced climate-related events, geopolitical tensions, and conflicts, with worldwide impacts. The re-emergence of trade protectionism adds another layer of uncertainty.

The issue of industrial resilience was already discussed in the megatrend of digitalization and GVCs, but this is not purely a supply-chain issue. It also highlights issues about industrial structure, diversification, technological capabilities, and social protection. From a statistical perspective, the key consequence is the need for flexible and responsive statistical systems that can react and adapt to emerging issues while at the same time preserving consistency. They should include a battery of industrial indicators that can capture both the short-term impact of shocks and the structural factors that shape resilience or vulnerability. This includes more timely indicators of production, employment, trade, and inventories, and information on exposures to specific risks. It also calls for greater use of highfrequency data, including from non-traditional sources. **==> picture [62 x 62] intentionally omitted <==**

## **5.2 Aligning industrial statistics with future needs** 

The megatrends described in Section 5.1 directly affect what industrial statistics need to measure and how they are produced. Many of the conceptual tools required to respond to these new demands already exist in the international statistical frameworks, including the updated system of national accounts (SNA) 2025 [93], the system of environmental-economic accounting (SEEA) [74], the fifth revision of the ISIC [94], the third version of the Central Product Classification (CPC) [95], and the forthcoming 2028 update of the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (HS). Other adjustments will require new methodological guidance and integration across statistical domains. This section outlines how these frameworks can be leveraged to keep industrial statistics relevant and fit for purpose amid ongoing and anticipated transformations in industrial activity. ## **Rethinking the scope and boundaries of industrial statistics** 

**==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

New and revised international standards provide a toolbox for modernizing industrial statistics 

As summarized in Section 1.2, current international standards define industrial statistics as covering mining, manufacturing, and utilities. This core scope has long provided a solid conceptual foundation and remains valid. However, the transformations discussed above 

--- end of page.page_number=132 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 120_ 

increasingly challenge the traditional boundaries of what should be considered _industrial_ for statistical and policy purposes. GVCs spread industrial activities across borders and blur the separation between sectors. They involve the participation of domestic, foreign, and multinational enterprises (MNEs) connected through complex production networks. Although international manuals provide definitions and guidance on global production arrangements, such as contract manufacturing, outsourcing, and factoryless goods production (FGP), applying them in practice is often difficult and may lead to counterintuitive outcomes. The green transition depends not only on what happens within manufacturing establishments, but also on upstream and downstream functions such as engineering, design, industrial R&D, maintenance and repair, recycling, and end-of-life management. Similarly, the digital transformation erodes the traditional boundary between manufacturing and services, as production processes become deeply integrated with software development, data processing, and platform-based business models. These developments suggest the need for information covering broader industrial ecosystems or production systems, rather than narrowly defined industrial sectors. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

The boundary between manufacturing and related services is blurring, challenging traditional sector-based measurement approaches 

A review of the scope of industrial statistics could therefore consider how to define and classify industrial services and activities that support or are closely linked to industry, while maintaining coherence with ISIC, CPC, and SNA. Flexible thematic groups, such as green industries or digital-intensive industries, could be developed to answer specific policy questions. This would enable industrial statistics to better capture emerging realities while preserving the core definitional structure that ensures cross-country comparability. ## **Classifications for a changing industrial structure** 

Classifications of activities and products are at the core of official statistics. They determine how establishments are grouped into industries and how goods and services are categorized, ensuring that national data can be compared internationally. The ISIC classification of economic activities and the CPC classification of products therefore play a central role in ensuring that industrial statistics remain aligned with ongoing transformations. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Classification systems are at the core of official statistics and are essential modernization building blocks 

ISIC Rev. 5, endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission in 2023–2024, preserves the broad structure of its predecessor while introducing some refinements to reflect new forms of production and the growing importance of services, digital activities, and environmental management. For industrial statistics, some of the improvements include:

- A finer breakdown of repair, waste management, and environmental services, supporting better identification and monitoring of “green” industries; 

- Enhanced classification of information and communication, data processing, and platform-based activities, improving the statistical visibility of digital services that are increasingly integrates with industrial production; 

- Clearer guidance on contract manufacturing, outsourcing, and FGP, helping ensure more consistent and transparent measurement of GVCs. CPC Ver. 3, adopted in 2024–2025, provides a revised and more detailed product classification aligned with ISIC Rev. 5 and other macroeconomic standards. For industrial statistics, key implications include: 

- Identification of green and low-carbon goods, circular economy products, and environmental services produced by industrial establishments;

These updates will allow trade statistics to better capture the evolving composition of manufactured exports and imports. For industrial statistics, this implies that surveys and administrative data used to compile industrial output and investment need to collect information on the expenditures on these assets; the bundling of physical goods with digital services or embedded software; and the integration of digital technologies into industrial production processes. These improvements will help industrial statistics to reflect more accurately the growing importance of digitalization, AI adoption, and the role of intangibles in industrial activity. The SNA update devotes substantial attention to globalization and global production arrangements, providing refined guidance on MNEs, special purpose entities, GVCs, FGP, merchanting, and outsourcing arrangements. This has several implications for industrial statistics:

- The focus on thematic or satellite accounts (e.g. on the digital economy) increases the demand for detailed data from industrial establishments. The SNA 2025 also broadens the national accounts framework to better account for well-being and sustainability, including more explicit treatment of natural resource depletion as a cost of production, distributional measures, and links to environmental-economic accounts. For industrial statistics, this will result in a more comprehensive reflection of the inclusiveness and sustainability dimensions of industrial production. ## **Integrating environmental-economic accounting into industrial statistics** 

Environmental pressures and the green transition feature prominently among the transformations shaping industry, but traditional industrial statistics remain largely focused on economic variables such as output, value added, and trade.
