--- end of page.page_number=136 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 124_ 

by industry and product. Second, environmental asset accounts record stocks and changes in stocks of individual natural resources in volume and monetary terms. Third, accounts for environmental protection expenditure, environmental taxes and subsidies, and environmental goods and services link environmental policy instruments and markets to industries and institutional sectors. The SEEA Ecosystem Accounting, adopted in 2021, extends this approach further by quantifying ecosystem extent, condition, and services in a way that can be linked to economic activity [105]. This framework directly addresses several of the measurement challenges that industrial statistics must overcome to remain future-ready. First, it provides a coherent mechanism to link industrial activities to their resource use and environmental pressures, including energy and water use, GHG and air pollutant emissions, waste generation, and material flows.


Final chunk number 445, content : 
This information is essential for tracking resource efficiency, environmental performance, and the decoupling between emissions and production. Second, it provides a way to identify industries producing environmental goods and services, which can be useful for monitoring activity in “green” industries and the transition to sustainable production. And third, it supports the analysis of how industrial activities affect ecosystems and the services they provide, including land-use change, degradation, and restoration. Despite these advantages, SEEA implementation remains uneven across countries and often partial in coverage, in part because of its significant data requirements. Moreover, environmental statistics are still often compiled separately from economic statistics, leading to inconsistencies and limited integration across domains. A more comprehensive and harmonized implementation of the SEEA offers significant potential benefits for industrial statistics. It would strengthen the capacity of NSOs to measure the green transformation, assess environmental impacts with greater level of detail, and provide policymakers with integrated information to design and monitor sustainable industrial strategies. ## **Linking industrial statistics with other domains** 

As emphasized throughout this chapter, many emerging policy questions concerning industry cannot be addressed using industrial statistics alone. Understanding the implications of industrial transformations for decent jobs, wages, innovation capacity, external competitiveness, inclusiveness, and other dimensions requires integrating information across multiple statistical domains. This integration could draw on several established international standards, including but not limited to: 

Two main manuals in the SEEA family: 

Central Framework and Ecosystem Accounting 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

The adoption of environmental accounting remains low worldwide, limiting its contribution to green industrial policymaking 

--- end of page.page_number=137 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 125_ 

- Labour statistics, guided by International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS) resolutions on statistics related to labour force, employment, working time, wages, and occupational classifications. Linking business statistics with labour force surveys and other demographic and social data could provide information to analyse the distributional and inclusiveness dimensions of industrialization, including gender and youth employment, informality, skills, and job quality. - R&D and innovation statistics, guided by the Frascati Manual [103] and the Oslo Manual [104], respectively. These frameworks define concepts, classifications, and survey methodologies for measuring R&D expenditure and personnel, as well as innovation activities in the business sector. Integrating these statistics with structural and performance indicators from industrial statistics would provide a more complete understanding of the role of innovation and intangible assets in industrial development. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Complex policy questions require industrial data to be integrated with labour, trade, and innovation statistics 

- Trade and balance-of-payments statistics, including the 2025 update of the Balance of Payments Manual [100] and forthcoming revisions to the International Merchandise Trade Statistics and International Trade in Services Statistics manuals. These standards offer guidance for measuring cross-border flows of goods, services, and capital, including digital trade and services supplied by industrial firms. - Energy statistics, which can be linked with industrial statistics to obtain detailed information on energy production and consumption by industrial establishments and on their progress along the energy transition [106]. Taken together, these options suggest that the future of industrial statistics may lie not in expanding as a standalone statistical domain, but in deeper synergies within an integrated system of economic, social, and environmental statistics. ## **5.3 Cross-cutting challenges in the production of industrial statistics** 

The adaptations described in the previous section would allow industrial statistics to better respond to the data needs arising from the transformations reshaping industry. However, these conceptual advances also interact with multiple, often simultaneous operational pressures faced by NSOs. This section highlights some of the most important cross-cutting challenges in the compilation and dissemination of industrial statistics that must also be addressed to maintain data quality, increase efficiency, and ensure industrial statistics remain fit for purpose. **==> picture [62 x 53] intentionally omitted <==**

The future role of industrial statistics lies within a broader integrated system, not in isolated efforts 

--- end of page.page_number=138 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 126_ 

## **Response burden, non-response, and declining survey participation** 

Business surveys are typically demanding for establishments. They request detailed information on output, inputs, employment, investment, products, and technologies, often at high frequency and for multiple reference periods, using concepts that do not always align with business accounting practices. At the same time, firms face increasing and overlapping reporting obligations, including tax, social security, regulatory, and other statistical requirements.


Final chunk number 446, content : 
These pressures are particularly acute for SMEs, which have fewer administrative resources. International frameworks highlight the importance of considering response burden when collecting statistical information [107; 108]. A related challenge is declining response rates. Many NSOs report increasing difficulties in recruiting and retaining survey respondents, particularly among small firms and in sectors with high turnover. The United Kingdom’s labour force survey, although a household survey, illustrates this trend: full response rates declined from 48.2 per cent in 2010 to 17.4 per cent in 2024 [109; 110]. Similar patterns are observed in many other countries. If not adequately addressed, these trends can introduce bias and threaten the representativeness of industrial statistics. To mitigate these challenges, many NSOs are adopting an administrative data-first approach, surveying establishments only when comparable data cannot be obtained from existing sources, such as tax filings, financial statements, or employment reports. Non-traditional data sources, including big data, could also serve as complements. Implementing such approach requires well-established data flows, robust data governance frameworks, and clear methodologies for integrating data sources. When surveys remain necessary, several improvements could help reduce burden and improve participation: careful survey design and sampling strategies that avoid repeatedly burdening the same units; the use of web-based questionnaires and pre-filled forms; responsive collection strategies targeted at highimpact non-respondents; and clear communication about the purpose 

## **Survey frames and complex enterprise structures** 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Response burden management is an increasingly important priority for NSOs 

**==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Survey response rates are declining all over the world, undermining the representativeness and data quality of official statistics 

Producing high-quality industrial statistics depends critically on the quality of the underlying survey frames. SBRs are widely recognized as the backbone of business statistics, providing coherent frames for sampling and integrating data across surveys and administrative 

--- end of page.page_number=139 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 127_ 

sources [111; 112]. However, in many countries SBRs remain incomplete or outdated. Gaps are common with respect to SMEs, industries with high firm turnover, and establishments operating in the informal sector. Globalization and new business models introduce additional complexity. Enterprise groups are becoming increasingly multifaceted, with operations spread out in multiple industries and jurisdictions. FGP and outsourcing blur the link between the location where goods are physically produced and the units that own the products, technologies, and intellectual property. These issues challenge the ability of SBRs and survey frames to correctly identify statistical units and to attribute industrial activity to the appropriate resident entities. Meeting these challenges requires prioritizing the coverage, quality, and maintenance of the SBR; establishing a dedicated large case unit (LCU); expanding the use of administrative data for business profiling; and aligning national practices with international guidance on enterprise groups and global production [112]. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

High-quality business registers are essential for sampling, data integration, and analysing business demography 

## **Data sources and data integration** 

While surveys remain indispensable in many cases, the pressure to reduce response burden and increase timeliness and granularity is accelerating the shift towards multi-source statistical systems. Administrative data, including tax records, social security registers, customs records, business licensing, and many others, can play a central role in this transition, especially for structural variables like turnover, trade, employment, and firm characteristics [113; 114]. At the same time, new types of data are becoming increasingly relevant for industrial statistics. Satellite imagery, scanner data, web-scraped data, and other digital traces hold significant potential for measuring specific aspects of economic and environmental activity (see, for instance, the resources available in [115]). A major challenge lies in linking survey and non-survey data sources. The adoption of unique identifiers that allow consistent linkage across datasets would significantly facilitate integration.


Final chunk number 447, content : 
When they are not available, probabilistic matching can achieve reliable results when based on robust methodologies. Additional challenges commonly arise, including data access restrictions, limitations in legal frameworks, and the presence of intrinsic biases or quality issues in nonsurvey data. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Industrial statistics increasingly combine surveys, administrative records, big data, and other non-traditional sources 

--- end of page.page_number=140 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 128_ 

## **Timeliness and quality trade-offs** 

Industrial statistics are used both for structural analysis and shortterm monitoring of economic activity. Data users increasingly expect timely, high-frequency indicators of industrial activity with minimal publication lags. Meeting these expectations requires balancing difficult trade-offs between timeliness, coverage, granularity, and accuracy. For industrial statistics, improving timeliness without jeopardizing quality often requires a combination of measures. These include, among others, redesigning survey instruments and collection modes; expanding the use of administrative and high-frequency data sources; and applying model-based estimation and nowcasting techniques to produce preliminary estimates. New methodologies, including machine learning tools, can greatly accelerate data production while maintaining or even improving quality. These include, for example, automated classification, anomaly detection, or imputation techniques [116]. ## Machine learning methods 

applied across the data production cycle can improve timeliness while 

maintaining or improving other dimensions of data quality 

## **Methodological modernization and process integration** 

In addition to new data sources and methods, addressing the challenges presented requires a modernization of statistical production processes and infrastructure. Applying a statistical business process model to industrial statistics can help identify opportunities for standardization, automation, and reuse of tools across surveys and domains, ultimately leading to improved efficiency and consistency. It can also contribute to a more robust data and metadata management, supported by stronger integration and clear governance structures [117; 118]. For industrial data in particular, given its complex classifications, multiple disaggregations, and frequent revisions, well-designed metadata systems are essential to ensure that users can correctly interpret statistical outputs and that data can be consistently linked across domains and over time. Strengthening these systems is therefore essential for making industrial statistics more agile, interoperable, and responsive to the evolving needs of policymakers and other users. ## **Dissemination, communication, and AI-readiness** 

There has never been a greater demand for reliable, accessible, and timely data. As evidence-based policymaking becomes more deeply embedded and as analytical tools grow more sophisticated, the need for disaggregated, high-frequency indicators continues to rise. At the 

**==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Statistical business process models can streamline industrial data production and support end-to-end modernization 

--- end of page.page_number=141 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 129_ 

same time, the way industrial statistics are disseminated and communicated is undergoing rapid transformation. Some users look for concise summaries and policy-ready dashboards, while others expect open, machine-readable datasets with clear licences, rich metadata, and tools that enable automated processing and reproducible analysis. Ensuring that dissemination systems serve this increasingly diverse spectrum of users is now a central challenge for producers of industrial statistics. Confidentiality and data protection remain essential considerations. As dissemination becomes more granular (by industry, region, firm size, or other attributes), the risk of disclosing sensitive information grows. Statistical offices must continue to apply robust confidentiality safeguards, including SDC techniques, when releasing detailed data to the public. **==> picture [62 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

Dissemination should cater both human and AI users through open, 

interoperable, and machine-readable data and metadata standards 

A new and rapidly growing dimension is the AI-readiness of official statistics. While dissemination platforms were traditionally optimized for direct human use, industrial data are now increasingly accessed by AI systems that retrieve, read, and synthesize information on behalf of users. This shift rises the importance of standardized formats, semantic consistency, consistent identifiers, and machine-readable metadata, enabling AI tools to interpret and combine statistical content correctly. Dissemination systems must therefore be optimized simultaneously for human interpretation and automated consumption, ensuring clarity, transparency, and interoperability [119]. ## **5.4 Conclusion and the forthcoming revision of the international standards for industrial statistics** 

This chapter has shown that industrial statistics are at a turning point. Structural transformations in industry, including the green and energy transition, digitalization, the reconfiguration of GVCs, labour market shifts, the rising importance of innovation, and growing concerns about resilience, are reshaping what policy makers need to know about industry and how industrial development should be measured. At the same time, statistical producers face mounting operational pressures related to response burden, non-response, integration of multiple data sources, timeliness, data quality, confidentiality, and dissemination. Both the megatrends reshaping industry and the mounting cross-cutting challenges call for a renewed approach to industrial statistics 

Section 5.2 described how many of the conceptual tools needed to respond to these demands already exist in the form of revised international frameworks and classifications. However, the current industrial statistics standards themselves still reflect an earlier generation of industrial structures, policy priorities, and statistical practices. They 

--- end of page.page_number=142 ---

_5 Industrial statistics for a sustainable industrial future 130_ 

no longer fully match the information needed to design, monitor, and evaluate industrial policy in a rapidly changing world. The existing manuals have provided a robust foundation for industrial statistics for many years. They standardized key concepts, classifications, and indicators; supported the development of national industrial survey programmes; and guided international reporting, including for SDG 9. However, they pre-date many of the conceptual, policy, and statistical developments discussed in this chapter, leaving important gaps where updated guidance is needed. In response, UNIDO and the UN Statistics Division have initiated exploratory work on the future of international standards for industrial statistics. The directions under consideration include: 

- Aligning definitions and measurement concepts in industrial statistics with the SNA 2025 and the SEEA, including for digitalization, globalization, and environmental and distributional aspects; 

## **Current industrial statistical standards** 

   - International Recommendations for Industrial Statistics (IRIS) [4] 

   - International Recommendations for the Index of Industrial Production (IRIIP) [99] 

   - List of Industrial Products (LoIP) [97] 

- Clarifying the scope of industrial statistics, including the treatment of industrial services and industry-related activities, drawing on updated SNA guidance; 

- Fully leverage updated classifications to identify green, digital, and high-technology industries and products; 

- Providing guidance on the measurement of R&D, innovation, intangibles, MNE activity, the informal economy, and other concepts within an industrial context; 

- Strengthening methodological guidance on the use of administrative and other data sources, the role of the SBR, and integration of industrial statistics with labour, innovation, trade, and environmental data; 

- Updating the list of industrial performance indicators to better reflect contemporary policy priorities and data needs. This would result in a new generation of international standards for industrial statistics, replacing the existing manuals. Importantly, this should not be seen as an isolated technical exercise, but as part of a broader global effort to adapt official statistics so that they remain relevant, coherent, and fit for purpose amid accelerating economic, technological, and environmental change. The transformations described in this chapter will continue to evolve, and statistical systems will need to remain flexible and forward-looking while at the same time maintaining consistency over time. By building on the strengths of current standards while addressing emerging demands in a pragmatic manner, the forthcoming revision can help ensure that industrial statistics remain a solid analytical foundation for evidence-based policies in support of an inclusive, resilient, and sustainable industrial future. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

The forthcoming revision of the industrial statistics manuals aims to align them with recently updated frameworks and make them more fit for purpose

## **B Explanatory notes** 

Unless otherwise indicated, _manufacturing_ refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section C, while the combined _mining and utilities_ sector includes sections B, D, and E of ISIC Rev. 4 [5].[INFO-CIRCLE] 

ISIC code numbers are accompanied by a descriptive title. For example, the descriptive title of ISIC division 16 is “Manufacture of wood and of products of wood and cork, except furniture; manufacture of articles of straw and plaiting materials”. However, the description is sometimes shortened for space considerations. In this example, ISIC division 16 may be described simply as “Wood products, excluding furniture”. A list of ISIC codes and their corresponding descriptive titles is given in Annex E.1. In the presentation of statistical tables and visualizations, individual countries and areas are referred to as economies. They are listed alphabetically, unless another ranking is considered more appropriate. Economies are classified according to their stage of industrial development and their geographical regions. Additional country groupings may be used whenever necessary. For additional information on UNIDO’s classification system, see Annex C. The lists of economies according to the main country groups used in the _Yearbook_ are provided in Annexes E.3, E.4, and E.5. In some cases, data on economic activity and traded commodities are classified according to technological intensity. For more details on the sources of these classifications, as well as the lists of highertechnology industries and traded commodities, see Annex E.2. Unless otherwise specified, data for China do not include Hong Kong SAR of China, Macao SAR of China, and Taiwan Province of China, which are reported separately. References to Kosovo should be understood within the framework of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999). References to Kosovo and to Taiwan Province of China are included exclusively for statistical completeness and do not imply any opinion whatsoever by UNIDO regarding their legal status. INFO-CIRCLE ISIC provides a comprehensive framework for collecting and reporting economic data for purposes of economic analysis, decision-taking and policy-making. ## **C Overview of methodological aspects** 

One of the most important objectives of UNIDO’s statistical databases and regular publications, such as this _Yearbook_ , is providing statistical information that facilitate international comparisons related to the manufacturing sector and the combined mining and utilities sector. Bearing in mind the requirements of international comparability when maintaining a common platform for global industrial statistics, the data presented were compiled using the international recommendations and the standards endorsed by the UN. Concepts and definitions are drawn from [4; 5]. ## INDUSTRY **ISIC** 

ISIC has provided guidance for developing national activity classifications since its adoption in 1948. It is an essential tool for international comparison of statistical data on economic activities. ISIC is the recommended international reference classification of productive activities. Since the adoption of the first version in 1948, the majority of countries around the world have used ISIC as their national activity classification or have developed national classifications derived from it. Besides, it has become an essential tool for comparing statistical data on economic activities at the regional and international levels. In this publication, information on industrial sectors and their groups are presented according to ISIC Rev. 4 [5], since this revision remains the most used classification of economic activities worldwide. Data reported in accordance with ISIC Rev. 3 [121] or other national/regional classifications of economic activities were converted to ISIC Rev. 4 using appropriate correspondence tables. A new version of the classification, ISIC Rev. 5, was endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission at its 54[th] session in 2023 [94]. All economies are encouraged to reflect this new classification in the coming years, as far as national requirements permit, in their industrial classification schemes. In some cases, UNIDO applies imputation methods when data are missing. The primary objective is extending the length of time series and enabling the calculation of country group aggregates. Minor discrepancies may occur due to data revisions or during the conversion and estimation processes. As a result, users may observe differences when 

UNIDO databases provide statistical indicators to facilitate long-term analysis of economic performance across economies 

--- end of page.page_number=157 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 145_ 

comparing data for the same reference year across various editions of the _Yearbook_ or when contrasting earlier and later data releases. The _Yearbook_ presents information sourced from a wide variety of data, including national accounts, structural business statistics, industrial performance indicators, and short-term statistics. These official data compiled by UNIDO were originally collected by individual national authorities and NSOs through surveys and censuses conducted periodically, as well as from business registers and other administrative sources. The data collected were generally complemented with estimations made by national experts. UNIDO relies on appropriate statistical benchmarking techniques to combine statistical information from multiple data sources in order to produce estimates with the highest degree of accuracy, reliability, coherence, and detail possible [4]. Quality dimensions of official statistics: Relevance, 

accuracy and reliability, timeliness and punctuality, accessibility and clarity, coherence and comparability 

Statistical indicators in the _Yearbook_ are presented using percentage distributions, cross-country averages, ratios and shares, real growth rates, and per capita measures. These indicators are designed to facilitate regional, international, and time-based comparisons. ## **National accounts and population** 

Industrial statistics based on the SNA provide a continuing flow of key information that is indispensable for the monitoring, analysis, and evaluation of an economy’s performance over time. The main economic indicators presented in the _Yearbook_ , including value added of the manufacturing sector (ISIC Rev. 4 section C) and those for the mining and utilities sectors (ISIC Rev. 4 sections B, D, and E), are obtained based on the SNA. They represent the net contribution of the respective sectors to GDP. Information on MVA and MUVA serve as significant benchmarks for measuring performance in those industrial sectors. In this publication, both MVA per capita at constant prices and the share of MVA in GDP are used as markers of a country’s level of industrialization and its progress towards structural transformation. UNIDO obtains data on GDP, MVA, and other national accounts aggregates mostly from the National Accounts Main Aggregates Database [122]. The database is compiled by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) from official national accounts submitted by NSOs, supplemented with estimates generated by UNSD experts, whenever appropriate. It includes information for more than 200 economies and is updated annually in December. Complete information on the estimation methodology is available in [123]. The base year of these data is currently 2015. ## INDUSTRY **National Accounts** 

Statistics based on the SNA provide a continuous flow of key information indispensable for monitoring, analysing, and evaluating an economy’s performance over time. --- end of page.page_number=158 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 146_ 

UNIDO Statistics complements this database with other national and international sources, as needed. In addition, UNIDO generates estimates of the main aggregates with the purpose of improving timeliness and facilitating comparability over time and across economies. Population figures are based on data compiled by the Population Division of the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) [84]. ## **Index of industrial production (IIP)** 

Another important economic benchmark featured in the _Yearbook_ is the IIP, which tracks economic trends by measuring growth of industrial production in volume terms, independent of price fluctuations. For many economies, the index is available with a breakdown of manufacturing industries at the 2-digit level of ISIC Rev. 4.


Final chunk number 453, content : 
While the focus is primarily on the manufacturing sectors (ISIC Rev. 4 section C), it often includes data on the mining and utilities sectors (ISIC Rev. 4 sections B, D, and E) as well. The time series extend back to 2005. Figure C.1 provides an overview of the economies for with the IIP are available. ## **Coverage of global value added by available quarterly IIPs** 

- Mining and quarrying (ISIC B): 83.2% 

- Manufacturing (ISIC C): 97.5% 

- Electricity (ISIC D): 76.3% 

- Water supply (ISIC E): 41.5% 

## INDUSTRY **Features of the IIP and UNIDO’s IIP databases** 

- The IIP measures the volume of industrial output in real terms, free from price fluctuations. - It is one of the most important short-term statistics (STS), used to keep track of economic activity in industrial sectors, including manufacturing. - It is usually available in quarterly and monthly frequencies, although with different coverage and level of detail. - UNIDO regularly collects and harmonizes IIP data from across the world. - It is available as the UNIDO IIP database [19], with a coverage of around 80 economies on a monthly basis and about 120 economies with quarterly data. - The database includes original and seasonally-adjusted data. The information is compiled by UNIDO from NSOs’ publications and other resources. For the majority of European countries, information on IIP was obtained from the Statistical Office of the European Union (Eurostat). Most national indices are calculated using the Laspeyres formula and a combination of volume extrapolation and deflation methods. The methodologies most commonly followed are described in [99]. ## UNIDO databases 

include 81 economies (95% of global MVA) with both monthly and quarterly IIP plus around 40 additional economies with quarterly IIP only

Currently, the base year of indices in the IIP database is 2015. ## **Manufacturing trade** 

The _Yearbook_ presents annual and monthly/quarterly manufacturing trade data to assess the international performance of manufacturing across the world. Trade statistics capture the physical movement of products across borders and reflect a key component of global economic integration and competitiveness. In principle: 

Both 

- Imports comprise all foreign goods entering a country, including purchases of goods manufactured abroad and re-imports (i.e.

domestically produced goods that were previously exported and later returned). re-exports and re-imports are included in trade statistics

_C Overview of methodological aspects 148_ 

- Exports include domestically produced goods and re-exports (i.e. foreign goods that were previously imported and later exported without significant domestic transformation). Two main data sources underpin the _Yearbook_ ’s trade statistics. First, yearly data on exports and imports come from the UNIDO Annual Manufacturing Trade Database [40], which contains country, region, and group-level aggregates of trade in manufactured goods, expressed in current USD. Time series generally extend back to 1995 and have full country coverage. The primary source is UNCTAD, complemented by additional official data where appropriate. Second, sub-annual manufacturing trade data, used to capture shortterm dynamics, are drawn from the UNIDO Monthly Manufacturing Trade Database [41]. Figure C.2 shows the economies covered in this database. Although the data are collected on a monthly basis, the _Yearbook_ reports them at a quarterly frequency to smooth short-term volatility. ## The UNIDO database 

includes 60+ economies (around 90% of global exports and imports) with monthly trade available 

## INDUSTRY **Features of the UNIDO Monthly Manufacturing Trade Database** 

- Trade data capture exports and imports in current USD. - These short-term indicators reflect the linkages between producers and consumers across borders within the global trading system. - Data are typically available at quarterly and monthly frequencies, though country coverage and detail vary. - UNIDO regularly collects and harmonizes trade data released by national authorities. - The database currently provides monthly information for approximately 60 economies. - The database includes original as well as seasonally-adjusted time series. UNIDO compiles this database from official releases by national authorities; for most European economies, the source is Eurostat. Values are expressed in current USD, converted from national currency when needed using monthly exchange rates published by the [120]. Quarterly and monthly trade data can be affected by calendar and seasonal patterns, which may obscure underlying economic trends. When necessary, UNIDO applies seasonal adjustment using the TRAMO/SEATS method in the JDemetra+ software [125; 124]. Further methodological information on this database is available in [127]. **Coverage of global manufacturing trade by available quarterly trade data**

## **Structural business statistics (SBS)** 

SBS provide important indicators concerning the detailed structure, economic activity, and performance of businesses over time, both at country and regional levels. These indicators are also presented in the _Yearbook_ . The information was originally collected and reported by individual NSOs, covering a wide range of variables.


Final chunk number 455, content : 
The comprehensive data originating from SBS enhance assessment and comparison of industrial performance across countries at a relatively detailed level of economic activity. However, the major statistical indicators exhibited here focus mainly on the manufacturing sector and the combined mining and utilities sector at the 2-digit level of ISIC Rev. 4. These statistics were collected by UNIDO through various sources. They include UNIDO’s _General Industrial Statistics Questionnaire_ sent 

## INDUSTRY **SBS** 

A clear and comprehensive SBS methodological framework promotes production of industrial statistics with increased efficiency and high data quality, amidst today’s dynamic business environment. --- end of page.page_number=162 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 150_ 

annually to NSOs, data compiled jointly by regional and international organizations such as Eurostat and the OECD, and relevant publications issued by individual national authorities. It is well understood that individual national data compilation schemes vary, which could affect comparability across economies. Hence, national authorities are encouraged to adhere to UN’s concepts and definitions on industrial statistics, whenever possible. Production (output) is an essential economic indicators in industrial statistics. While some data are still reported using census concept covering only activities of industrial nature, current recommendations call for approximating the national accounts measurement by including revenue from activities of a non-industrial nature. Manufacturing output refers to the more refined or higher value merchandise for use or sale. It is the end-product of industrial processes that use labour, machines, tools, and chemical and biological processing or formulation 

Output cannot be directly observed from the accounting records of enterprises/establishments [4]. The value of output in the case of estimates compiled on a production basis comprises: 

- a) The value of the sale of all products of the establishment; 

- b) The net change between the beginning and end of the reference period in the value of work in progress and stocks of goods to be shipped in the same condition as received; 

- c) The value of industrial work performed or industrial services rendered to others; 

- d) The value of goods shipped in the same condition as received less the amount paid for these goods; and 

## INDUSTRY **Census and gross output** 

The difference between census output and gross output is the exclusion or inclusion of the output from the activities that are nonindustrial in nature. - e) The value of fixed assets produced during the period by the unit for its own use. In the case of estimates compiled on a shipment basis, the net change in the value of stocks of finished goods between the beginning and the end of the reference period is also included. Gross output is equivalent to census output plus the revenue from activities of a non-industrial nature. Valuation methods of output vary across countries/areas. The main difference is the inclusion or exclusion of taxes and subsidies on products and production (see Figure C.3). - _Values at factor costs_ exclude taxes on production (taxes that the producing units are liable to pay as a result of engaging in production) and includes subsidies on production (subsidies that resident enterprises may receive as a result of engaging in production, with the exception of direct subsidies on products). - _Values at basic prices_ equal values at factor costs including taxes on production and excluding subsidies on production. - Finally, _values at producers’ prices_ equal values at basic prices plus taxes on products (taxes payable per unit of a product, excluding value added tax (VAT)) minus subsidies on products 

Value at factor costs excludes taxes on production and includes subsidies on production 

Value at basic prices = Value at factor costs + taxes on production - subsidies on production 

Value at producers’ prices = Value at basic prices + taxes on products (excl. VAT) - subsidies on products

5]. Another important economic measurement is value added. In SBS, the value added of manufacturing industries is a survey concept that refers to the given industries’ net output derived from the difference of gross output and intermediate consumption/input. Items covered in the latter include: 

- a) value of materials and supplies for production, including the cost of all fuels and electricity purchased; and 

- b) the cost of services received (mainly payments for contract and commission work and repair and maintenance work). If input estimates are compiled on a “received” rather than on a “consumed” basis, the result is adjusted for the net change between the beginning and the end of the period in the value of stocks of materials, fuel, and other supplies. The estimates of value added are gross of depreciation and other provisions for capital consumption, unless otherwise stated. Similar to output, the valuation of value added may be at factor costs, at basic prices, or at producers’ prices, depending on the treatment of indirect taxes and subsidies as described above and summarized in Figure C.3. Beyond output, value added and employment are essential economic measurements

The interested reader can find the full description and definition of the variables in [4]. Additionally, the terms primarily reflect the situation of a producer in manufacturing. Figure C.4 provides a visual overview of the key components of output, intermediate consumption, and value added, as well as their linkages. One more important statistical concept presented in UNIDO’s databases and in this publication is employment. This is one of the central elements in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Within the framework adopted at the 19[th] International Conference of Labour Statisticians in 2013, employment is defined as work performed in return for pay or profit [129]. It has long been recognized as a pathway to economic development, social inclusion, and well-being. Estimates on the number of employees include both full-time and part-time workers, excluding working proprietors, active business partners, unpaid family workers, and home workers. The figures reported usually refer to the average number of workers during the reference year, obtained as the sum of the “average number of employees” during the year or the total number of employees measured for a single period of the year. ## INDUSTRY **Employment** 

Industrial statistics on employment are essential tools for measuring progress towards national and international policy goals. National authorities may use the data on the number of persons engaged when those for the employees are not separately available. However, both terms are not interchangeable. Figures for persons en- 

--- end of page.page_number=165 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 153_ 

gaged cover employees, working proprietors, active business partners, and unpaid family workers. It is worth noting that this publication also uses employment estimates obtained through household or labour force surveys; although these estimates are more timely and may provide a more complete coverage than employment estimates from SBS, they are based on different statistical units and not available with the same granularity by industry of economic activity. Finally, it is important to highlight that in this publication, national accounts data, SBS, and other sources may be combined with the objective of providing comprehensive statistics for analysing and comparing industrial performance across country groups at a relatively detailed level of economic activity. For instance, it is possible to construct indicators with the combined information from the IIP and value added estimates obtained from SBS. ## INDUSTRY **SBS vs. IIP** 

SBS refer to low-frequency data (annual or less frequent) that are comprehensive but not very timely. IIP relates to high-frequency data (quarterly and monthly) that are timely but have less detail and reduced coverage. For each economy and industrial division, value added estimates were generated by applying IIP figures to the 2015 value added base weights. These weights were estimated by UNIDO using various national and international sources. For more country-specific SBS, readers can refer to the databases available at the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3]. ## **Competitive industrial performance (CIP) Index** 

The CIP Index is a composite indicator that measures the capacity of countries/areas to increase their presence in international and domestic markets, while developing industrial sectors and activities with higher value added and higher technological level. It is constructed by combining eight variables across three dimensions: 

- a) _Capacity to produce and export manufactured goods._ This dimension captures a country’s ability to increase the presence of its manufactured goods in international and domestic markets. It covers comparable measures of the country’s manufacturing production and exports, namely MVA and manufacturing exports in per capita terms.


Final chunk number 457, content : 
These indicators allow for cross-country comparisons, independent of the differences in population or economy size. - b) _Technological deepening and upgrading._ The second dimension measures the technological complexity of manufacturing processes in a country by using two composite sub-indices. First, the degree of industrialization intensity that estimates the complexity of production processes. This indicator consists of the share of MVA originating from MHT industries and the share of MVA in GDP. Second, export quality, another composite indicator 

## Three dimensions of the CIP Index 

**==> picture [96 x 96] intentionally omitted <==**

--- end of page.page_number=166 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 154_ 

that measures the quality of the integration process of the country’s manufacturing sector. This indicator is estimated based on the share of MHT manufacturing exports in total manufacturing exports and the share of manufacturing exports in total exports. - c) _World impact._ The third dimension serves as a proxy of economies of agglomeration, scope, and scale present in a country’s manufacturing sector. It captures the world impact based on two indicators: the country’s share in world MVA and in world trade of manufactured goods. All variables are first standardized to a [0, 1] interval. Scores for each dimension are obtained by calculating the geometric mean of the underlying variables. Finally, the overall CIP score is calculated as the geometric mean of the scores for the three dimensions. The higher the score in any of the variables, the higher the country’s industrial competitiveness and its rank in the overall CIP Index. The detailed conceptual framework and methodology of the Index are described in [130]. The Index’s scores, ranks, and underlying indicators are available in the UNIDO Statistics Portal [34]. ## **Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 9 indicators** 

Following the adoption of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the global indicator framework for SDGs was developed by the UN Statistical Commission through its Inter-agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators (IAEG-SDGs). This was adopted by the UN General Assembly in July 2017 and is contained in the Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on Work of the Statistical Commission pertaining to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development [131]. The latest reference metadata information for all SDG indicators is available in [132]. The current global SDG database can be consulted in [133]. The current edition of the CIP Index evaluates the industrial performance of 153 economies

SDG 9, one of the 17 global Goals, is composed of eight targets and 12 indicators aiming at building resilient infrastructure, promoting inclusive and sustainable industrialization, and fostering innovation. UNIDO is a custodian agency of six industry-related SDG indicators under Goal 9: 

- 9.2.1 Manufacturing value added as a proportion of GDP and per capita 

- 9.2.2 Manufacturing employment as a proportion of total employment 

- 9.3.1 Proportion of small-scale industries in total industry value 

- 9.3.2 Proportion of small-scale industries with a loan or line of credit

UNIDO has developed advanced tools for monitoring the performance of countries/areas towards achieving the industry-related targets of the SDG 9. These include an overall composite index, the SDG 9 Industry Index described below, as well as a progress metric and an outlook assessment. They have the objective of identifying lagging cases and thus support economies in their successful implementation of ISID. The data and relevant analytical tools are available in the UNIDO Statistics Portal [20]. Detailed methodological notes about these tools are available at [28]. **==> picture [62 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

## **SDG 9 Industry Index** 

The SDG 9 Industry Index is a composite indicator that summarizes countries’ performance on the industry-related targets of SDG 9. It combines the information of the indicators for which UNIDO is the custodian agency and for which sufficient data are available (i.e. the two series of indicator 9.2.1, plus 9.2.2, 9.4.1, and 9.b.1).


Final chunk number 458, content : 
A short explanation of the Index’s calculation is presented below. A more complete description on the methodology can be found in [28; 134]. All indicators are first normalized through the min-max method to standardize the variables for further data aggregation, as they have different measurement units. The normalization is applied with three caveats: (i) the minimum and maximum values for normalizing each indicator are calculated over the entire sample of observations, which consists of all countries with available information over the period from 2000 to the latest year; (ii) to avoid the excessive influence of outliers in the transformation, the observed minimum and maximum values are capped at three standard deviations from the mean; (iii) an inverse normalization is applied to SDG indicator 9.4.1 ( _CO2 emission intensity of manufacturing_ ), so that all normalized indicators follow the same direction. SDG indicators on small manufacturing 

lack sufficient data coverage to be included in the SDG 9 Industry Index 

After these steps, normalized indicators have a range of [0, 1], with zero indicating the case with the lowest performance and one indicating the case with the best performance. All normalized indicators have the same direction: a higher value indicates a better performance. Finally, since the normalization is calculated using common parameters, the resulting indicators can be used for comparisons across countries and time. --- end of page.page_number=168 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 156_ 

The Index score is then calculated as the geometric mean of the five normalized indicators. Geometric aggregation allows to limit compensability among indicators. However, it has the disadvantage that a country with a value of zero in one normalized indicator (i.e. when it coincides with the minimum value observed in the sample) also has a composite Index equal to zero in that period. It is worth noting that all indicators are aggregated under an equal weighting scheme. This choice makes the Index transparent and facilitates interpretation [135]. Ranks are also calculated to facilitate country comparison. SDG 9 Industry Index is a summary measure of inclusive and sustainable industrial development as declared in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development 

As described in the methodology summary above, the construction of the Index requires available information for all indicators. The Index currently covers 138 countries for the period from 2000 to 2022. ## **Country/area classifications** 

The main purpose of the UNIDO country classification is defining a relatively homogeneous set of country groups that have common features in terms of their stage of industrial development, determined by objective criteria derived from official indicators of industrial performance. It adheres to the basic principles of statistical classifications, as defined in [136]. The country groups are revised annually with the objective of reflecting countries’ current economic situation, while the classification methodology remains stable. More information on the classification methodology can be found in [38]. UNIDO country 

is based on a combination of income groups and industrialization indicators 

The main country classification proposed by UNIDO divides countries/areas according to a combination of their income level and their stage of industrial development. It therefore relies on two parameters: (i) per capita income levels, sourced from the World Bank’s 2025 income groups [137]; and (ii) structural transformation metrics (MVA per capita in constant USD, historical maximum of the share of manufacturing employment in total employment, and exports of MHT products per capita), calculated from UNIDO databases. This classification system allocates countries/areas among five groups: 

- _High-income industrial economies_ : Countries/areas that have achieved a high national income through a development path that resulted in highly industrialized economies. - _High-income industrializing economies_ : Countries/areas with a high income level but with relatively low levels of industrialization. - _Medium-income industrial economies_ : Countries/areas classified as medium-income economies that have already achieved positive outcomes in terms of structural transformation indicators. Five UNIDO country groups: two groups of industrial economies and three groups of industrializing economies 

--- end of page.page_number=169 ---

_C Overview of methodological aspects 157_ 

- _Medium-income industrializing economies_ : Countries/areas classified as medium-income but that still remain at comparatively low levels of industrialization; these are some of the economies that could benefit the most from prioritizing industrial development in their policy strategies. - _Low-income economies_ : Countries/areas that remain at low income levels and also underperform in industrial development indicators; these economies would greatly gain from an accelerated structural change process that could help them escape the development trap. Emerging industrial economies includes the most dynamic low- and middle-income economies in terms of industrial performance 

This classification has the objective of summarizing large amounts of country-level data into relevant insights and common trends observed in countries facing similar development challenges. The list of economies according to these five groups is included in Annex E.4. A special economic group proposed by UNIDO is that of emerging industrial economies (EIEs). These are the most dynamic low- and middle-income economies in terms of their industrial performance. It includes economies that have continuously registered positive spells of growth in MVA. This group includes 12 economies in 2025: three middle-income industrial economies, six middle-income industrializing economies, and three low-income economies. The list is given in Annex Table E.5.1. Countries/areas are also classified according to geographical region. UNIDO follows the UN Standard Country or Area Codes for Statistical Use (M49) [138]. According to this standard, all world economies are assigned to one main regions, which are then further divided into subregions. These regional groupings are, inter alia, the main classification system used for SDG indicators. The complete classification is given in Annex E.3. **==> picture [136 x 60] intentionally omitted <==**

Geographical regions follow the official UN classification of countries and areas for statistical use: M49 Standard 

Finally, the report also considers the three country groups with specific development challenges, according to official UN lists. These are LDCs, LLDCs, and SIDS, presented in Annex E.5. --- end of page.page_number=170 ---

## **D UNIDO Statistics and the International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics** 

## **D.1 UNIDO Statistics** 

Following the recommendations of the United Nations Statistical Commission, UNIDO has the mandate to compile and disseminate international statistics on the manufacturing, mining, and utilities sectors. This involves the regular collection, screening, and validation of industrial data from official sources and presenting them according to harmonized definitions and classifications. UNIDO generates analytical indicators based on official data, which can be used to monitor a country’s prevailing performance and progress in terms of ISID. The statistics are disseminated through various databases available at the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3], as well as publications such as this _Yearbook_ . These products offer statistical information to a wide range of users, including national governments, international development partners, academic and research institutions, as well as the business and statistical communities. Priority is given to quality assurance of statistics, especially in terms of international comparability and alignment with UN recommended concepts and classifications. As a custodian agency of six industry-related indicators under SDG 9, UNIDO has been actively involved in the process of developing and monitoring the global indicator framework for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. UNIDO contributes to the _UN SDG Global Database_ [133], reports to the IAEG-SDGs, and collaborates with countries on improving data availability and quality for better tracking their progress towards the 2030 Agenda. The organization cooperates closely with other international agencies, namely the ILO on employment; the International Energy Agency (IEA) on CO 2 emissions; and the World Bank on access to finance, to produce data and compile the corresponding SDG indicators. Furthermore, UNIDO publishes the _SDG 9 Industry Index_ , benchmarking countries’ performance towards achieving the industry-related targets of SDG 9 [134]. achieving industry-related SDG targets by using the tools available at the UNIDO Statistics Portal [3]. These insights are summarized in a biennial UNIDO report, presenting progress achieved towards the industry-related SDG 9 targets [39]. Industrial statistics are essential for formulating industrial development strategies and policies, analysing structural change and monitoring economic growth. UNIDO shares its expertise in industrial statistics with national and regional statistical offices by providing technical assistance and trainings on a wide range of topics. By implementing customized programmes to target countries’ specific needs, UNIDO assists in strengthening the institutional capacity of NSOs and line ministries to collect industrial data, maintain business registers, set up short-term statistical indicators and information systems, carry out data analyses of industrial performance, and track progress on SDGs. UNIDO furthermore provides capacity development activities on the usage of empirical data for economic analyses, which are relevant for promoting industrial development through evidence-based policymaking. ## **D.2 The International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics** 

This _Yearbook_ presents a summary of the most recent data in industrial sectors. It outlines the current performance and latest developments, allowing the reader to analyse patterns of growth, business cycle fluctuations, and longer-term trends, including progress towards structural change, ISID and SDG 9. While the _Yearbook_ focuses on aggregate global trends observed in industrial sectors, it also highlights the main regional trends and sector-specific developments. More detailed information for specific regions and country groups are presented in Factsheets accompanying the _Yearbook_ . This publication relies on visualizations and short analytical texts to summarize the prevailing situation in global industry and to highlight key insights extracted from the data. It is essentially sourced from information that is available on UNIDO Statistics Portal [3]. Interested readers are invited to visit this resource to access the full datasets and related statistical products. All data presented in this _Yearbook_ were compiled bearing in mind the coherence of industrial statistics derived from various sources, the requirements of international comparability, and the standards of this work endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission. Concepts and definitions were drawn from international recommendations applicable to industrial statistics [4] and the classification of economic activities according to ISIC [5]. _D UNIDO Statistics and the International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics 160_ 

This is the thirty-first edition of the _International Yearbook of Industrial Statistics_ , published by UNIDO since 1995. For historical reference, this publication replaced two reports: the _Handbook of Industrial Statistics_ [140], which was published biennially by UNIDO until 1992, and the _United Nations Industrial Statistics Yearbook Volume I (General Industrial Statistics)_ [141], which was discontinued after its 1991 edition was published in 1993 by UNSD. These changes were introduced in line with the recommendations of the UN Statistical Commission at its 27[th] session. This four most recent editions of the _Yearbook_ feature several novelties compared to earlier editions. The current format represents an effort to modernize this long-standing publication, expanding its coverage to include all aspects of industrial statistics. It merges the contents of earlier editions of the _Yearbook_ (see [142] for the last edition under the previous format) and the biennial report _World Statistics on Mining and Utilities_ (see [143] for the last edition), at the same time expands its coverage to include the CIP Index, SDG 9 indicators, and other industrial performance indicators. ## **Concepts and definitions** 

## **C | E | F | G | H | I | L | M | S | U | W** 

## **C** 

**CO2 emission intensity** Indicator computed as the ratio between CO2 emissions from fuel combustion and the value added of associated economic activities. It can be computed for the entire economy (total CO2 emissions per unit of GDP) or for specific sectors, notably the manufacturing sector (CO2 emissions from manufacturing per unit of MVA). 25 

## **E** 

**Economies of scale** In economics, this term refers to the reduced cost per unit that arises from a higher production level. 5 

**Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply** This sector refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section D. It includes the provision of electric power, natural gas, steam, hot water, air-conditioning supply and the like through a permanent infrastructure of lines, mains and pipes. This section also includes the operation of electric and gas utilities, which generate, control and distribute electric power or gas. 4, 18, 186 

## **F** 

**Factoryless goods production (FGP)** Factoryless goods production represents a distinctive organizational model within the broader landscape of global manufacturing arrangements. A principal controls the production of a good by undertaking the entrepreneurial steps and providing the technical specifications required to produce the good, but outsources all or most of the material transformation process required to produce the output [151]. x, 120 

## **G** 

**Gross domestic product (GDP)** GDP basically derives from the concept of gross value added. GDP is the sum of gross value added of all resident producer units plus the part (possibly the total) of taxes on products that is not included in the valuation of output, less subsidies on products [152, p. 34]. x, 5 

## **H** 

**Human Development Index (HDI)** Long-standing indicator measuring human development, defined as the process of expanding people’s freedoms and opportunities and improving their well-being.


Final chunk number 549, content : 
The HDI is a composite index of three dimensions: 1) the ability to lead a long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth; 2) the ability to acquire knowledge, measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling; and 3) the ability to achieve a decent standard of living, measured by gross national income per capita. A higher HDI value indicates a higher human development level. This indicator is calculated and maintained by UNDP [16]. x, 7 

## **I** 

**Index of industrial production (IIP)** Indicator that describes changes in the volume of goods produced in industrial sectors over time. Its main purpose is to provide a measure of short-term changes in value added over a given reference period. However, since it is difficult to collect high-frequency data to accurately measure value added, gross output measures such as the value of production or turnover data are more commonly used. The IIP, being a volume index, is not influenced by price fluctuations [99, p. 11]. x, 18, 146 

--- end of page.page_number=198 ---

- **Industrial statistics** Field of statistics related to the characteristics and economic activities of all resident units in the reporting country that are primarily active in the following productive activities: 

      - a.


Final chunk number 550, content : 
Mining and quarrying (ISIC Rev. 4 section B); 

      - b.


Final chunk number 551, content : 
Manufacturing (ISIC Rev. 4 section C); 

      - c. Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply (ISIC Rev. 4 section D); 

      - d. Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (ISIC Rev. 4 section E). - Industrial statistics form part of the broader domain of structural and short-term business statistics [4, pp. 2 and 12]. 4, 5, 159, 160 

- **Industry** This term refers to the set of all production units engaged primarily in the same or similar kinds of productive activity [5, p. 9] The ISIC provides the international guidelines for cataloguing economic activity into specific industries, such as agriculture, mining, manufacturing or services. 4 

- **Industry value added (IVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of industrial sectors to GDP. x, 13 

- **Inter-agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators (IAEG-SDGs)** Working group tasked by the United Nations Statistical Commission to develop and implement the global indicator framework for the SDGs and the Targets of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It is composed of representatives from Member States from all regions, with custodian agencies participating as observers and experts. 23 

- **ISIC** The International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities, abbreviated as ISIC, is a standard classification of economic activities arranged so that entities can be classified according to the activity they carry out. Currently, the fourth revision of ISIC [5] is the most commonly used, and it is the reference used throughout this Yearbook. The hierarchically structured ISIC Rev. 4 classification contains sections, divisions, groups and classes. The ISIC classification is maintained by UNSD. x, 4, 121 

## **L** 

- **Large case unit (LCU)** A large case unit is a specialized unit within an NSO that focuses on ensuring the quality and consistency of data for large establishments, especially MNEs. x, 127 

- **Least developed country (LDC)** The LDC category was established by the United Nations (UN) General Assembly in 1971. The UN defines LDCs as countries that have low-income levels and face severe structural impediments to sustainable development. x 

## **M** 

- **Manufacturing** This industry refers to ISIC Rev. 4 section C.


Final chunk number 552, content : 
It includes activities related to the physical or chemical transformation of materials, substances or components into new products, although such a definition cannot be used as the single universal criterion for determining what constitutes manufacturing (see [5] for more details on activities included and not included in manufacturing). The materials, substances or components transformed are raw materials that are products of agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining or products of other manufacturing activities. Substantial alteration, renovation or reconstruction of goods is generally considered to be manufacturing. The output of a manufacturing process may be finished in the sense that it is ready for utilization or consumption, or it may be semi-finished in the sense that it is to become an input for further manufacturing. 4, 18, 93, 146, 186 

- **Manufacturing value added (MVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of manufacturing to GDP [153, p. 5]. xi, 6 

- **Mining and quarrying** This industry corresponds to ISIC Rev.


Final chunk number 553, content : 
4 section B. It includes activities related to the extraction of minerals that occur naturally as solids (coal and ores), liquids (petroleum) or gases 

--- end of page.page_number=199 ---

   - (natural gas). Supplementary activities aimed at preparing the crude materials for marketing are also included, if they are undertaken in conjunction with mining, for example, crushing, grinding, cleaning, drying, sorting, concentrating ores, liquefaction of natural gas and agglomeration of solid fuels. 4, 18, 93, 146, 186 

- **Mining and utilities value added (MUVA)** This is a national accounts aggregate measuring the exclusive and exhaustive contribution of mining and utilities sectors to GDP. xi, 89 

- **Multinational enterprise (MNE)** A multinational enterprise, sometimes also called multinational corporation (MNC), just multinational, or international corporation, is an enterprise producing goods or delivering services in more than one country. It has its management headquarters in one (or rarely more than one) country, the home country, while also operating in other countries, the host countries [154]. xi, 120 

## **S** 

- **Short-term statistics (STS)** Infra-annual production-related statistics collected to monitor the business cycle. They are suitable for the short-term evaluation of supply, demand and production factors [4, p. 3].


Final chunk number 554, content : 
Although available more frequently and in a timelier manner, they usually cover only some variables of interest and are published with a limited level of detail. 146 

- **Statistical confidentiality** Principle 6 of the _Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics_ [155] stresses that data collected by national statistical agencies are to be strictly confidential and used exclusively for statistical purposes. Many NSOs therefore implement national rules on statistical confidentiality. The two main reasons for declaring data to be of primary confidentiality are: 

   - a. too few units in a cell; 

   - b. dominance of one or two units in a cell. The limits of what constitutes ”too few” or ”dominance” vary between statistical domains. Statistical confidentiality is ensured through appropriate methods: 

- **Physical protection:** data is securely stored and not accessible to anyone without explicit authorization. - **Statistical disclosure control (SDC):** methods for reducing the risk that statistical units are identified when the statistical data is being published, including: 

   - **Tabular data protection:** for aggregate information on respondents presented in tables (using suppression, rounding, combinations and interval publication). - **Microdata protection:** for information on statistical units (using local suppression, sampling, recoding, top and bottom coding, rounding, rank swapping and microaggregation). xi, 89, 187 

- **Structural business statistics (SBS)** These are production-related statistics that are collected and compiled to determine the structure, activity, competitiveness and performance of enterprises at national, regional and international levels. They generally provide annual information with respect to a reference year [4, p. 3]. Although available only annually and published with some delay, they usually cover a large number of variables at a highly granular level. Other common abbreviations used by NSOs are ABS (annual business statistics/survey) or AIS (annual industrial survey). xi, 96, 149 

- **Sub-annual Manufacturing Trade Data** Manufacturing trade is a key component of global trade, accounting for the majority of traded goods and offering valuable, timely insights into a country’s productive structure and the competitiveness of its manufacturing sector. xi 

- **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development [17], adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, provides a shared blueprint for peace and prosperity 

--- end of page.page_number=200 ---

for people and the planet, now and into the future. At its core are the 17 SDGs, which are an urgent call for action by all countries in a global partnership. They recognize that ending poverty and other deprivations must go hand-in-hand with strategies that improve health and education, reduce inequality and spur economic growth—all while tackling climate change and working to preserve our oceans and forests. xi, 3, 154 **Goal 9** Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation. 3, 9, 13, 20, 29–31, 44, 54, 82, 130, 154, 155, 158, 159. - **System of environmental-economic accounting (SEEA)** An international statistical framework that organizes data to show the interrelationships between the economy and the environment, as well as the stocks and changes in stocks of environmental assets as they bring benefits to humanity. It provides a standardized approach with consistent definitions and classifications, similar to the system of national accounts (SNA), to measure environmental assets and their contributions to the economy [74]. xi, 114, 119 

- **System of national accounts (SNA)** A coherent, consistent and integrated set of macroeconomic accounts, balance sheets and tables based on a set of internationally agreed concepts, definitions, classifications and accounting rules [156]. xi, 119, 188 

## **U** 

**UNIDO industrial statistics databases** UNIDO Statistics currently maintains a variety of databases, as described below. These can be accessed at the UNIDO Statistics Portal. 158 The **Annual Manufacturing Trade Database** [40] contains aggregate data at the country, region and group level for variables related to the trade of manufactured goods. The database provides historical time series in current United States dollar (USD). The data are collected primarily from the United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD); other sources of official data may be used when appropriate. 61, 158. The **Competitive Industrial Performance (CIP) index** benchmarks the ability of countries to produce and export manufactured goods competitively. 158. The **Industrial Demand-Supply Balance Databases (IDSB)** [139] contain disaggregated data on the manufacturing sector, including a correspondence to international trade data. 158. The **IIP Database** [19] contains monthly, quarterly and annual data on the index of industrial production for the manufacturing as well as mining and utilities sectors. 146, 158. The **Industrial Statistics Databases (INDSTAT)** [35; 36] contain disaggregated data for selected variables on the manufacturing, mining and utilities sectors. 52, 158. The **Monthly Manufacturing Trade Database** [41] contains monthly data on manufacturing trade with special emphasis on higher-technology goods. 61, 158. The **National Accounts Database** [9] contains aggregate data at the country, region and group level for several national accounts indicators related to industrial economic activity. 158. The **SDG 9 Database** [20] contains the industry-related indicators of SDG 9. 158. ## **W** 

**Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities** This industry, corresponding to ISIC Rev.

4 section E, includes activities related to the management (including collection, treatment and disposal) of various forms of waste, such as solid or non-solid industrial or household waste, as well as contaminated sites. Activities of water supply are also grouped in this section, since they are often carried out in connection with, or by units also engaged in, the treatment of sewage. 4, 18, 186
